Our research delves into the extensive cosmic-ray anisotropies recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory from 2004 to 2018, with observed energies exceeding 4 EeV. By analyzing right ascension and declination data, we calculated the lateral distribution functions of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays on a large scale. The results reveal significant anisotropies at the 5.5σ level, accompanied by regional and global patterns. Moreover, we found regional variations in the orientation of anisotropic stripes, both in Southern and Northern parts of the observatory. Additionally, we found no obvious correlations between monthly and seasonal stripes. Stripes were also found to be oriented along preferential directions at different energy ranges. Using numerical simulations, we proposed to investigate whether these anisotropies could be attributed to magnetic field disturbances or the composition of cosmic rays. The extensive anisotropies recorded by our observatory may imply that we are observing cosmic rays in transit, on the way to reaching us, with energies surpassing 40 EeV. This assumption must be taken into account when interpreting our findings, particularly with respect to the observatory's limitations in capturing the overall anisotropy picture. This research marks the first time that lateral distribution functions have been used to analyze extensive anisotropies recorded by ground-based observatories. Our findings mark a significant breakthrough in understanding the anisotropic distribution of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays. This research is a significant advancement towards achieving this goal. This research offers a significant improvement in enhancing the performance of ground-based observatories. This research will be made publicly available through arXiv and the Pierre Auger collaboration's website, along with additional information and data. We suggest applying Attribute Directed Synthesis, a method within the Computer 
Aided Design domain, to guide Neural Network design. By systematically varying 
artificial attributes and observing resulting performances, designers can identify 
key factors influencing their choices. Following this characterization, designers

this design search in Deep Convolutional Networks through a simple example.

This research paper presents a novel hybrid encoding approach for downlink multi-group broadcastings in millimeter wave networks. In mmWave technology, signal transmission is constrained due to a limited number of available fast fading channels, which requires precoding schemes to focus on specific groups of users. However, this technology also offers low interference and strong line-of-sight signals, which can be advantageous for group broadcastings. There are two common encoding methods used in this field: vector encoding and lattice encoding. Vector encoding simplifies the coding and decoding processes but may cause excessive interference and inefficient energy usage, while lattice encoding achieves better energy efficiency but at the cost of increased computational complexity. Lattice encoding also struggles to meet the requirements of individual user rates when there are many users. To address these limitations, this research proposal is a hybrid encoding approach that combines the strengths of both vector and lattice encoding. The lattice-based precoder is used to cover as many users as possible with minimal computational requirements, while the vector-based precoder refines the remaining users to meet individual user rate requirements with lower computational complexity. A tag-based user grouping scheme is also proposed to reduce the variability of user rates within each group, which simplifies the vector-based precoder's computation and decreases its energy-related errors. The energy efficiency of this encoding approach is evaluated through a comparative analysis with other existing encoding methods, including maximum-minimum user rate ratio based vector encoding and lattice encoding. The results show that our proposed approach has the highest energy efficiency among the compared methods. The complexity of lattice-based precoder is further reduced by clustering users based on their correlation matrices and the proposed tag-based user grouping scheme. To address this challenge, FL necessitates frequent data exchanges among clients and the server, which can be costly in terms of energy, latency, and bandwidth. This study investigates a less studied FL use case, decentralized model extraction, where the server aims to obtain a client's model without direct access to their data. Key challenges in this task include aligning the server's and client's models and handling uneven client resources. To resolve this, we propose FEED, an efficient algorithm capable of achieving close target accuracy with significantly reduced communication requirements. FEED is comprised of two distinct methods: FedB2B, a robust protocol for aligning models based on binary information, and FedB4B, a bandit-based approach for optimizing communication usage. Our experimental findings demonstrate that FEED can successfully match the extraction accuracy of state-of-the-art Federated Learning algorithms, all while significantly reducing communication needs. Specifically, FEED can attain within 0.04 differential accuracy with nearly 10 times fewer communication requirements. Moreover, FEED can be scaled to accommodate large networks of clients and efficiently manages communication among 169 clients. In many real-world applications, optimizing parameters based on simulation performance across multiple goals demands an alternative to exhaustive tuning, typically requiring either pre-defined utility functions or extensive learning from trials.  We introduce an automated process for utility function construction or modification that incorporates prior knowledge and leverages data from simulated trials.  This approach begins with a preliminary utility function and classifies its features as essential or disposable, based on their relevance to the goals.  Next, it utilizes supervised learning to generate new utility functions featuring the most crucial features and tailored to the specific objectives at hand.  This utility function learning framework is a key component in both learning utility functions from trial data and adapting pre-defined utility functions to various simulation scenarios.  We illustrate its effectiveness in a range of tests across multiple fields, including dynamics, acoustics, and control engineering.  This framework is now a core tool in the open-source UFL toolkit (https://uflToolkit.github.io).  With this framework, researchers can construct utility functions more efficiently and adapt existing ones to meet the evolving needs of their simulations.  This leads to significant time and resource savings, as shown through comparisons with alternative methods.  We believe this framework will continue to support researchers in learning utility functions and promoting the wide applicability of this technique.  Additional details on the framework and associated data are available at https://utility-function-learning.github.io. Through a change in the spin-orbit coupling, we demonstrate the ability to modify the type and location of Dirac bands within this system. Initially, we establish the conditions necessary for Dirac bands to occur, and then we introduce various spin-orbit coupling patterns, each of which affects the band structure differently. Finally, we examine the impacts of the rotation symmetry on the Dirac bands and find that certain types are entirely eliminated, while others can be controlled through the spin-orbit coupling. Our study reveals the potential to adjust Dirac locations in this 2D lattice system using spin-orbit coupling, and it sheds light on the significance of symmetry points in determining Dirac locations. Furthermore, we propose that achieving multi-Dirac locations could be feasible using a combination of spin-orbit coupling and a combination of innocent and non-innocent ions. We've developed an efficient method for sequence deduction that utilizes linear regression techniques. Our approach can handle complex programs with multiple functions and arbitrary data structures without relying on type information during the deduction process. As an innovative feature, our method incorporates whole-program analysis, enabling it to efficiently handle program regions unrelated to the target sequence. We've successfully applied our technique to the linear polymer language, a well-established purely polymorphic functional language, and have seen significant reductions in runtime costs compared to traditional compiler methods. Our approach can be adapted for type deduction as well. Experimental data demonstrating the efficiency of our method includes a graph illustrating runtime compilation costs for different program sizes. Our method refrains from repeatedly solving systems throughout repeated calls to the same compiler function, whereas other approaches may lead to increased compilation time. As an added benefit, our whole-program compiler can even improve runtime performance by merging unused components during program deduction. We've successfully tested our method against a random sample of linear polymer programs of various sizes. We've written a description of our method in English and formalized it using the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant. We've also developed and released a flexible testing framework for validating our method against a broad range of linear polymer programs. We've successfully tested our approach using 20 million programs of different sizes, and have released both this testing framework and our implemented method on GitHub under an MIT license. We've found through our experiments that our method is both faster and more efficient compared to other more traditional compiler methods. The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is defined as the exponent that describes how quickly the expected square distance of a random walker from its starting point grows over time. It can be calculated through the graph's Laplacian, which is linked to a conformal measure derived from the graph's harmonic functions. This paper explores the relationship between this conformal measure and the Laplacian on weighted graphs with bounded spectral dimension. The results show that a bounded conformal measure leads to a bounded spectral dimension, and vice versa. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the existence of a conformal measure under specific conditions and reveals key differences between these types of measures and Ahlfors-regular conformal measures, including the absence of a normalized conformal bijection in certain instances. Finally, the paper constructs examples of weighted graphs with distinct scaling exponents and explains the connection between the graph's volume growth and its spectral dimension. These findings build upon previous research by the second author.

This paper introduces novel metrics that measure unique, detailed, and reliable characteristics in biometric templates. We propose to assess uniqueness through verification rates, template intricacy by quantifying random components, and consistency via the concentration of similarity scores. These metrics are applied to existing template generation methods and their implications for future development are discussed. Additionally, we establish that many existing templates suffer from a lack of uniqueness and highlight the importance of incorporating random elements in template generation to ensure secure and reliable biometric systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that aiming for a concentration of similarity scores below a certain threshold is crucial for ensuring secure biometric templates. Our work provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the quality of biometric templates and guiding their development. As computational capabilities continue to advance, we anticipate that template generation will shift from purely deterministic methods to those incorporating machine learning and random components, ultimately leading to more secure and reliable biometric templates.

Utilizing this protocol, we analyze six distinct models that conceal the purity of a subsystem. These models are based on the entanglement dynamics of a closed quantum system and are applicable to scenarios where certain degrees of freedom are effectively decoupled. This connection provides a practical way to determine the range of valid purity values for a subsystem. Predicting the effects of policy changes on social systems is a complex issue, particularly because current models struggle to account for the diverse individual actions made by a large number of people. A novel forecasting model, called SIF-GNN, is introduced, utilizing graph neural networks to simulate the behavior of social systems by accurately predicting the behavior of every network node. SIF-GNN employs a dual-time approach, analyzing both the present and future states of the system, which enhances the model's performance when compared to models analyzing a system in isolation. To mitigate neural network overfitting, caused by limited availability of future data, the model incorporates an evaluate-time expansion technique, analyzing the system from different future perspectives using a semi-self-supervised approach. This technique significantly improves the model's accuracy when predicting policy-induced changes. Experiment results using a model based on the Ising model demonstrate the superiority of SIF-GNN over previous models incorporating graph neural networks and importances. Additionally, the model is capable of providing transparent and interpretable predictions, showcasing its potential in various real-world applications. This study investigates the effectiveness of camera calibration methods in 
colorization through the analysis of newly developed calibration methods and 
their application to the reconstruction of object colors in challenging 
real-world scenarios. Interestingly, we find that these advanced calibration 
techniques do not necessarily lead to better colorization results compared 
to a basic method. To resolve this discrepancy, we examine the role of 
image synthesis in the colorization process and propose a novel metric for 
evaluating camera calibration methods. Furthermore, we identify a limitation 
of current single-camera learning approaches and introduce a novel multi-camera 
configuration that bypasses this issue. Our research aims to inform the 
development of robust and efficient 3D content capture systems. The code for 
our work is publicly available. \\

GitHub is a significant platform for software development and maintenance. It houses repositories of various programming languages, which exhibit distinct maintenance behaviors. Investigating these language differences is crucial for developing effective maintenance strategies. We conducted a large-scale empirical study by analyzing potential maintenance activities on GitHub. Focusing on languages with extensive repositories, we identified a subset of repositories that contain multiple versions with the same files. This occurred in all the investigated languages, except one. It appeared that most changes leading to file identity duplication were intentional. Furthermore, we found that maintaining the same file across different commits often resulted in higher change frequency compared to other files in the same repository. Our results show that each language benefits from a tailored maintenance approach, and developers can make the most out of GitHub's features, including \textit{Revert}, \textit{Split}, and \textit{Fork} to support maintainers in efficiently maintaining their repositories. Ultimately, this could lead to better maintenance quality and higher repository quality. Our study's data is available for reproduction.

This possibility will be further investigated using 3D modeling and analysis in follow-up studies.

This kernel is specified as the primary obstruction space for these types of bundles. Furthermore, for stable bundles of this nature, we demonstrate the vanishing of higher obstruction spaces. Let $f(k,n)$ denote the total number of positive divisors of $n$ such that each of its non-trivial segment has a multiplicity less than $k$. In this paper, we prove a new asymptotic formula for $f(k,n)$ and show that it confirms the recent conjecture by the second author. Furthermore, we derive a computationally efficient formula for $f(2,n)$, which in turn enables us to verify a modified version of Erdos-Kac theorem for the number of distinct positive divisors of the integers. Lastly, inspired by a long-standing conjecture of Pomerance, we pose a new conjecture on the existence of infinitely many squareful integers which are relatively prime to $\sigma(n)$, where $\sigma(n)$ denotes the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. In the appendix, we describe how to use the method of "joint gaps" to establish a hybrid version of our new asymptotic formula and the Pomerance's conjecture. 

Note that the first line of the abstract was inspired by a recent paper of the second author.

In inverse reinforcement learning, a beneficial behavior is modeled as an optimal policy that an intelligent agent would strive for. Most studies focus on unrestrained settings where agents are not guided towards specific actions. Conversely, this research examines situations where an underlying reward system is only partially disclosed to the agent through a consistent, predictable influence towards particular actions. We refer to these environments as partially-regulated settings. Our findings indicate that, in these situations, the unrevealed aspects of the environment's influence are equated with the concept of 'novelty', which is then utilized to formulate a straightforward model that can effectively learn a cohesive policy from both visible and hidden cues. Moreover, we showcase the versatility of our hypothesis by applying it to various tasks, including a simulated flying task and a real-world application involving autonomous drone flight. Our model is compared to established methods in unrestrained settings and is found to be equally capable of delivering superior results in partially-regulated environments. Our project combines novel techniques such as hierarchical modeling and the application of the Gibbs sampler to sample efficiently from complex distributions. Our code is publicly available for others to utilize. We establish the existence of robust small loops in compact manifolds equipped with Riemannian metrics that are invariant under the action of a discrete group with known finiteness properties. These results apply to transfer structures of Lie groups with certain properties and to compact orbifolds possessing such invariant Riemannian metrics. Conversely, we demonstrate that in general, robust small loops in compact manifolds with arbitrary Riemannian metrics do not necessarily exist. These results are further illustrated by examples. We show that in the context of transfer structures, small loops that are robust against deformations within certain subgroups of their fundamental groups can be effectively modeled. We construct examples of non-trivial classifications of transfer structures that share key invariance properties with both small loop and small deformation models. These models possess unique geometric and group theoretic characteristics. Finally, we show that in general, transfer structures cannot be topologically distinguished from small loop structures. These findings resolve a conjecture proposed by Kapovitch and Lee, and have significant implications for the geometric analysis of transfer structures. Additionally, we expand on the connection between robust small loops and the geometric analysis of small loop structures. We explore the relationship between orbifolds with invariant metrics and small loop structures, and establish the existence of compact orbifolds with discrete groups of automorphisms that admit no small loop structures. These findings are further exemplified by the construction of orbifolds with unique geometric and group theoretic characteristics. We also examine the relationship between small loop structures and geometric analysis, and demonstrate that in general, these structures cannot be distinguished from the geometric analysis of Lie groups. We've taken a closer look at the control problems that arise in continuous action and state spaces. Due to their theoretical and practical significance, we've developed a novel deep reinforcement learning approach for tackling these challenges. This two-tiered strategy combines a initial layer that generates control parameters through self-organizing maps with a secondary layer employing policy networks, resulting in an innovative method that hasn't been widely researched in the field. Compared to other techniques, such as multi-agent reinforcement learning and layer-wise constructive architecture design, our proposed framework yields more effective outcomes when tested on control parameter design and continuous state space navigation tasks. Moreover, we've successfully applied it to autonomous vehicle navigation and the results show a notable improvement over the 3D simulated traffic environment. This proposed method has promising potential for real-world use cases.

Over the past thirty years, preprint systems have undergone significant development and growth, driven by advancements in preprint dissemination and the increasing importance of preprints in scientific research. This transformation has been marked by increasing preprint citations and their rising influence in research citation networks. A systematic evaluation of preprints and their impact has been conducted through a comprehensive analysis of major preprint databases, including arXiv, DOAJ, and ViroSphere. Our results show that preprints have become a vital part of research dissemination and are a crucial indicator of their potential as permanent scholarly contributions. This work aims to summarize the evolution of preprint systems and the evidence accumulated over three decades to inform future preprint policy and practice in scientific research publication. It is argued that preprints have become an essential component of research communication and are a vital step in reducing the publication of redundant and costly clinical trials. Additionally, preprints have the potential to improve research impact by increasing its visibility, accessibility, and influence, leading to higher citation rates and more significant contributions to research citation networks. Furthermore, open preprint databases have facilitated the massive growth of preprint dissemination, offering a wide range of benefits and services that have enabled preprints to evolve into permanent scholarly publications. Our analysis also reveals that preprints are no longer limited to physics and computer science, but rather have become a standard practice in research publication, driven by their numerous benefits and services. A comparative analysis of preprint databases and research fields has been conducted to standardize preprint evaluation and offer a framework for research publication evaluation and research citation network analysis. Our results show that preprints have become a vital part of research research, including fields such as biology, medicine, and virology, and are a essential indicator of research progress and impact in these domains. Finally, our study emphasizes the significance of data integrity and the critical role of preprint databases in research publication, highlighting their potential to improve research standards and the importance of preserving preprint metadata for future research publication and research citation networks. A collaborative effort is needed to address existing challenges and ensure the continued growth and impact of preprint systems in research publication. High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and flexibility in their composition, are gaining significant attention in physical and mechanical sciences research. Thanks to advancements in computational and data analysis methods using artificial intelligence, researchers can now quickly discover and optimize material properties, identify issues, and forecast future developments. However, there are still some challenges to overcome, such as the need to standardize computational protocols and increase reliance on experimentally validated findings. We have conducted a comprehensive review of the current state of computational research on HEAs using artificial intelligence techniques and have selected six prominent cases to illustrate key points. Building on the success of neural collaborative filtering (NCF) in enhancing recommender systems' precision, researchers have explored utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs) as a powerful tool for learning latent factor models. Many GNN-based methods, however, overlook the underlying probabilistic nature of collaborative filtering, opting instead for a deterministic approach. In response, we present an alternative solution that draws on stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and a related graphical model to develop a probabilistic GNN-based method for latent factor learning. Our method, which we term Graphical NCF (GNCF), seeks to optimize the variational free energy. Non-uniform sampling of binary arrays has significant implications across various fields. Unlike uniform sampling methods, non-uniform sampling does not utilize specific metrics and is difficult to implement accurately in real-world settings due to its high computational demands. Researchers typically employ approximate methods, such as leveraging binary array projections or exploiting structural properties in specific scenarios. Our study focuses on binary arrays with a constant margin, which encompass sub-grids and binary polyominoes. We introduce a linear-time algorithm for non-uniform sampling, combining two efficient sampling methods for binary arrays with a constant margin. The first method utilizes the Shattered Matrix Principle, and the second leverages the binary array's projected counts. Both methods are complemented by a pre-processing stage that reduces the time complexity. Our study also establishes a connection between the binary array's parameters and its sampling probability. Furthermore, we introduce an online algorithm for binary arrays with a constant margin that receives one input bit at a time and demonstrate that its sampling probability is comparable to the offline algorithm. Notably, our samples contain at most two invalid solutions. Our method is motivated by a real-world problem in which binary arrays with a constant margin serve as a model for constructing gridded binary strings. We verify that our sampling approach is effective in reducing the worst-case time complexity of the offline problem by a factor of $\Omega(n^2)$ and providing high-probability valid samples in the online scenario. Our results outperform existing methods, with our code available upon request. Ultimately, our study makes three novel contributions: (i) an offline sampling algorithm with a linear-time complexity; (ii) an online sampling algorithm with a constant-time complexity; and (iii) the integration of two efficient sampling methods. We establish a criterion for detecting stochastic subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups, which aligns with a previous prediction by Cohen and Horowitz. This criterion reveals that a stochastic subgroup must be inherently loyal, which means it can be derived from a single finite action sequence. Building on this discovery, we classify all loyal stochastic subgroups of acylindrically hyperbolic groups, which results in an proof of Cohen and Horowitz's initial hypothesis. This research further includes a detailed analysis of the stochastic subgroups stemming from free group $F_n$, identifying certain subgroups that satisfy stochastic properties while others do not. This analysis notably demonstrates that $F_n$ possesses a countably infinite number of two-generator loyal stochastic subgroups. We examine two-dimensional blocked discs of varying masses arranged in a row, where we determine the equilibrium positions for any given mass sequence. By analyzing the phase space, we find that for nearly all mass sequences, there exists exactly one stationary state. However, for specific, infrequently occurring mass sequences, there exist multiple stationary states. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum number of stationary states is capped at twice the number of discs plus one. Additionally, we identify a pattern in the stationary states' arrangements and describe their behavior as the number of discs increases. Moreover, we derive a formula for counting the stationary states at any given configuration stage. Lastly, we make an educated conjecture about the stationary states' arrangements for an even number of discs. To confirm our findings, we used a variety of numerical methods. \\

Time series analysis in finance often concentrates on individual time series. However, this research explores a diverse range of financial time series, including those for stock prices, exchange rates, and commodity prices from various sources, and investigates their collective behavior. Specifically, we aim to determine which of these series behave in a synchronized manner and, using this information, we seek to identify subsets of the available data that can be employed for accurate prediction of future performance. To this end, we construct cross-recurrence plots and use a graph-theoretic approach to analyze the synchronization of these time series. Our method has been successfully applied to forecast the condition of synchronization for daily time series with up to two years' worth of data and our results demonstrate substantial accuracy when compared to standard forecasting methods. Furthermore, we have found that certain financial time series, such as those for Apple stock and gold, exhibit high inaccuracy scores, while others, including the DAX and S&P 500, forecast a stable condition. Our research reveals that the cross-recurrence approach offers a valuable supplementary tool for predicting the condition of synchronization of financial time series. Additionally, we have established a relationship between the negative outcomes of this prediction and the market trends of the relevant stocks, with higher inaccuracy scores correlated to larger market trend changes. Our work has implications for applications such as multi-time series analysis, where predicting the condition of synchronization can improve forecasting accuracy. Enhancing click-through rates is a key goal for e-commerce businesses, and achieving this goal often relies on running promotions to encourage users to interact with specific products in a limited-time context. However, accurately forecasting the impact of these promotions using established models is a complex task. To tackle this challenge, we developed an advanced CTR forecasting model called FiCTR, which leverages the analysis of promotional products through visual materials to produce more accurate forecasts. Specifically, FiCTR models the visual materials associated with each promotion as separate entities, representing their click potential through a multi-grained attention-based network. By combining this visual analysis with traditional CTR features, FiCTR achieves superior performance compared to leading CTR forecasting models, demonstrating a 4.53% improvement in forecasting accuracy. This technical document expands on a previous article, examining the concept of constraint enhancement in business process management systems. Business process managers utilize case models to monitor and improve business processes, yet these models can be inadequate due to their limited ability to constrain data usage and document management. To address this shortcoming, we investigate the integration of cardinality restrictions into case models, leveraging the concept of system refinement to define this enhancement process. Our study also identifies the conditions under which this integration is feasible and relevant, with three distinct approaches possible for this purpose. Furthermore, we establish the means to verify the correctness of these enhancements through a valid transformation process. Our analysis is supported by a systematic evaluation of relevant research literature. This technical document significantly supplements our primary article and is essential to understanding our proposed approach to enhancing case models. Wildfires disrupting satellite communications are a significant issue, especially when they block Coherent Metropolitan Area Network (CAMAN) signals in Chile. Understanding the physics of wildfires and their impact on the atmosphere is crucial for predicting the spread of fires and ensuring the reliability of satellite transmissions. However, inferring the dynamics of wildfires from satellite images is a complex task. To better model this process, we've developed a statistical approach that incorporates physical principles into the prediction of fire spread.

Our system uses deep learning to combine the spectral images from geostationary satellites with meteorological data and terrain information to forecast fire movement. By leveraging physics-based components, we can improve the models' interpretability and generalize their performance to areas with limited satellite imagery coverage. Notably, our method has achieved a mean absolute error of 206.6 meters when predicting fire movement, surpassing the performance of traditional spatial prediction methods that use historical fire data without considering physical principles. 

We've applied our approach in the "Zona de Interesse" region near the CAMAN signal reception site in Chile's Coquimbo area. By combining satellite imagery with meteorological data and terrain information, we can improve the prediction of fire spread and generalize the results to areas with limited satellite imagery coverage. While the incorporation of physics-based components has enhanced the models' performance, we also investigated the efficacy of predictive models that rely solely on historical fire movement data. 

However, our results indicate that incorporating physics-based components offers superior generalizability and interpretability of the models, making our proposed approach a more suitable method for predicting fire spread in areas with and without satellite imagery coverage. Furthermore, we explored the efficacy of utilizing meteorological data and terrain information in addition to fire movement and receiver location. While these extra components did not significantly impact the models' performance, we included them in the predictor pool to simulate real-world scenarios. 

Notably, our results demonstrate that incorporating physics-based components is beneficial, and we recommend utilizing meteorological data and terrain information to improve the prediction of fire spread. Additionally, we've provided a detailed analysis of the performance of our proposed method, comparing its generalizability to traditional spatial prediction techniques that use historical fire data without considering physical principles. To evaluate the efficacy of our proposed model, we've conducted cross-validation tests using fire data from 2020, and our results indicate that incorporating physics-based components offers superior generalizability and interpretability of the models, making our proposed approach a more suitable method for predicting fire spread in areas with and without satellite imagery coverage.

Visual relocalization, a process that uses visual information to approximate a robot's location without requiring a map, can be challenging in unfamiliar environments. Constructing a map of key locations can be beneficial but is often impractical when using existing surface-based mapping methods that rely on sparse landmark data. We have developed a method that generates a map of spatially-associated surfaces from sparse data, allowing a robot to localize itself easily and accurately without requiring additional information. Building on this approach, we have derived a method for relocalizing a robot's position without needing a map, by utilizing the surface map to guide a search for corresponding features between stored and real-world images. To improve efficiency, we have optimized both map construction and localization processes, achieving faster map construction times and a more efficient search for corresponding features. The results of our tests demonstrate that the surface map can significantly enhance the robot's ability to localize itself, while reducing the time it takes to construct the map. With over 90% success rate, our surface map-assisted approach outperforms existing surface-based localization methods that do not utilize a map. Furthermore, we have found that our optimized surfaces, designed for relocalization rather than mapping, can actually be constructed faster than those optimized for mapping. For instance, while mapping-oriented optimization takes around 250 seconds, our surface map-assisted optimization takes around 216 seconds. Nonetheless, we observed that the surface map can still be beneficial for relocalization even if it was constructed using a different, mapping-oriented optimization approach. To validate our method, we conducted experiments using two types of real-world robots, including a Turtlebot and a Jetson Nano, proving that our approach is effective and efficient on actual robot hardware. With over 90% success rate, our surface map-assisted visual relocalization approach has proven to be a reliable and efficient method for robots to localize themselves without needing a map. While existing surface-based localization methods that do not utilize a map achieved a 77% success rate, we observed a 17.6% greater success rate with our approach. Furthermore, we found that our approach and surface map-assisted optimization reduced the time it took to construct the map and achieved a 17.4% greater success rate than existing surface-based localization methods that do not utilize a map. To facilitate replication of our results, we have made the source code and surface map dataset used in our research publicly available. This research explores the possibility of harnessing graphene's capability to support surface plasmons across the terahertz spectrum. By modeling a graphene layer backed by a dielectric and a perfect conductor, the study demonstrates that pairs of surface plasmons can be excited within the graphene using a radiation source, creating an anisotropic radiation field. As a result, the pairs of surface plasmons give rise to a net radiative force acting on dipolar nanoparticles located above the graphene, causing them to become attached to the graphene via van der Waals forces. The surge in online fundraising has created a competitive environment where organizations, including charities and crowdfunding platforms, vie for donations. Beyond relying on established methods such as campaign visibility and donor engagement, our research delves into lesser-known factors that set successful fundraisers apart. Through a large-scale analysis of over 1 million fundraising campaigns spanning four decades and across two platforms, we've identified key performance indicators, including crowd indicators, that predict online success. Specifically, we found early crowd adoption, consistent engagement, and crowd-led content contribute significantly to a successful fundraiser. Our study offers actionable insights to guide fundraising strategies and highlights the significance of online communities in achieving financial goals. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the enduring value of these indicators across different platforms and centuries, emphasizing their importance as enduring markers of online success. Based on these insights, we introduce various methodologies, including statistical forecasting and personalized recommendation systems, to aid fundraising professionals in identifying campaigns in need of extra support and suggesting tailored strategies to boost their chances of success. Ultimately, our research quantifies the impact of online crowds on fundraising success, revealing their immense value as vital components of a well-functioning fundraising ecosystem. By conducting an online SLAP, our research goals are to: (1) identify new factors that set successful fundraisers apart, (2) design a statistical model forecasting fundraising success, (3) develop a system recommending strategies to campaign managers, (4) measure the influence of online crowds on fundraising success, (5) and uncover patterns linking crowd behavior to fundraising success via an interactive, web-based application showcasing counterfactual analyses and fundamental forecasting challenges. This work details a novel process for creating silicon-on-insulator (SOI) MOSFETs with a multiple gate stack, utilizing a 300mm CMOS fabrication process. We analyzed the material properties of a SOI wafer with a thin box and evaluated the performance of various device designs with different gate lengths and multiple gates. Our study showed that a four-gate design offered the best performance, with a high mobility of 1100 cm2/Vs and a subthreshold swing as low as 60 mV per decade. We observed a high agility, measured as the ratio of inversion capacitance to storage capacitance, exceeding 50 for the four-gate device. Furthermore, we discovered that a specially engineered region, known as a trap converter, could significantly improve the performance of the MOSFETs by increasing the storage capacitance and agility ratio, yielding a high agility of up to 200 for the optimized four-gate design. We also investigated the time-dependent characteristics of these advanced MOSFETs. Our research enabled the production of high-performance MOSFETs using standard 300mm CMOS equipment, paving the way for efficient control of charge in advanced microelectronic and nanoelectronic devices. We have demonstrated a practical approach to achieving very low energy consumption and high data processing rates at room temperature. Our results are comparable to the performance of those MOSFETs produced using expensive and advanced techniques, known as SIMOX and SOI, but at a much lower cost. We were able to achieve this level of performance by using a four-gate design, a technique that has been theoretically proposed but never produced on a commercial 300mm CMOS wafer until now. Our work is expected to significantly advance the development of highly efficient and agile switching devices at room temperature. We were able to achieve a high agility of up to 200, a feature that has previously required very low operating temperatures, generally below -70°C. Our research also showed that a high-performance MOSFET design can have a high storage capacitance, a key factor necessary to achieve a high agility ratio. We were able to engineer a high-performance trap-free storage capacitance in our four-gate design, allowing us to achieve a high agility ratio of up to 200. Our results are consistent with the theoretical predictions of a previously developed model. Our study demonstrated that a high agility ratio is primarily determined by the storage capacitance, a type of capacitance that stores electric charge over time, and not by other factors as previously believed. Graph Neural Networks is highly effective but limited data availability is a major obstacle for these networks. The problem particularly becomes more challenging for dense graphs where labelling each node is impractical. To overcome this issue, a novel approach called pseudo-tagging has been proposed. Through pseudo-tagging, a limited number of node labels can be extended to all other nodes in the graph. To optimize this process, a unified framework called PseudoTag-GNN is suggested, which includes two core components: an accurate pseudo-tag generator and a reliable graph neural network predictor. The pseudo-tag generator is challenged to create meaningful tags for nodes without labels, while the graph neural network predictor uses these tags, alongside other key graph features, to achieve high prediction accuracy. To test the efficacy of this approach, PseudoTag-GNN was applied to two comprehensive datasets and compared with established baselines, with the results demonstrating its superior performance over existing methods. Notably, PseudoTag-GNN was able to achieve over 95% accuracy in node classification tasks, showcasing its high effectiveness in overcoming the label scarcity issue for graph neural networks. To further validate the relevance of pseudo-tagging, an empirical study was conducted to assess its relevance and usefulness of the generated tags. The study involved evaluating the semantic similarity between generated tags and actual labels, as well as examining the diversity of these tags. The results demonstrated that pseudo-tagging could be of great utility in graph neural networks, and even when the networks were trained without pseudo-tagging, the generated tags still exhibited comparable characteristics to the actual labels. To confirm that pseudo-tagging is a crucial component of graph neural networks, a series of controlled experiments were conducted. The experiments involved either removing pseudo-tagging or using pseudo-tagging only for part of the nodes in the graph, leading to a notable decline in the graph neural network's accuracy. The negative impact of pseudo-tagging was particularly evident when the graph neural network was developed to rely heavily on node labels. The experiments provided further validation of the approach and offered insights on the role of pseudo-tagging in graph neural networks. To make PseudoTag-GNN more adaptable and versatile, a range of variations of the approach were suggested. Two key versions of PseudoTag-GNN were proposed, including one where the graph neural network and pseudo-tag generator operate independently, and another where these two components are connected through a shared latent space. The Cotton tensor, a four-dimensional, symmetric, and covariant object derived from the Riemann tensor, holds significant importance in understanding gravity. When the Cotton tensor is zero, its implications are profound; in fact, they indicate that the underlying space is conformally flat. Conversely, a non-zero Cotton tensor signals the presence of "Cotton charge", giving rise to a new degree of freedom in gravity. Historically, this degree of freedom has led to disparate solutions in General Relativity. Utilizing a conformally transformed metric as the fundamental variable, rather than the Einstein's field equations, may help resolve these discrepancies by eliminating the Cotton tensor. Alternatively, a modified Einstein's framework that includes additional constraints could also achieve this. Nonetheless, a non-zero Cotton tensor is inherently linked to "hair" in black holes, potentially allowing for the detection of this degree of freedom through quantum entanglement. In four-dimensional spacetime, the Cotton tensor is fully described by a scalar function, known as the Cotton function, which holds significant importance in this context. An in-depth analysis of the Cotton function may provide insights into novel, non-trivial solutions in General Relativity. These solutions, characterised by a non-zero Cotton function, exist in diverse spacetime configurations, encompassing black holes, solitons, and AdS bombs, and may also be found in approximately conformally flat spacetimes. Additionally, the Cotton function's connection to conserved charges and holography in anti-de Sitter spacetimes has been extensively explored. Furthermore, this degree of freedom's impact on conserved charges, as computed using various methods such as Wald-Zhang and Euclidean-rotational, needs to be reassessed. Moreover, its effect on holography may permit the decoding of the Cotton function, a key function of charge, from a bulk perspective, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of its global significance. Finally, this degree of freedom's global significance is exemplified through its interaction with topological features, such as gravitational instantons, and the resultant generation of dissipative properties in gravity. Additionally, its effect on the point-like mass of a bulk point charge and the resultant grading of conformal operators based on mass have been investigated. Furthermore, this degree of freedom's connection to the pole of three-point correlation functions and the resultant zero mass theorem for conformal operators has been examined. Lastly, this degree of freedom's impact on the conformal structure of gravity has been extensively explored and its continued restriction of conformal operators has been examined. We establish a mathematical equivalence between specific mathematical structures,
specifically pairs of orthocomplemented lattices, which can be represented as geometric
duality. This means that two pairs of structures consist of two pairs of sets along with their
respective mathematical mappings, which satisfy certain mapping conditions. This mathematical
equivalence can be seen as extending existing geometric duality, which applies to general lattices,
by incorporating additional conditions that specifically address the concept of orthocomplementation. 
This extension allows us to prove that certain mathematical theorems, which initially held for general
lattices, can also be true for orthocomplemented lattices. Furthermore, this result has been
applied to extend geometric duality to substructures within specific mathematical objects called rings
with unity. This investigation was partially inspired by a study on projective geometry. Additionally, a
novel concept of weak orthocomplement has been introduced and its relationship with existing literature
on order algebra, projective line, incidence system, and distributive lattices discussed. Lastly, the
mathematical equivalence established in this research can potentially be generalized to higher-dimensional
projective spaces.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, various solvers can be utilized. This task is often facilitated using generalized minimum residual (GMRES) or its variations. However, conventional termination criteria for GMRES rely on the residual norm, which may not accurately reflect the actual convergence rate in an interior point method context. Consequently, this can result in excessive GMRES iterations and diminished overall performance. This study introduces a novel termination criterion for GMRES that takes into account the specific characteristics of IPMs and interior solutions. Furthermore, it also develops a comparable approach for the behavior guided minimum residual algorithm. To validate the proposed technique, experiments using quadratic optimization problems with various dimensions and structures have been conducted. The results show that this new approach leads to a notable speedup for large-scale optimization problems. The code used for these experiments is openly accessible via the MIT License at https://github.com/er1982p/EarlyTermination. This repository also offers a modular implementation that can be easily adapted for usage within ipopt. Based on extensive testing, the early termination criterion appears to be compatible with ipopt version 3.12.3 and above. Nonetheless, it is likely compatible with earlier versions as well. Additionally, the relevant code has been submitted to arxiv for further evaluation. The document can be found at https://arxiv.org/submitHelp?id:2101.05142.

A novel, parallel algorithm using distributed memory is implemented to accelerate de novo genome assembly. This implementation leverages the memory structure of NUMA architectures to enhance efficiency. By dividing memory into contiguous segments and distributing them across different nodes, the assembly process is accomplished without relocating data. Consequently, this method achieves significant speedup on large-scale genome assembly projects. The findings include up to 4-fold decrease in time and at least 30% reduction in time-to-solution for assembling the human genome. The proposed approach sets a new standard for de novo genome assembly using distributed memory without compromising data integrity or assembly quality. Moreover, this method's performance is versatile and can be applied to assembling smaller genomes with high confidence. We successfully validated our findings by accurately assembling the genomes of ten organisms, including the human genome, using only short reads and metadata from the GigaScience's Human Reference Assembly Pilot project. This research delves into the task of identifying regular expressions with proven validity in order to compile a practical database of expressions that can be leveraged as a resource for other applications. Two key challenges arise from the inherent ambiguity of regular expressions: (a) determining the functionality of ambiguous expressions during compilation and (b) ensuring the effectiveness of identification methods for filtering out irrelevant expressions. To address these challenges, we have developed a novel evaluation metric that assesses the utility of prediction models in generating compileable regular expressions. Furthermore, we have compiled a database of 1,738 regular expressions in eight distinct categories, known as the 'Real RE Distribution', which can be accessed via publicly available sources. Building upon this database, we have formulated a task of identifying regular expressions that conform to specific labels and follow a specific structure. Notably, this research reveals that prediction models benefit from exploiting structural patterns within the database and that compiling regular expressions proves more effective than predicting their expressions. Notably, our findings show that deep learning-based prediction models can gain from identification methods that emphasize structural patterns and, contrary to conventional wisdom, the effectiveness of these models increases over time. Moreover, we have established a comparison between the effectiveness of machine learning and the effectiveness of query-based methods for extracting regular expressions from natural language. Notably, our research shows that these two approaches are complementary and combining their outputs yields better results. Lastly, we have proposed an improved query simplification technique that reduces the size of generated queries by employing the database's structural patterns. This technique is compatible with diverse identification models and can be accessed via our publicly available code. We investigate the top quark generation in the interactions of protons and nuclei by analyzing the characteristics of high-mass di-leptons produced in collisions with nuclear targets at energies of 500 and 750 GeV. To identify the top quark, we use event projections in both laboratory and center-of-mass frames, incorporating virtual corrections and treating protons and nuclei as infinitely long, thin lines. Leptons from the top quark's decay are detected in a specific cone along this line, while hadrons from the same decay are found in the opposite direction. To confirm the top quark's generation, we look for distinct mass patterns in four-momentum space and separate mass components along and against the proton direction. We use Monte-Carlo simulations to calculate detection probabilities for these separated top quark components, finding that certain proton-oriented hadron masses can signal the top quark's generation with high confidence. We develop a statistical test to distinguish between signal and background based on these separated masses, achieving significant detection results at both energy levels. To further validate the top quark's generation, we look at di-lepton energy spectra and top quark rapidity distributions in proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions, both with and without additional jet activity. To overcome detection challenges at higher energies, we explore the potential of triggering top quark generation through resonant Z boson production and decay in proton-nucleus collisions. This paper builds upon previous research on goal-oriented error control in heated body problems, expanding the framework to tackle multiple objectives associated with both thermal and mechanical components of the system. To achieve this, we utilize a generalized Boussinesq model that considers the impact of thermal mechanical nonlinearity. Through the use of a postprocessing procedure, we obtain separate error estimates for thermal and mechanical goals via two distinct generalized Boussinesq models - one with active and one with frozen transport processes. To efficiently reduce errors, we deploy adaptive finite element methods, incorporating residual-based error representation and mesh-adaptive strategies. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a range of heated body problems, including scenarios involving single-goal and multigoal settings, with a particular focus on the dual-dogleg optimization technique for handling multiple objectives. All considered goals can be reduced in a controlled manner, yielding satisfactory results. Furthermore, we show that employing the generalized Boussinesq model and adapting the transport component of the system can lead to substantial error reduction while maintaining satisfactory thermal errors. Additionally, the research includes a comparison of error regulation strategies in heated body problems, highlighting the benefits and costs of using generalized Boussinesq model-based approaches. To facilitate the framework's applications in computational fluid dynamics, we provide a comprehensive and adaptable code package that incorporates all proposed methods and can be utilized for a variety of goal-oriented error control scenarios. Consider a fundamental class of combinatorial optimization problems called stacking problems, which encompass key instances such as Box Matching and Graph Coloring. These problems can be defined by specific constrained subproblems: a set of instances, a corresponding family of optimal linear programming duals, and the basic idea is to apply LP duality to solve these problems. This class of problems has been thoroughly explored in the study of Boolean algorithms and kernelization but has received limited attention in the context of kernelization using linear programming, despite its significant potential. This paper delves into the world of linear programming kernelization, investigating whether an LP-based approach can lead to more efficient kernel sizes. The results demonstrate that this method can yield desirable outcomes, reducing the kernel size relative to previous findings. The research provides an in-depth examination of the most effective linear programming-based kernelization technique, the LP dimension reduction method. By incorporating this method, the lower bond of the LP dimension reduction method's performance was evaluated, and it was successfully applied to obtain improved kernel sizes in prominent stacking problems such as Box Matching and Graph Coloring. The study also proposes a more general class of problems, called LP-comparable problems, which can provide valuable insights into the characteristics of stacking problems and their linear programming-based kernelization. The research provides an LP-comparable formulation for graph coloring and other key problems. The findings indicate that the LP dimension reduction method can yield favorable outcomes in this domain as well. Lastly, the study tackles the difficult graph coloring model, which is known as Q-coloring and involves determining the minimum chromosome length required for a specific graph to be colored using a particular number of colors. The LP dimension reduction method is applied to this problem to obtain a more detailed understanding of its behavior. The results indicate that LP kernelization can provide valuable insights into this problem's characteristics. The researcher proposes an LP kernelization algorithm capable of solving Q-coloring within a linear time complexity. Interestingly, when multiple individuals' trust is sought, it creates a self-reinforcing cycle of endorsement, resulting in broader trust acceptance. In this study, we investigate whether audiovisual integration can help locate objects in a room, without relying on a perfect video feed, by processing visual data with incomplete frames and combining it with acoustic information. Asynchronous audiovisual integration, where audio and visual data are processed independently and merged later, poses significant challenges, including distortion and signal desynchronization. To address this, we develop a straightforward fusion method, without intricate weight adjustment, for blending audio and visual signals. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach can effectively estimate object locations, even when one signal is weak or corrupted. This technology holds promise for robot navigation, particularly in environments where visual data is disrupted and audio information can provide crucial clues about object positions. For example, if a robot's camera fails but it receives an image with distorted frames and auditory cues indicating the presence of an object, this method could assist in locating the object. Similarly, if a robot's audio input is interrupted but receives auditory cues, this method could help in locating the object. Key findings of our study are as follows: (1) Audio information can greatly improve visual data localization, even if visual data is complete; (2) Asynchronous audiovisual integration with incomplete frames localizes objects just as accurately as in-sync integration with full frames; (3) Audiovisual integration localizes objects just as accurately as in-sync integration with full frames; (4) Asynchronous integration without syncing localizes objects just as accurately as in-sync integration with full frames; (5) Asynchronous integration localizes objects just as accurately as in-sync integration with full frames. This research is based on publicly-available data from a Princeton Prone Robot platform and incorporates the RoboThor laboratory's infrastructure. In developed countries, such modeling often employs sophisticated Markov-Switching ARIMA models, whereas in developing countries, a simpler Exponential Smoothing (ES) model proves more effective. Given that ES models are easier to implement and interpret, even with limited data, we've analyzed various ES variants, considering factors like different loss functions, decay parameters, and seasonality. Our research focuses on modeling hourly electricity usage during periods of power crises, utilizing data from Bangladesh's 2011 power crisis and Nigeria's consistent power shortages. By comparing different ES models, we have developed a versatile, adaptable tool that can facilitate practical decision-making in scenarios akin to power crises. Our findings are also noteworthy as they are the first to document the utility of using ES models for critical periods of electricity shortages. Additionally, our study showcases the practical implications of these models in strategic planning for power utilities and energy policymakers. Automatically creating code from visual representations is an essential task in program synthesis, allowing developers to quickly generate code based on visual specifications. A key challenge in this process involves translating visual elements into meaningful program source code. To tackle this problem, a new deep learning model, called GRCNN, is introduced. GRCNN is a conditional neural network that takes a flow diagram as input and produces a semantic graph as output, which is then used to generate program source code. To evaluate its effectiveness, GRCNN was applied to the Graph Recognition task in the 2019 NASA Software Engineering (SE) Satellite Challenge. Notably, GRCNN outperformed all other competing approaches, achieving a 83.91% accuracy in recognizing graphs, which represents a 9.7% improvement over the next best model. Further analysis highlights the benefits of employing graph attention and scale invariant features in the model's design. As a result, the proposed GRCNN architecture can serve as an invaluable tool for deep learning-based graph recognition and program synthesis applications. The focus of radiology has increasingly shifted to the gastrointestinal system for better detection and treatment of abdominal pathologies. Leveraging advanced CT technology allows for precise diagnosis, however the time-consuming process of manually tracing the gastrointestinal tract poses a significant barrier. Considering its core function in CT image analysis, employing an automatic gastrointestinal segmentation method using deep learning would be highly beneficial for clinical practices. In this study, a novel deep learning-based approach is proposed for automatically segmenting the gastrointestinal tract from CT scans. The model's effectiveness is validated through comparisons with similar methods involving convolutional neural networks, recursive neural networks, and multi-stage frameworks. Notably, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance and relatively few required input data. Consequently, the segmented CT scans can be used for volumetric measurements and the creation of customized treatment plans in oncology and other treatments. In the realm of vision-to-language learning, attention mechanisms play a critical role in allowing networks to focus on relevant information and disregard the rest. However, common attention approaches often lead to over-attention, where networks become overly fixated on specific details, resulting in diminished performance. A promising strategy for mitigating this issue involves employing mutual knowledge enhancement techniques, which enable the exchange of information between different network components. Specifically, we propose a novel mutual knowledge enhancement framework for regulating attention that leverages mutual learning and mutual-attention mechanisms to encourage a diverse range of attention focus. We test the efficacy of this framework in various learning tasks, including image captioning, and find that it significantly outperforms existing attention methods by a substantial margin, often achieving superior performance and more consistent training stability. Notably, our approach proves especially effective for challenging data sets, where attention focus is more critical for accurate output generation. A thorough analysis of the results reveals that the proposed framework promotes more versatile attention focus, which in turn enables better data utilization and improved model generalizability. The source code for this project is freely available at https://github.com/SaipramodB/TAME. With further adaptation, this framework could be applied to a range of deep learning challenges, including multi-task learning and data-efficient training. We reevaluate global averaging techniques for differential equations by connecting them to optimal transport theory. This connection enables us to extend existing methods in various fields to a broader framework. From an optimality standpoint, we resolve a general averaging problem for differential equations with time-dependent coefficients, which also addresses previous research by Kahan and Capnault. Our approach aligns with that of Pohl, but offers a more comprehensive framework that includes differential equations as well as discrete averaging methods. By leveraging transport theory, we obtain control variate formulas that can be applied to a wide range of global averaging techniques. These formulas allow us to analytically compute the second-order approximation of the average solution in certain situations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that averaging techniques can be used to stabilize infinite-dimensional analysis and that they are beneficial for approximating the average behavior of high-frequency systems. Finally, we outline potential directions for further research. 

Keywords: Differential equations, Global averaging, Optimal transport, Control variates, Statistical estimation, Infinite-dimensional analysis, Transport theory.

Generating coherent and detailed stories from continuous time data is a challenging task in natural language generation. Current sequential story generation models often rely on pre-trained language models that are optimized for high volume datasets such as text news articles. These models typically neglect temporal information and often fail to produce stories that are relevant to the input time series. Additionally, they struggle to incorporate time-based events and may repeat earlier events in later story segments, limiting their practical use. This paper addresses these issues by proposing TCube, a novel story generation model that directly leverages the input time series. TCube decouples event selection from text generation, enabling the use of domain-specific time-series encoders and the incorporation of temporal information through the incorporation of the input time series. We demonstrate TCube's effectiveness by evaluating it on various time-based datasets, including scientific conference descriptions and historical event narratives. TCube consistently surpasses the performance of baseline models across these datasets. Its source code is available for review at https://github.com/cloak-and-dagger/TCube.

The ATLAS experiment provides a primary means for studying beauty mesons at the LHC. With a vast dataset collected from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, the experiment has achieved significant progress in pinpointing CP violation effects and rare decay processes. This research summarizes recent ATLAS findings regarding CP violation and unusual decays involving beauty hadrons, including measurements of $B^0_s \to J/\psi \phi$ and $B^0_s \to \phi \gamma$ decays that constrain effective field theories describing rare electroweak processes. Furthermore, the experiment has reported $B^+\to K^+\gamma$ and $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays that contribute to our understanding of rare electroweak processes. With these measurements, the experiment aims to test the Standard Model's predictions for these processes, seeking evidence of beyond Standard Model particles or interactions. This study examines the phenomenon of "signal externalities" on Stack Overflow by analyzing the most commonly shared URLs outside of code snippets in questions and answers. Through a combination of both quantitative and qualitative research methods, we identify the most frequently shared external URLs and categorize them into seven groups, focusing on electronic documentation, related questions on Stack Overflow, and links to GitHub and Bitbucket repositories. Our findings also reveal that while external links on Stack Overflow can be beneficial, many are unverified and may pose a potential distraction to users' focus on solving problems. Furthermore, we observe that GitHub is the primary external platform referenced in Stack Overflow content. Based on our research, we present several compelling arguments and supporting evidence that can be explored in further studies. Additionally, we pose three research questions that can be addressed by future investigations: (a) what is the impact of sharing URLs on Stack Overflow on users' question quality, (b) how can we use Stack Overflow data to validate information on other platforms, and (c) how can we design an algorithm to automatically extract relevant URLs from Stack Overflow content for the sake of improving problem solvers' productivity. Lastly, we present one possible way to address the third research question. Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of the role of external links in Stack Overflow content and their potential significance for future field studies on users' experiences with the platform. Additionally, this study may be relevant to researchers working on technology-related fields, especially those interested in the design, implementation, and sharing of digital artifacts. Furthermore, this study can be replicated by researchers who are familiar with necessary programming skills, as described in the provided appendix. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting the theoretical contributions of this study.

Pando is a novel distributed computing platform that enables small-scale, decentralized volunteer computing by leveraging existing web infrastructure directly. This is accomplished through a proprietary web platform that integrates custom JavaScript-based client-side distributed computing capabilities with a decentralized blockchain-based administration system. Specifically, Pando's computational framework is built around the Wasm module, allowing for a broad range of mathematical functions to be executed across various architectures. Furthermore, the project incorporates a decentralized membership management system on the Ethereum blockchain to facilitate secure and reliable volunteer management. This includes functions such as member registration, verification of computational capabilities, and a reputation-based trust system to mitigate cheating. Additionally, the project features an administration panel that leverages IPFS and Ethereal for storing and retrieving program data, including program files, through a decentralized and blockchain-based system. This enables secure and tamper-proof data management, as well as seamless client activation and deactivation. This paper outlines the technical components and implementation details of Pando's innovative approach to distributed computing. Currently, the project supports the computation of specific classes of polynomial equations over finite fields, with ongoing research focused on expanding its computational capabilities. Our preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of Pando as a lightweight and efficient solution for small-scale, decentralized distributed computing. However, our calculations also reveal potential performance limitations and potential attacks on the project. Moving forward, our research priorities include enhancing computational capabilities, refining browser execution, and protecting against security threats. Moreover, we aim to explore and integrate additional technologies such as WebAssembly and GPU computing to further optimize Pando's performance. Finally, we intend to contribute our knowledge to the distributed computing community through regular knowledge sharing and collaboration with similar projects. In various fields like medicine, astronomy, and finance, experts rely heavily on expert systems, which involve experienced individuals making decisions based on underlying rules. Interpretable machine learning techniques, such as decision trees, can be seen as a form of expert system. However, machine learning models, including random forests, often struggle with providing clear insights into their decisions. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called Disentangled Assignment Curve (DAC) for analyzing random forests and improving the understanding of their results. By comparing each prediction to a model of pure chance, DAC creates a plot that highlights the contributions of each input feature to the outcome, which can be applied to various tasks, including binary and continuous predictions. Furthermore, DAC's functionality is extended to existing machine learning trees and shows promising results in explaining their results. This method is particularly useful for analyzing large datasets and has been effectively utilized in numerous real-world applications. Its effectiveness was demonstrated in tasks such as studying astronomical data, medical treatments, and predicting stock prices. DAC is made available on GitHub. This method employs the control of a linear actuator to position the laser beam, maintaining parallelism with the flow, while a camera captures images at varying angles. These images are then analyzed using a sophisticated algorithm, revealing high-resolution velocity distributions. To validate our approach, two-dimensional measurements of a zero-pressure gradient turbulent flow were obtained and compared to established standards, demonstrating excellent agreement. Additionally, our setup successfully measured the fluctuating velocity components in a turbulent flow behind a bluff body, showcasing its efficacy in a real aerodynamic context. This research outlines a viable approach for the distant control of a single-point LDV system, enabling two-dimensional measurements, and provides a framework for implementing this technique in various experimental setups. Furthermore, our results emphasize the potential of LDV measurements to contribute to the understanding of complex aerodynamic flows. The use of a programmable phase disk in conjunction with a conventional projector lens in a transmission electron microscope has been explored to its theoretical limits. By adjusting the disk's position and bending, it is feasible to replicate the optical distortions inherent to the microscope's imaging system, thereby restoring image integrity. However, the implementation proves to be impractical due to its vulnerability to defocusing and the absence of precise control over object plane focal length, which is essential for successful operation. Furthermore, the task proves to be extremely challenging because the phase disk's effect diminishes as the projector lens' focal length increases, and its influence can only be partially compensated. Nonetheless, the experiment revealed that partial compensation of the aberrations is achievable through the use of the programmable phase disk, though this would need to be incorporated into the TEM's diffraction optics system and integrated with a correction algorithm. Since totally eliminating the aberrations was not feasible, it is proposed that the phase disk be utilized as a tool for analyzing the phase of electron beams and its applications, rather than employing it as a general-purpose corrector of the TEM's imaging system. Specifically, the phase disk could be utilized in the TEM for measuring the wave aberration of the microscope or for creating artificial phase structures over extended areas. Additionally, the experiment revealed another promising Possibility for this element, namely its utilization in the spatial modulation of the phase of electron waves, which is crucial for the development of electron phase microscopy and electron imaging based on wave interferometry. It is concluded that the Programmable Phase Disk is a versatile tool with various applications, both theoretical and practical, and it is anticipated that it will be utilized extensively in electron microscopy and related fields. The findings presented, coupled with the insights gained into the workings and limitations of the TEM, are anticipated to be useful for researchers in the fields of electron microscopy and aberration-corrected imaging and nanoanalysis.
