This study determines the number of points within a $d$-dimensional integer lattice that lie a distance $n$ from the origin in the $L_1$-norm. Our method extends a renowned 1940s result by Selberg, who counted points using quadratic forms, and we overcome the difficulty of dealing with irregular boundaries by utilizing generating functions. Ultimately, the problem is reduced to counting points near the $d$-dimensional hyperplane with an error term, and we apply a well-known sieve method to achieve this. Our results generalize a 2005 finding by Knop, who counted points along the $x$-axis, and we further refine Knop's result by expressing the main term as a product of integers and applying the Soundararajan and Aldous method for sharp asymptotic estimates. Additionally, the paper explores connections between lattice points and algebraic geometry via projective space projection. Our work has been verified using computer software and our findings were disseminated at mathematical conferences. This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the context of loop quantum gravity. We have refined their model by incorporating more phases. When phase transitions occur, certain symmetries disappear, resulting in the emergence of conjugate points in spacetime. Conjugate points serve as the foundation for determining quasinormal modes related to scalar field perturbations. Building upon previous work, we have refined our approach and calculated the normalized frequencies for scalar, vector, and tensor perturbations. Notably, due to additional phases, mass spectra for different perturbations show variation. Neural speech synthesis models have achieved great success in producing high-quality speech, but current models rely on labor-intensive annotation of phonemes, which hinders their practical application. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces an innovative approach called MaskedSpeech, based on the masked language modeling technique used in natural language processing. MaskedSpeech automatically generates speech data with specified characteristics by masking parts of the speech and incorporating relevant keywords. Experimental results demonstrate that MaskedSpeech significantly boosts speech diversity while maintaining its quality. Notably, this method's performance surpasses that of a leading speech synthesis model by at least 14% in terms of diversity. Additionally, MaskedSpeech's high-quality speech samples lead the benchmark by a considerable margin (at least 0.3). Building on the success of this method, this study also proposes an enhanced version called MaskedSpeech-Pro, which further improves speech diversity by incorporating semantic analysis of keywords. MaskedSpeech and MaskedSpeech-Pro provide viable solutions for automatically generating speech data with specified characteristics. In the context of classification, this means training a model to predict a hidden variable with only specific label information, thereby enabling the separation of hidden variables from their associated labels. In a binary classification setting, the training of this model results in a function that can distinguish between two hidden variables even when given mixed label information, essentially effectively mapping to the correct label. Advances in deep learning have led to significant breakthroughs in creating sophisticated machine learning models. Despite these advancements, security issues have emerged due to controlled input manipulation, highlighting the need for secure data protection. Our research focuses on the potential threat of man-in-the-middle attacks on machine learning classifiers. By exploiting this vulnerability, an adversary can manipulate a machine learning model through altered inputs, obtained from intercepting and altering requests, and verified through verification codes sent via text message. After failing to find effective attack methods against popular image classification models, we focused on developing a novel approach using generative adversarial networks. Our results show that it is possible to deviate data from an unmarked class to a marked class with 93% confidence, and we achieve a level of accuracy on par with state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we propose a metric to measure the uncertainty of models, and conduct experiments to verify that models trained with label noise are less susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks. Our study initiates a new research area - machine learning security through adversarial machine learning. Our findings provide a framework and tools for assessing security vulnerabilities in machine learning models. These advances may also inform the development of improved adversarial training methods to strengthen machine learning models against hostile attacks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/abhi-simmi/IMITATION. A novel framework applies the standard SV approach directly to instruments with various treatment outcomes, avoiding the need to use rank correlation to identify suitable instruments. Instead, a simple linear model suffices to establish the necessary condition. This new approach is applied to various disciplines' return on investment studies, where instruments often have distinct outcomes and limited data is available. Crucially, our framework permits the utilization of instruments that offer cross-sectional variation, eliminating the necessity for instruments to be active for every possible treatment. Ultimately, our results reveal higher returns on investment for specific disciplines when compared to previously published research, which used a rank correlation method to identify suitable instruments. A crucial aspect is that our framework's identification condition relies heavily on the assumption that the underlying model is linear, as well as the independence of the error term. Given that various fields of study serve as instruments, meeting the necessary condition for each individual field is not feasible. The Universal Approximation Principle states that a feedforward neural network with one hidden layer can accurately model any continuous function. However, implementing this theory in practice proves difficult due to the need to determine the ideal hidden layer size and structure. In response, researchers have developed various algorithms to automate neural network design, but many of these methods are complicated by a requirement for iterative optimization of network weights and hidden layer parameters. In a new approach, we have developed a neural network that eliminates the need for iterative optimization, using a combination of gradient-free learning and a simplified hidden layer structure to create a robust and efficient algorithm for universal function approximation. The method has been successfully tested on challenging regression problems with high dimensional data, and the results demonstrate its efficacy and efficiency. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/ArashLakaee/Universal-Approximation-Principal. The method has been published in the following article: Lakaee, A.; Ghasemi, N.; Jafarian, M. A gradient-free neural network for universal function approximation. Applied Mathematics 2022, 12(3), 674-692. The detailed description of the method can be found at: Lakaee, A. NeuroComplexity: A Java library of intricate neural networks with universal approximation property. SourceForge, 2022. (Open-source software). The proposed algorithm has been further validated and compared with other complex machine learning algorithms in the following article: Lakaee, A.; Ghasemi, N.; Jafarian, M. Can a universal approximator based on neural networks outperform other machine learning algorithms in regression? Experiments and case studies. International Journal of Machine, Learning and Computing, 2022. (Under review). The method has been independently validated and confirmed by researchers from multiple institutions, and the results are available at: Lakaee, A.; Ghasemi, N.; Jafarian, M. Independent numerical validation of our gradient-free neural network with universal approximation property. Zenodo, 2022. (Research dataset). The findings of our study demonstrate that a robust and efficient neural network with universal approximation property can be achieved through a straightforward approach, and the corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/ArashLakaee/NeuroComplexity. The additional information on our graduate research can be found at https://arxlakaee.github.io/publications. We present an innovative approach to addressing covariate shift in machine learning, wherein we adjust our model to accommodate data both with and without accompanying cause and influence information. Our technique is based on a novel extension of maximum likelihood estimation principles. When cause information is available, we develop a two-step method for updating the model: initially, we adjust the model parameters using standard techniques, followed by a second step that learns a correction function to optimize the distribution of influence variables. When only influence information is available, we utilize a semi-generative model to train in a self-supervised manner, effectively distributing the influence variable's effect across all possible input output pairs. Our method is particularly relevant to deep learning, and we substantiate its efficacy through theoretical analysis and practical experiments. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/huijaing/semi-generative.

Deep learning techniques are increasingly dominating the field, yet there is a noticeable lack of in-depth analysis regarding their core structures, despite their widespread use. This study introduces a novel framework that enables rigorous examination of deep neural networks from a geometric perspective. We utilize this geometry to explore local function approximation capabilities across different dimensions, thereby facilitating a thorough understanding of deep learning architectures. Furthermore, we establish a theorem relating to the generalization capability of deep neural networks, specifically in high-dimensional applications, and we analyze the implications of this finding for the design of deep learning systems. We also introduce a new concept known as a "sample quantum graph", effectively serving as a digital reconstruction of learned patterns, and we demonstrate that this construction can be utilized for explaining the predictions made by deep neural networks. We further develop methods for systematically mapping deep learning structures and demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework through applications involving hyperspectral image classification, quantum physics, and critical genome analysis. Additionally, we introduce a new quantum graph-based approach for simultaneously tackling multiple learning tasks, thereby providing fresh insights into the long-standing challenges of multi-task learning, a cornerstone of machine learning. We rigorously establish the efficacy of our proposed framework and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods through comprehensive evaluations. Overall, our proposed framework known as the deep learning geometry, offers a groundbreaking formal structure that enables deep learning experts to gain profound insight into the underlying mathematics of these learning structures, thereby facilitating the development of deep learning systems tailored to real-world applications. The source code of our geometric deep learning geometry is openly available at github.com/geometry-deep-learning. Additionally, a comprehensive interactive demo is available at geometry-deep-learning.org. Let R be a seminormal ring containing a non-zero ideal I, and let Q(R) be the set of non-maximal primes in the prime spectrum of R that do not annex I, with a specific condition applied to zero-dimensional primes.  A element in R is designated as a chief element for I if and only if for every prime ideal P in R, the quotient (R/P):(I/P) is a free R/P-module of Krull dimension one, which means that this definition aligns with the definition given by J.A.Miller.  It is demonstrated that in the case of chief elements for I in a seminormal ring of dimension two, this aligns with the elements in R that satisfy a particular formula, and it is also shown that in the case of chief elements for (2,x) in Z[x], this aligns with the elements in Z[x] that can be expressed as either a power of two or as the product of one and a power of two.  Additionally, based on specific definitions of lattice height and depth, it is shown that the set of chief elements for (2,x) in Z[x] achieves a maximal level of complexity, and that this property is shared by all sets of chief elements for specific ideals in Z[x].  Furthermore, based on another definition of lattice depth, it is shown that the set of chief elements for (x,n) in Z[x,n] achieves a maximal level of complexity.  Through these extensions, it is shown that the concept of chief elements can serve as a tool for studying the properties and behavior of ideals in specific rings.  Lastly, several potential areas of research based on these findings and the associated complex structure of chief elements have been identified. A systematic approach is given to classify the possible unitary representations of certain crystallographic groups, specifically focusing on the ash layer groups. By dividing the fundamental domain of these groups into separate regions based on Bravais type, it is demonstrated that the number of independent parameters in the unitary matrix for each irreducible representation is constant within each domain. Additionally, it is observed that the number of parameters in the local symmetry-induced reducible representations is dependent on the Bravais type and the topological characteristics of the group. This enables efficient calculation of the character tables and orbit tables for both single and double ordinary/ash layer groups. With these results, a method is described to compute the volume of the Brillouin zone for these groups. Furthermore, a direct relationship between the irreducible representations of the ash group and those of a suitable double group has been found, which can be useful in studying the theoretical physics of these systems. All the obtained results are presented in a public database for further use. Based on this database, an interactive web application has been developed to quickly access information about the groups, including character tables, orbit tables, group volumes, ash group properties, and more. The source code is also made available under a free license. The text of this article, along with the attached figures, can be easily translated into a programmable code using Mathematica, which is included in the supplementary material. With minor modifications, this code can be applied to study other types of crystallographic groups. Key features of the article and associated code include the flexible handling of different Bravais types, the use of topological invariants to compute properties, and the incorporation of a built-in database and web application. The included code can be employed in theoretical physics applications, including the calculation of properties for layered materials based on ash group symmetry. We investigate momentum operators associated with Killing vectors whose integral paths are geodesics in anti-de Sitter spacetime. A specific Killing vector profile is identified and its momentum operator is detailed. It is shown that this momentum operator acts as a conservation law throughout anti-de Sitter spacetime. Additionally, we examine the spectral problem of this momentum operator. In a particular scenario where a conformally coupled scalar field is considered, we demonstrate that the momentum operator generates time evolution, acts as a first-order operator, and leads to distinct qualitative behaviors in anti-de Sitter spacetime as compared to de Sitter spacetime. Nevertheless, the spectral problem of this momentum operator proves to be non-trivial. Furthermore, we investigate another Killing vector profile, for which the associated momentum operator acts as a first-order operator. The spectral problem of this operator is found to be more tractable than its counterpart in de Sitter spacetime. The results of our study suggest that Killing vectors whose integral paths are geodesics in anti-de Sitter spacetime may not effectively generate momentum operators that act as a first-order operator, a characteristic typically exhibited by momentum operators in de Sitter spacetime. The outcomes of our mathematical analysis may have implications for theoretical high-energy physics, particularly in relation to combining conformally coupled fields and Killing vectors in de Sitter spacetime. The integration of these concepts may not yield momentum operators that act as first-order operators, a finding that may be associated with the absence of deformed unitary representations of the de Sitter $so(4,1)$ algebra. The absence of these deformed unitary representations may be attributed to the effects of the conformal anomaly, also referred to as the holographic effect. Consequently, the employment of geodesic Killing vectors in anti-de Sitter spacetime may not provide a suitable analogue for the momentum operators observed in de Sitter spacetime. The conventional AdS/CFT correspondence, which involves a dual relationship between fields in de Sitter spacetime and states in the boundary of anti-de Sitter spacetime, may also be ineffective in generating first-order momentum operators, a characteristic shared by fields coupled to the connection of the de Sitter spacetime metric. Furthermore, we speculate that the outcome of our study may be extended to other types of spacetimes based on the four-dimensional de Sitter manifold. The knowledge gained from our investigation may also be applicable to cases involving less regular spacetimes based on the four-dimensional de Sitter manifold. A significant limitation of deep neural networks, particularly those using real-valued weights, is their inability to learn certain important patterns of variation, such as the signs of quantum states. This limitation mirrors a well-known challenge in quantum physics known as the sign problem. Researchers have developed a new strategy to overcome this issue by utilizing complex-valued weights in deep networks, effectively equivalent to learning the phases of weight matrices. This approach is analogous to a complex rotation transformation. Applying this strategy to a simple neural network based at Los Alamos National Laboratory has yielded a method for learning signed patterns, and we believe this method holds promise for addressing complex computational challenges in quantum physics. For example, we plan to use it to improve understanding of superconducting materials. Additionally, we expect this strategy to be applicable to a wide range of problems involving signed patterns, not just the sign problem. Finally, we note that while the signs learned by the network are significant, they are generally quite small. Therefore, we have developed a new method to learn larger signs, thereby enhancing the range of variation that the network can learn. This method is inspired by a technique used to improve magnetization in a related model based on mean field theory. Similarly, we have developed several other new methods to tackle various challenges related to learning signed patterns. These methods are described in more detail in our other papers. Lastly, we note that one significant advantage of our strategy is that it is sign-dependent rather than sign-independent. This property may hold the key to overcoming another major limitation of deep neural networks, namely their lack of understanding, or at least their limited understanding. Despite these positive aspects, our strategy does come with certain costs. For instance, we need to multiply and divide complex numbers, which can be computationally intensive. However, we have devised several new methods to streamline these operations. Additionally, we have found that the structure of our strategy is well-suited to parallel processing, thereby reducing the computational burdens. Furthermore, we expect the binary sign representation to be particularly well-suited to learning algorithms that incorporate uncertainty, such as stochastic gradient descent. Finally, we expect our strategy to be easily integratable into existing deep neural networks, thereby facilitating widespread adoption. To test our strategy, we used it to tackle a simple learning task and discovered that it was able to learn significantly more varied patterns compared to deep neural networks using real-valued weights. We explore various composite models where the Higgs and flavon fields are made up of Goldstone bosons derived from symmetry, with the flavon acting as a source of electroweak breaking. By employing a flavon doublet with $SU(2)_L\otimes SU(2)_R$ global symmetry, we generate small vacuum expectation values while avoiding an unwanted electroweak symmetry breaking. Alternative models featuring a singlet flavon and discrete symmetries are also examined, along with an analysis of top quark partner masses in both cases. Depending on the mechanism of flavon electroweak symmetry breaking, different mass scales are produced - either an electroweak scale or a TeV scale for top quarks. We calculate the predicted cross-sections for top quark partners in both scenarios, indicating possible detection or non-detection in upcoming experiments. Specifically, in the case of discrete symmetries, the TeV scale for top quark partners corresponds to $\mathcal{L}_f\sim 10^{-8}$, while $\mathcal{L}_f\sim 10^{-10}$ corresponds to an electroweak scale for top quark partners. Furthermore, we investigate the requirement for flavon decay branching ratios into gluons and $\gamma\gamma$ that would allow it to decay completely within the TeV range. Additionally, in composite Higgs models where the minimal flavour violating operators are sufficiently suppressed, we analyze flavon interactions with high-scale supersymmetry and a hidden $Z'$ boson. Lastly, under these conditions, the possibility of supersymmetry or hidden $Z'$ boson detection in the near future is considered. For this, we use the cross-sections and luminosities of the HL-LHC and future colliders, such as HL-LHC, FCC-hh, FCC-pe and CepC. Specifically, we determine that the HL-LHC has the required sensitivity to detect the hidden $Z'$ boson across a wide range of masses and couplings, while the sensitivity of the FCC-hh and CepC far surpasses that of the HL-LHC. Conversely, we fail to detect the $Z'$ boson at the FCC-hh and CepC in the scenarios where the supersymmetry is at a very high scale. Our understanding of high-level computer-generated reality experiences, particularly in Virtual Reality, is largely based on how real-world perceptions are re-created. Research has focused on how to manipulate user perceptions, but little is known about the underlying physical properties of VR. This paper shifts its focus to exploring the physical aspects of VR and proposes the concept of shadow aspect to describe alterations in user perceptions. We demonstrate the utility of this notion through a new application in VR interaction, where we have successfully improved interactivity by implementing a method of creating dynamic shadow fields. We observe significant advancements in user experience, as evidenced by experimental results. Furthermore, the shadow aspect is shown to be a versatile tool, as it can be applied to enhance the interactivity of existing interactive environments without altering their core features. The effectiveness of this approach is also reflected in the results of our conducted user study. The shadow aspect thus offers a valuable framework for designing and enhancing user experiences in VR by revealing the hidden physical means to influence perceptions and interactions. By utilizing a zero-dimensional model, researchers examine how planetary core formation unfolds when a more massive, rotating protostar breaks apart and gives birth to twin cores with distinct properties. This study delves into how the core's final mass is determined in relation to factors like initial protostar mass and angular momentum. Notably, the research reveals that more massive initial protostars yield larger planetary core masses, while those with higher spin rates produce smaller cores. Specifically, the relationship between initial mass and angular momentum is pinpointed as the key variable that dictates the core's mass. This discovery holds significant implications for the potential masses of metal-rich, iron-poor planets that could one day be discovered through transit missions. 
The researchers further expand their model by investigating various scenarios in which both core mass and angular momentum are affected. This is particularly evident when the parent core's enveloping disk is dense enough to shelter a substantial planetary core. Conversely, when the core is overpowered by the growing disk, both core and angular momentum are diminished. This phenomenon is shown to occur when the core's initial spin rate is relatively slow. However, when it spins rapidly, the core itself becomes the new center of a smaller, more tightly wound disk, ultimately resulting in both core mass and angular momentum being preserved. 
The researchers analyze various other scenarios, including cases in which both core mass and angular momentum are affected at distinct times. This is particularly evident when massive planets develop in highly eccentric, irregular orbits following a collision with a nearby core. Such a collision can result in core mass and angular momentum being both gained or lost, leading to a temporary deviation from normal behavior. This study offers crucial insights into the possible masses and spin rates of planets that could one day be observed through transit missions, and paves the way for a deeper understanding of the exoplanetary core mass function. This, in turn, may ultimately shed light on the emergence of habitable worlds and super-Earths. 
The researchers also discuss other areas for future research and examination, including how planetary core formation is affected when initial protostars are bound together by magnetic fields, and what happens when cores at varying distances from the star's center of rotation interact in a physical sense. Moreover, the impact of stellar winds on core development and angular momentum, as well as the effects of late-stage storm systems on core and planetary development, remain largely unexplored and await a more in-depth analysis. This new type of attack surpassed existing bounds, successfully decrypting encrypted data with high accuracy in a few milliseconds using a single processor core. Due to the extremely short duration, traditional countermeasures like frequency analysis became ineffective. This study proposes an economical solution to mitigate this vulnerability, utilizing a lightweight framework that can be implemented on modern embedded devices across various platforms without significantly impacting performance. This framework can also be adapted for use in cryptographic frameworks. The proliferation of social media has led to an overwhelming amount of user-generated data, 
which can be utilized to acquire real-time spatial and temporal insight into public events. 
Current approaches to event detection are hindered by several limitations: they mostly rely on 
popular microblogging platforms, using crude spatial and temporal summarization methods, 
and incorporating user-generated information such as event images. 
To address these shortcomings, we have developed an event recognition framework that utilizes 
sensitive spatial and temporal analysis, integrates multi-media data, and utilizes geographic coordinates. 
In this framework, we automatically identify and categorize events in real-time, and describe 
the approach to detecting public events from user posts on the Chinese social media platform, 
Weibo. 

Due to privacy concerns, Weibo caps the geographic area containing user posts at a 
circle with a radius of 3 km. As a result, events that span this distance are merged by the 
system, and events that require a larger area are split. 
To overcome these limitations, our approach utilizes a Poisson distribution-based method to 
calculate the probability of occurrence for events of a given size, and employs a decision 
threshold to determine whether an event has reached the required size. 
Further, to separate close events, we have developed a algorithm based on the distance 
and square root of time, and utilize user-posted images to refine event analysis. 
However, incorporating user images leads to increased noise, which is removed through a 
set of predefined criteria. 
The effectiveness of our approach was validated through experiments involving 160,062 
events covering an area of Shanghai and Ningbo, and spanning a period of one month. 
As a result, our system achieved accuracy and recall rates of 87.62% and 84.18% respectively. 
Or, viewed from another angle, our approach achieved recall rates of 82.16% and precision rates of 89.3%. 
Overall, our system remained accurate and efficient, even when event separation difficulty increased. 
Notably, incorporating Weibo images led to significantly higher recall rates. 
Finally, system scalability was validated through experiments involving reduced datasets, 
which revealed that our system remained accurate and efficient with datasets of any size. 
Consequently, the developed framework can be directly employed on larger social media platforms. 
However, some modifications would be required if the approach were applied to smaller platforms. 
Alternatively, a hybrid method could be used to combine elements from both the large and small platform scenarios.

In early 2020, widespread COVID-19 cases led Chinese citizens to greatly rely on mobile devices for information about epidemic prevention measures and the latest news. Unfortunately, this led to an influx of digital rumors that could pose significant harm to public safety. Notably, these digital rumors were often disseminated by prominent social media figures, reaching large audiences quickly. To combat this issue, Chinese authorities began officially releasing official information about the spread of COVID-19. This research analyzed user posts on the Chinese micro-blogging platform, Weibo, to better understand the dissemination of digital rumors within China during the pandemic. Our study identified key characteristics of these digital rumors, revealed the impact they had on the public's behavior, and examined the effectiveness of government dissemination efforts. Additionally, we developed and tested a model to assess the spread of digital rumors across social media networks. Our analysis showed that digital rumors often led Chinese citizens to adopt unsafe behaviors, and although government dissemination efforts were costly and reached millions of users, they had a limited impact on halting the spread of these digital rumors. However, when combined with refutal tactics, government dissemination efforts greatly reduced the range of spread. These findings provide critical insights for policymakers and public health officials seeking to control the dissemination of digital rumors and protect public safety. Moreover, these conclusions have significant practical applications, as demonstrated by recent government practices discussed in the paper. Finally, our research is conducive to other countries due to its broadness and versatility. Keywords: Digital Rumors, COVID-19, Weibo, Spreading Mechanism, Impact Assessment, Epidemic Social Media. Dimensionality reduction techniques are widely used in hyperspectral image analysis but the optimal method for reducing complex spectral dimensions is yet to be established. In this research, several renowned methods, along with Autoencoder networks, are evaluated based on their influence on hyperspectral image classification performance. Specifically, six methods were chosen for their frequent application in hyperspectral analysis: Principal Component Analysis, Principal Axis Sampling, Principal Curves, Autoencoders, Self Organizing Maps, and Local Linear Embedding. To assess these methods' effectiveness, experiments were conducted using datasets from various remote sensing platforms, including hyperspectral images provided by the Air Force Laboratory, a UNIS specifications dataset derived from Google Earth, and a hyperspectral dataset from the University of Pavia, along with corresponding true-color RGB images. The results showed that principal axis sampling retains the most manifold features in the reduced-dimensional space followed by principal curves, autoencoders, local linear embedding, and self-organizing maps. However, principal curves and autoencoders performed better than local linear embedding and self-organizing maps. Additionally, principal component analysis produced the worst outcome. When evaluating the spectral classification performance of these methods, principal axis sampling and principal curves achieved better results than autoencoders and self-organizing maps, with similar outcomes to local linear embedding and a slight improvement over the pairwise similarity metric. Ultimately, principal component analysis yielded the worst outcome. The success of principal axis sampling and principal curves in retaining manifold features in the reduced-dimensional space indicates their potential in hyperspectral analysis for comprehensive feature retention. Based on these findings, autoencoders could be preferred over principal component analysis and self-organizing maps in applications where morphological structures are prominent. Conversely, principal curves may be more suitable than autoencoders and self-organizing maps in environments with complex geometry. Recent breakthroughs in natural language understanding have paved the way for applying general task frameworks, like SOAR, to a wide range of specific challenges. However, task frameworks can be characterized by extremely broad and flexible input/output relationships, making it difficult to identify reliable connections between tasks. To tackle this issue, we develop a systematic approach for defining task-related narratives and use this framework to analyze and reduce the scope of task frameworks, limiting them to logically narrower problems, like zero-shot data labeling. This methodology can be applied to any task framework and helps to prevent overly general solutions, thereby facilitating more manageable and practical solutions. We implement this approach with a new system, SOAR-Zero, for zero-shot data labeling, significantly improving model efficiency while maintaining accuracy. The code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/ashish9610/soar-zero. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive guide to reducing task frameworks in the appendix. A typical method for modeling extreme events involves considering the occurrences as coming from a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While using the "mean of the distribution of the counts" as a parameter for Bayesian estimation has the advantage of being unbiased and consistent, this approach can lead to inefficient posterior computations due to the non-convergence of the Markov chain Monte Carlo method. There is also a higher chance of underestimating the extreme event frequency. We present an alternative method that converts the original parameter to one that affects the log-intensity function of the Poisson process, resulting in improved Markov chain Monte Carlo performance and a more accurate estimation of the extreme event frequency. This new method has the advantage of being computationally efficient and providing accurate results, particularly for low-frequency data. Our empirical study demonstrates that the new method outperforms the original one in both frequency and severity estimation. Our research further shows that the new method has detectable weaknesses that could be exploited by skilful attackers in Bayesian estimation attacks. There is a practical solution provided to mitigate these weaknesses. Our study's findings are validated through simulations and the analysis of well-known extreme event datasets. Our research integrates the new method into the extreme value theory framework, enabling frequency and severity estimations that are more accurate than before. For instance, our research reveals that the new method provides a more precise estimate of the 100-year flood in London, a more accurate estimate of the tail parameter in the Pareto distribution for certain rainfall data, and a more reliable estimate of the extreme value distribution parameter for low-frequency outcomes in Bayesian estimation. Our research compares the new method to the original parameter in terms of posterior concentration, efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo samples, estimation errors, and a new measure of extreme event frequency. Our study's findings are documented in a user-friendly format to facilitate the implementation of the new method in practice. Our research demonstrates the new method's benefits and provides a practical guide for its application in the estimation of frequency and severity extremes. Our research extends the theoretical results to include the estimation of the new method's rate parameter. Our research provides a practical solution to validate the new method's performance. Our research shows the new method's robustness to changes in its parameters. Our research demonstrates the new method's applicability to various scenarios. Our research provides a thorough comparison of the new method to other extreme value theory methods. Our research integrates the new method into the extreme value theory framework. Our research shows the new method's superiority to other extreme value theory methods through a series of simulations.

This aims to address a long-acknowledged gap in being able to effectively deal with corrupted data in RL. Our research contributes positively to the offline RL community by providing effective tools for handling corrupted data and reveals areas for further improvement. In this research, we make a novel observation that certain types of texts are more likely to be deemed out-of-distribution than others, and we propose a method to identify these high-risk categories.  Furthermore, based on these high-risk categories, we devise new metrics to gauge a language model's performance under out-of-distribution conditions.  Our research is the first to provide empirical evidence linking certain types of texts with out-of-distribution status, and our study offers novel evaluation metrics that are correlated with actual out-of-distribution performance.  Notably, our study reveals that existing state-of-the-art language models struggle to process texts in categories like'math', 'technology', and'science', thus highlighting areas for future research and development. We introduce an innovative algorithm for computing generalized convolutions with a summand count exceeding a billion within a fraction of a second, outperforming traditional brute-force methods by several orders of magnitude. Our approach, based on dividing the convolution function into smaller segments and combining the results, reduces memory usage and mitigates the inherent inefficiency of recursive methods. We compare the efficiency of our method against two alternative techniques: an iterative approach and a random access method. These efficient computation methods pave the way for the development of more sophisticated statistical tools, facilitating the exploration of new mathematical concepts and applications. Utilizing a model of atmospheric escape, we found GJ 229B's properties align with a top-heavy formation mechanism. A fundamental tool in electronic monetary markets is the double auction mechanism, with various adaptations proposed to improve its efficiency and robustness. However, current double auction mechanisms fail to prevent fraudulent activities such as bidding manipulations that can result in significant financial losses. To address this gap, we introduce a new, flexible double auction protocol that combines a novel demand assessment technique and a double auction model featuring double tokens. This novel approach prevents the threat of bidding manipulations through comparative analysis of bidding behavior, while ensuring the same level of user freedom and market efficiency as traditional double auctions. Furthermore, we develop a prototype implementation and conduct rigorous experiments to validate the efficacy of our solution. The results show that it is possible to achieve both security and efficiency in electronic monetary markets. The details of our experiment, including its design, are presented in the paper. The findings indicate that our security approach does not impair the efficiency of double auctions. Despite these efforts, understanding the dynamic relationships between player expertise, training methods, and the characteristics of chess openings remains a complex task. To shed light on this phenomenon, researchers have collected 317,858 chess games played at a high level of expertise from a popular online chess community, and employed a cluster analysis method known as Aggregate Analysis. This study uses data analysis techniques to determine how expert chess players use different openings in various ways, and examines both the structures of these openings and their usage patterns across multiple factors. Ultimately, the researchers were able to identify distinct and meaningful groups, or "manifolds," of chess openings based on both their internal structure and the way they are employed in actual games. This study provides new insights on the complex nature of chess openings and how they are played at a high level of expertise, and opens up new directions for research using data-driven methodologies to understand strategic behaviors in games. VPS is based on a novel concept of gauge invariance with geometric roots. VPS predicts that particles like the Higgs, W and Z bosons are sourced by a quantum field known as the Hilbert-Poincaré field (HPF), whose fluctuations give rise to three of the fundamental forces. Moreover, the theory indicates that gravitons are an implicit consequence of HPF fluctuations. VPS provides a natural and elegant framework for describing gravity and the other fundamental forces in a simplified and intuitive manner. Furthermore, the article highlights that VPS is a gauge-invariant version of the Einstein-Hilbert action, eliminating the ambiguity associated with the action's choice of gauge. VPS is comprised of two theories: the classical VPS (CVPS) and the quantum VPS (QVPS) theories. The CVPS theory is notable for its robustness in describing a theory of gravity and the other fundamental forces without fluctuations, whereas QVPS serves as a predictive model of quantum gravity and the other fundamental forces. Additionally, the article demonstrates that QVPS is consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics and general relativity. Moreover, the article highlights that both CVPS and QVPS theories are resistant to the continuum changes in the Poincaré algebra, thereby maintaining their gauge invariance. These challenges can potentially be resolved through the use of QVPS theory even in the absence of matter sources. We have developed new methods to apply SPARSEGRID, a framework for creating planar graphs, to upward drawing problems. By utilizing these methods, we have obtained parameterized algorithms for producing upward straight-line drawn trees and directed acyclic graphs, whose time complexity depends on the treewidth or number of DD-wedges in the input graph rather than the number of vertices. Specifically, for trees with vertex labels, we can create an upward straight-line drawing in O(n^2) time, expanding upon a previous quadratic-time algorithm for unweighted trees. For trees with direction labels, we can produce an upward directed straight-line drawing in O(n^2) time. Furthermore, we have obtained an upward straight-line drawing of a directed acyclic graph in O(n^3) time, improving a previous outcome-based approach. These results demonstrate that upward drawing problems can often be resolved through batch processing procedures, simplifying the concept of planarity and often leading to significantly faster algorithmic solutions. To achieve these outcomes, we have developed novel applications of the SPARSEGRID framework, incorporating concepts from graph embedding, combinatorial algorithms, and parameterized complexity. The resulting techniques should be applicable to more general problem classes and could provide a useful module for authors of upward drawing algorithms. The research presented here also explores new areas of the CHB-unfolding hierarchy and establishes a novel parameterization of the upward compatibility problem. This paper provides an in-depth look at the history and evolution of cellular technology and touches on future developments, such as sixth-generation (6G) systems, which will involve the integration of artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and other emerging technologies. This study introduces the concept of a dynamic hypergraph as a framework for modeling complex networks, where edges can encompass various structures. Building on previous work with evolving graphs, we develop algorithms for creating and managing the databases for dynamic hypergraphs and demonstrate their effectiveness through a range of theoretical analyses. Furthermore, we examine the computational challenges presented by our methods, revealing that some problems associated with dynamic hypergraphs are inherently more complex than their graph-based counterparts. To resolve these issues, we adopt a strategy of "approximation through substitution," utilizing simpler structures such as graphs to approximate the behavior of dynamic hypergraphs. Through this approach, we are able to demonstrate the feasibility of our methods. Specifically, our findings include the following: (1) online algorithms for dynamic hypergraphs can be at least twice as effective as their graph-based counterparts; (2) clearing the minimum weight edge in every time step is a key component in achieving optimal performance; (3) specific online algorithms using graphs to approximate the hypergraphs can yield comparable results and even slight improvements. These findings highlight the fundamental differences and similarities between the management of dynamic graphs and hypergraphs. To confirm the relevance and practicality of our solutions, we conduct experiments using real-world airline schedule data. Our research thus provides valuable insights for designing and managing the databases of dynamic hypergraphs. Furthermore, we identify the maximum scalability gap that can be achieved through online clearance, and we introduce the concept of $\alpha$-clustering, a measure of hypergraph topology that affects the efficiency of fractional clearing, and establish the relationship between $\alpha$-clustering and the hypergraph's fractional clearing performance. To showcase the applicability of our theoretical findings, we apply $\alpha$-clustering to analyze the airline schedule data. Our study thus provides the foundation for further research into the efficient management of databases for dynamic hypergraphs and other complex network structures. Through this research, we acquire important practical knowledge about clearing the real-world airline schedule data. Our work thus enables others to utilize the fractional clearing approach, and we provide known bounds for the efficiency loss and improvement factors associated with online clearance algorithms. Furthermore, we introduce the $\alpha$-clustering measure, which is essential for evaluating fractional clearing performance and has practical applications in analyzing the efficiency of clearing methods on specific hypergraphs. This study presents the results from SEM-TAB-FACTS, a new fact validation and discovery task focusing on tabular data in scientific papers. For proof discovery, participants were asked to identify which rows contained supporting evidence for claims made in the provided text. In the fact validation subset of data, human annotators marked whether a given claim was valid or not, with the model's performance compared to these annotations. We provide an overview of the task's methodology, data, and participant performance. 
The data collection process involved three stages: 
First, researchers compiled a dataset with annotated tables and written claims, which were then used to create a classification model for reference. 
Second, a set of claims and tables were generated automatically based on existing data. 
Third, human annotators marked whether each claim was valid or not, which led to additional annotated data. 
Finally, the complete set of data, including both human and model annotations, was used to create the dataset for SEM-TAB-FACTS. 
In total, six systems from four different groups took part in the task, which involved two subtasks: proof discovery and fact validation. 
Notably, all three successful systems in the proof discovery subtask used a similar approach, which consisted of combining table evidence with external knowledge. 
In the fact validation subtask, one system demonstrated particularly high performance, achieving 69\% F1 score, which is close to human-level at 72\% F1 score. 
More information about the task can be found at https://github.com/ashariz/SEM-TAB-FACTS. 
The data will also be shared with the public through https://github.com/ashariz/SEM-TAB-FACTS/tree/master/Data. 
It is planned to maintain this repository indefinitely.

Understanding why a deep neural network made a prediction is difficult. In this study, we developed a method to interpret the decisions of DNNs by utilizing concept analysis and inductive logic programming. This approach analyzes DNNs layer by layer, providing insights into how binary class predictions are made. Through experiments, we found that DNNs use a straightforward strategy to combine concepts from different layers to make decisions. This discovery led us to create a more efficient method for understanding DNNs, one that doesn't require re-training the network. We successfully applied this approach to multiple DNNs and observed that the resulting explanations accurately represent the underlying decision-making processes. Furthermore, we found that DNNs making binary classifications in the same domain often share similar decision-making structures. Based on this observation, we propose a merger of DNNs that integrates their decisions in a unified and interpretable way. This novel method has significant potential for understanding and optimizing the performance of individual DNNs within a family of prediction models. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a popular choice for representation learning in node graphs. However, they have a significant shortcoming - they neglect the distinct characteristics of graph structures. Recent research has introduced Graph Attention Networks (GATs) as a superior alternative to GCNs, as GATs prioritize node attributes over graph structures. We identified a flaw in this replacement - the over-emphasis on node attributes in GATs also obscures the underlying graph structure. Our study aims to address this issue. We begin by assessing the effectiveness of GCNs and GATs across 13 benchmark datasets. Notably, GCNs outperform GATs in 9 of these benchmark datasets. We then propose a hybrid model, SP3 GCN, which combines the strengths of GCNs and Personalized PageRank (PPR) algorithms. SP3 GCN is a GCN-based deep learning framework that preserves graph structures, and we demonstrate its potential through experiments. Our findings indicate that SP3 GCN surpasses state-of-the-art models, including those for semi-supervised and unsupervised node classification tasks. Additionally, we analyze the parameters and training procedures of SP3 GCN, as well as its underlying graph structure and related loss functions. We also provide a comprehensive comparison with GCNs and GATs to highlight the superiority of SP3 GCN. Through this research, we aim to rectify the misconception that GCNs are inferior and showcase the importance of graph structures in machine learning. Furthermore, we identify novel approaches to enhancing the representation of node graphs, as well as the underlying graph structure. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yelundg/SP3-GCN. In this study, we employ a combination of experimental and theoretical findings to clarify the epitaxial mechanisms underlying the growth of Heusler layers on graphene/sapphire substrates. We demonstrate that thin films of graphene on sapphire provide an ideal foundation for the epitaxial growth of these materials, given their large mismatch and ability to supply dopants. We examine the epitaxial techniques of van der Waals, pinhole, and volume epitaxy in detail, and highlight the significance of van der Waals forces and lattice matching between films and substrate in achieving precise epitaxy. Notably, the equilibrium between different epitaxial techniques is largely influenced by the thickness of the graphene layer. We use first-principles simulations to investigate the epitaxial models of LaPtS and LaAgS, revealing that a 2-3 monolayer thick graphene base is essential for precise epitaxy. However, further aggregation of graphene layers leads to distant epitaxy with high precision. We also observe that pinhole and volume epitaxy increase in significance as the thickness of graphene increases. Ultimately, the choice of Heusler layer depends on the optimal balance between these different epitaxial techniques. For example, LaPtS exhibits a combination of 50% distant and 50% volume epitaxy with a 4 monolayer thick graphene base, while LaAgS displays 50% pinhole and 50% volume epitaxy with a 6 monolayer thick graphene base. We verify these theoretical predictions through the analysis of high-resolution transmission electron microscopy images and demonstrate that these results are consistent with the experimental data. Together, these findings indicate that thin films of graphene on sapphire provide an ideal foundation for the epitaxial growth of Heusler layers through a combination of precise and less precise techniques. Additionally, these results underscore the significance of understanding the underlying physics behind different epitaxial mechanisms in reducing the mismatch between films and substrate. We believe that these findings will significantly contribute to the development of this class of materials. Additionally, these results are expected to extend beyond the field of Heusler materials and be applicable to other topological materials as well. We envision that our findings will be useful in navigating the diverse range of epitaxial techniques used in van der Waals, pinhole, and volume epitaxy. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) have long been urged to upgrade their networks to meet growing online content demands. However, many ISPs hesitate, citing the high costs involved. To bridge this gap, a new model has emerged where content providers compensate ISPs for improved network quality. This cooperation benefits both parties: ISPs benefit from upgraded networks, while content providers gain access to higher bandwidth and better quality for their users. Notable examples of such agreements include Google's partnership with CityFi and Facebook's connectivity initiative. This paper explores the potential of this cooperative model, investigating factors like varying content popularity and how different distribution policies affect user experience and revenue. Notably, results show that content providers can reap more profit when users have equal access to high-quality content, and that giving priority to popular content over others can decrease the overall network quality and the content provider's profit, despite initially increasing short-term revenue. Conversely, prioritizing all content equally tends to result in lower short-term profits but provides long-term benefits by maintaining a higher quality experience and ultimately boosting the content provider's profit. These findings provide meaningful insights for content and service providers considering such profit distribution agreements. Furthermore, this study offers a framework that enables these parties to quantify the effects of different policies and identify the most beneficial strategies to pursue. Finally, while this research focuses on a content-provider-pays model, its findings are general enough to be applied to other scenarios where profit distribution agreements come into play. Potential variants of this model include scenarios where the service provider acts as a mediator between multiple content providers and proposes a new contract to the content providers to establish a fair and profitable revenue distribution policy. These are topics for further study. Moreover, our study can be extended by considering more complex systems, such as systems with multiple tiers or those where the service provider acts as a mediator between content providers. These are topics for further study. This study investigates why bidders in practice appear to be less aggressive in auctions when their rivals' bids are easily accessible, a phenomenon that has economic theory struggle to replicate. Through a series of lab-based experiments designed to test the robustness of this finding, we demonstrate its presence across multiple auction types and sizes, notably finding that bidders tend to bid more conservatively when facing well-informed opponents, as opposed to those lacking such information. Our analysis suggests that a straightforward increase in the bidder's revenue is not the primary driver of this observed effect. Rather, when confronted with the possibility of being exploited by an informed opponent, a bidder may develop a heightened sense of risk aversion, a sentiment shared by our participants as expressed in post-experiment feedback. These findings emerge across various auction scenarios, with our results revealing a particular gaze from professional bidders in a particular type of auction. Ultimately, we demonstrate that increasing the difficulty for bidders to detect their opponents' knowledge does not significantly alter the trustworthiness effect. This study's results are the first to document the trustworthiness effect in a multi-round auction setting and its extension to revenue maximisation. Additionally, we discovered that proxy bidding may serve as a meaningful training ground for the trustworthiness effect. Furthermore, we found that the impact of bid visibility may decline as bidders become more experienced. Lastly, we demonstrate that the trustworthiness effect remains consistent across auctions conducted through an online platform. This study's findings are significant and contribute to our understanding of the trustworthiness effect, shedding light on its underlying mechanisms and multiple auction contexts. Moreover, we documented the bid variability of actual bids submitted by professional bidders in auctions without constraints. Finally, we explored the proxy bidding phenomenon, a by-product of our experimentally-created auction environment. Additionally, we discovered that the impact of bid visibility may be influenced by the number of rounds in an auction. Artificial Neural Networks, including Generative Adversarial Networks and Variational Autoencoders, demonstrate capabilities in creating aesthetically pleasing and realistic images. However, the artistic merit of generated images is ultimately subjective and cannot be fully automated. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach, the Delight Model, a GAN-based framework that learns to create images based on both adversarial and reinforcement learning principles. Through a simplified yet effective mechanism, the Delight Model incorporates feedback from a diverse set of pre-trained neural networks, each mimicking a specific art critic's perspective. As a result, it is capable of producing images that not only please human eyes but also align with various artistic agendas. Moreover, we showcase the Delight Model's capabilities by generating images that are both visually appealing and grounded in reality using a pre-trained VAE as a generator. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through qualitative and quantitative analysis of generated images. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/yelab-ucb/DelightNeuralArtistry. Additional generated images can be found at https://delight.ucb.edu. Experimental findings illustrate the significance of diverse artistic perspectives and the potential for generated images to be more visually appealing and artistically meaningful. To our knowledge, the Delight Model represents the first neural network system to incorporate multiple artistic agendas and incorporate human artistic preferences into the training process. The Delight Model's integration of various artistic agendas and preferences has been patented (US Patent Application 21/491759). The model's capabilities have been presented at conferences, including the 2022 Computer Vision Conference, and will be presented at the 2023 Neural Information Processing Systems Conference. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed neurological disorder in children and adults. ADHD diagnosis heavily relies on Behavioral questionnaires, which are limited to providing partial insight into the individual's condition. Recent advancements in Deep Learning technology have shown promise in aiding ADHD diagnosis using Neuroimaging data. Our investigation shows that enhancing rs-fMRI data with Spatial or Temporal features yields minimal improvement in ADHD classification using Deep Learning models. Notably, combining Spatial and Temporal features results in the optimal performance of 79.45% accuracy across various algorithms. Our novel implementation of Temporal feature extraction method has potential applications in enhancing ADHD diagnosis, as well as other Psychiatric disorder classification. In contrast to traditional continuous time epidemic models, a new discrete-time SISI model is proposed for analyzing disease spread, where the model's parameters are based on distinct time steps for both disease transmission and recovery processes. The model's equations are developed and its basic epidemic parameters, such as the basic reproductive number $R$, are defined and calculated in terms of the epidemic threshold $\lambda_c$ and the ultimate infection prevalence $\lambda_1$. The latter prevalence represents the prevalence at a specific time $t=mc$, where $c$ is the time-step interval. Furthermore, a numerical study is presented to verify the findings by comparing them with the outcomes of the continuous-time SISI model. The proposed discrete-time SISI model provides simplifications that can benefit computational simulations and theoretical analyses. Moreover, its application is more aligned with microsimulations that are commonly utilized in epidemiology. The proposed model has the potential to streamline such computations. The epigraph representation of the epidemic equilibrium in the discrete-time SISI model was previously reported; however, it is now demonstrated that this representation is no longer applicable to the distinct-time model, and instead, a new cactus representation is developed for capturing the epidemic equilibrium perfectly. Finally, both the SISI model's applications in social networks and its associated complexity are discussed. Although complex, the discrete-time SISI model has the advantage of simplifying complex microsimulations that are typically more computationally demanding and challenging. Lastly, it is argued that there is still value in studying the basic epidemic models to gain a deeper understanding. The work presented here contributes to this goal. The model's results and theories presented here are the original contributions of the studyspecific research. The provided code is compatible with MATLAB R2021a. This paper introduces MadDog, a comprehensive online system that facilitates
the identification and explanation of acronyms within incoming text or speech data,
enabling users to leverage its services via a secure, protected interface accessible
over HTTPS. MadDog encompasses two interconnected components: the Dog and the
Bull. The Bull constitutes the backend of MadDog, embodying the system's core
technology to process acronym requests and provide clarifications through returned
JSON responses. On the other hand, the Dog represents the frontend of MadDog, which
is comprised of a lightweight web application built using modern frontend
technologies. This paper details both MadDog's underlying methodology and the system
itself, in addition to highlighting the benefits derived from integrating the MadDog
service into existing Spoken Web Accessibility initiatives. Moreover, we also
describe the MadDog service architecture, incorporating Distributed Acronyms Recognition
and Explanation (DARE), a developed component that facilitates the MadDog service
at the University of Washington campus. DARE now serves as the Bull for MadDog, a
DARE-based service that powers the MadDog system. Furthermore, we also report on
the performance of MadDog in the Spoken Acronym Recognition task, showcasing its
capabilities. Finally, MadDog is made accessible to the public through
https://madog.uw.edu.pk. This research was funded by a grant from the Qatar National
Research Fund (7-Src-222-2-14). We express our gratitude to Qatar Disability Affairs
Department for their support and cooperation, particularly in evaluating the system
with Disability users. Additionally, we appreciate the guidance and support from
Professor Shadi Al Masaouin from the College of Engineering at Qatar University.

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is crucial for understanding the operation of quantum machines that generate work through microscopic arrangements. Research has established that quantum correlations are necessary for achieving optimal thermoelectric performance, yet this property is rare in systems lacking interactions. However, interactions can give rise to unusual thermoelectric behavior. We investigated whether quantum interactions could enable novel thermoelectric functionality, and our research reveals that they can. Using a quantum Hall junction model incorporating interactions, we demonstrate interaction-induced thermoelectric toggling, where a single voltage bias produces multiple current responses, and also achieve heat rectification through a single quantum channel. These findings illustrate how interactions can give rise to intricate thermoelectric properties, promoting the development of interacting quantum systems as a platform for quantum thermodynamics. Additionally, these results provide potential applications for switching and heat control at the quantum level. \\

Both algorithms work under the assumption that the maximum eigenvalue of the state's density matrix is less than one. The first algorithm utilizes O(\sqrt{N}) quantum queries to achieve an approximation within a factor of N^{\frac{1-\epsilon}{2}} for any \epsilon > 0. The second algorithm requires O(N^{\frac{1+\epsilon}{2}}) quantum queries to yield an approximation within a factor of N^{\frac{1-\epsilon}{2} \cdot N^{\frac{1+\epsilon}{2}}} for any \epsilon > 0. Interestingly, when \epsilon goes to zero, this approximation factor simplifies to N^{\frac{1}{2} - N^{\frac{1}{2}}}. Both of these results significantly outperform previous classical approximations that were known to be possible. The first algorithm leverages a modified version of Brascamp-Lieb inequality, incorporating recent findings by Ozel-Osborne-Osborne. The second algorithm relies on a novel approach derived from Shor's polynomial factorization algorithm. The efficiency gains observed in both algorithms can be attributed to innovative reductions that exploit the low eigenvalue constraint. The outcomes also reveal potential connections between entropy and randomness. Compared to supervised and fully supervised techniques, the proposed method demonstrates improved performance with reduced training data requirements. Experimental results validate the efficacy of this method.

Real-world shading contains compact, predictable, and shadowed areas which can be accurately represented through subspace modeling, yet its application in computer vision and graphics has been limited due to the non-differentiable nature of traditional shadow calculation methods, hindering its use in optimization-based techniques. We introduce an alternative, differentiable method for computing shading, using a neural network that effectively captures the essence of real-world shading. This model, known as NEAR, enables an alternative method for imaging and rendering tasks that takes into consideration the inherent properties of real-world shading. NEAR leverages a multi-scale neural network design that mimics the characteristics of real-world shading, specifically treating compact, predictable, and shadowed areas separately. By applying a differentiable approximation to classical shadow mapping, NEAR achieves a significant improvement in both computational efficiency and accuracy compared to prior methods. NEAR's integration with an optimization-based technique allows us to successfully solve challenging inverse problems in computer vision and graphics, even when current methods fail. Our work proposes an effective and differentiable approach to imaging and rendering issues involving real-world shading. Additionally, NEAR's code is publicly available at https://github.com/jbardin/neural-shading. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that NEAR surpasses traditional methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency, and provides a viable solution to optimization-based techniques for computer vision and graphics applications. NEAR's integration of a differentiable shadow calculation and subspace modeling capabilities, as well as its design inspirations and enhancements, are thoroughly explained. Through quantitative and qualitative assessments, we demonstrate that NEAR consistently produces superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods. NEAR's enhancements to classical shadow mapping, as well as its improvements in shading representation, are quantitatively evaluated and shown to significantly improve the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, NEAR's application in computer vision and graphics tasks is extensively demonstrated through over 30 numerical experiments that confirm its superiority and showcase its potential to solve a range of optimization-based techniques. Finally, the neural network's performance in a specific task is discussed, revealing that NEAR consistently produces more accurate results compared to state-of-the-art methods. To estimate origin-destination (OD) demands, we propose an approach that utilizes Google's traffic data. This data is broken down into small time frames, each containing traffic counts that can be associated with specific routes. To accurately estimate OD demands, we break them down into origins, destinations, and paths. Under the assumption that an OD pair travels along the shortest path, we can represent an OD matrix as a graph where flows along unique paths contribute to the overall demand. Given that Google's traffic data is inherently biased towards heavy travelers, we develop an iterative method that utilizes Thompson sampling to weight each path by its likelihood of being underrepresented. This process is computationally intensive, so we offer an accelerated version that utilizes Skew Normal regression for rapid estimation. This method yields comparable results while drastically reducing computational demands. Numerical studies demonstrate that our approach accurately estimates OD demands even in complex scenarios. Furthermore, the approach can easily incorporate additional information, such as historical OD demands, to enhance estimation precision. Experimental results show that incorporating this information enhances estimation precision. All numerical studies were conducted using Python 3.6, with the code available upon request. 

Keywords: Origin-destination demands, Thompson sampling, Skew Normal regression, Statistical estimation, Iterative refinement, Traffic analysis

Through both mathematical analysis and simulations, our study reveals that as the strength of an oscillator's connections changes, it inevitably transitions between two primary states: either having its oscillators move in unison or have their phases disconnected. Notably, the transition into a synchronized state can occur through two distinct mechanisms - either by increasing the strength of connections within the ensemble or by adding more connections within it. Furthermore, our analysis shows that as an oscillator is isolated from the others, it either begins to move in unison with them or has its phase become completely disconnected. The discoveries from our research provide a broader understanding of how diverse oscillator arrays behave. Additionally, our work is also relevant to the study of biological systems, where it sheds light on the mechanisms behind two commonly observed phenomena - where either a whole array or just a single element becomes synchronized. Finally, our results are applied to a specific example of a system consisting of mechanically coupled pendulums, where we demonstrate that the discovery of synchronized dynamics can lead to a significant reduction in energy consumption - namely, by tuning the pendulums' movements such that they moves in unison, which in turn reduces the required energy for maintaining their motion. This discovery has potential implications for various biologically-relevant schemes of synchronized swings during foraging. Moreover, this research may inspire the development of novel algorithms for automatically adjusting the timing of video captures to reduce power consumption. Lastly, our study provides an important discovery for applications such as hearing aids - by altering the timing of when electric signals are sent from these devices, we can make them more power-efficient while maintaining clear and understandable audio for the listener. In recent years, large-scale text and image datasets have driven innovation in natural language processing and computer vision.  Despite the abundance of these datasets, there is a notable shortage of comprehensive sheet-music datasets that could enable the development of universal musical representations.  Existing research in musical notation automatically converts sheet-music into text-based representations, but these models lack the pre-trained capabilities of their language model counterparts.  This paper introduces MusicTM-Dataset, a multi-format dataset comprising complete scores, sheet-music excerpts, lyrics, and corresponding audio recordings.  Designed to support the development of pre-trained, universal musical representations, MusicTM-Dataset consists of 20,913 complete works and 493,110 sheet-music excerpts from four major sheet-music providers.  To enhance data quality, MusicTM-Dataset incorporates three pre-trained encoders: musical notation, verse, and audio.  Experimental results using various pre-training objectives confirm that the dataset can facilitate the development of universal musical representations.  Additionally, the research demonstrates that pre-trained encoders trained on MusicTM-Dataset demonstrate enhanced generalization capabilities when evaluated using different modalities.  Furthermore, the research introduces MusicTM-Pretrained, a pre-trained model based on the T5 architecture that integrates the three encoders.  Comprehensive testing validates the pre-trained model's accuracy and showcases its potential to integrate sheet-music, text, and audio representations.  Future work using MusicTM-Dataset could focus on combining pre-trained encoders and incorporating structural information from sheet-music to further enhance data quality. One fundamental aspect of data analysis involves understanding connections between entities. In the context of structural data, this requires a thorough examination of nodes and edges that comprise the data set. For large data sets, users may become disoriented, leading to misplaced focus on irrelevant elements. To aid in data analysis, researchers have developed various techniques. This study utilizes Ontodia, a tool for visualizing Linked Data, in conjunction with word embeddings to enhance users' comprehension of Linked Data entities. However, word embedding implementations are limited in the Ontodia framework. To address this limitation, we have implemented a new Ontdia add-on that integrates the Wikidata Entity Schema Atlas. This atlas utilizes word embeddings and Wikidata to identify and analyze entity associations. We have successfully integrated it into Ontdia, as demonstrated in a data analysis exam demonstration. The integration of this atlas offers several benefits, including standardized annotations and discoverable connections. Additionally, we have freed up memory within the Ontdia framework, thereby improving performance. This improved functionality is now accessible to users via a dedicated menu option. Furthermore, we have developed a menu option that enables users to customize which Wikidata classes are incorporated into Ontdia data exams. This customization is applied to the Ontdia schema atlas. To validate our approach, we have conducted a comparative analysis of our method, employing word embeddings, against traditional Ontdia data exams. Our results demonstrate that incorporating word embeddings into Ontdia data exams leads to (1) a 30% decrease in redundant connections, as visually identified by human analysts, and (2) an average 69% increase in detected properties, as automatically analyzed by the Ontdia schema atlas. Furthermore, we have identified and released several memory-related issues within the Ontdia framework, and provided solutions to mitigate these problems.
