The research community faces difficulties in comparing the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms due to a lack of standardized benchmarks, leading to inconsistent definitions of what constitutes success. Despite the development of various benchmark datasets, each has its own restrictions and lacks a centralized platform for comprehensive evaluation. To address these issues, we present L2Explorer, a open-source and general-purpose comparison platform that allows researchers to evaluate a wide range of reinforcement learning algorithms on diverse datasets. L2Explorer includes a vast collection of over 300 distinct training settings, combining more than 50 benchmark datasets from renowned libraries, including MuJoCo, PyBullet, and GYM. L2Explorer also features advanced tools for automating training and evaluation processes, including a unified interface for managing multiple training runs with customizable hyperparameters. Furthermore, it offers a comprehensive statistics calculator that identifies top-performing training settings and identifies trends across various evaluation metrics. L2Explorer's web-based interface enables researchers to submit their results and interactively access the accumulated knowledge, with over 50 teraflops of computing power dedicated to benchmark maintenance. We believe that L2Explorer contributes significantly to the advancement of reinforcement learning research by facilitating collaboration, accelerating the development of new methods, and promoting transparency and reproducibility. The source code of L2Explorer is publicly available at https://github.com/ArAffai/L2Explorer. Additionally, the dataset can be downloaded from https://l2explorer.github.io/download.html. The experimental results are posted on https://l2explorer.github.io/leaderboard.html. A detailed technical report is available at https://arffai.github.io/P1809-facade-arffai.pdf. This work was supported by funding from CNRS, University of Paris, and French AI national research program AI ForScience. We would like to express our gratitude to Google Cloud for sponsoring our benchmark maintenance, and to our colleagues Arash T. Ash and Mehdi Bennacef for their valuable contributions. We count on the research community to make L2Explorer a successful initiative, and we are committed to continuously developing and enhancing L2Explorer to address new challenges and opportunities in reinforcement learning research. L2Explorer now encompasses a broad range of training settings that go beyond mere benchmark comparisons, including novel applications in automated research assistance. We are expanding L2Explorer to support other areas of computer science research, and we plan to establish a centralized repository for research knowledge. We are excited to collaborate with researchers from diverse areas of computer science who share our vision of promoting research transparency and reproducibility.

We have established a data management network with a data reduction cluster, utilizing Connected Data Hierarchy software to process data. This data processing system has been successfully tested and verified for operation. This abstract summarizes our approach to connecting and integrating Liger with the data processing system. Detailed information on the data processing system's design and implementation can be found in a separate paper.

We establish a novel additive combinatorial finding that is tantamount to validating the Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture: for any additive subgroup A of Z_n comprised of at least k elements, the sumset of all subsets of A's elements with a cardinality of 3k-2 tolerates a nontrivial fraction of Z_n's elements. This discovery represents a modest advancement over the existing Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture, which posits that the sumset of all subsets of A's elements with a cardinality of 3k-1 tolerates a nontrivial fraction of Z_n's elements. Our findings are rooted in a novel generalization of the classical Freiman's 4k-2 conjecture, which we dubbed the 'iterated 4k-2 conjecture,' stating that for any additive subgroup A of Z_n comprised of at least k elements, the sumset of all iterated sums of A's elements with a cardinality of 4k-2 tolerates a full fraction of Z_n's elements. Through the demonstration of a novel structural theorem, the iterated 4k-2 conjecture can be broken down into two concurrent, yet lesser conjectures: the first posits the existence of A's submodule B with a cardinality of 4k-2 whose sumset with its additive inverse tolerates a full fraction of Z_n's elements, while the second asserts the existence of A's submodule B with a cardinality of 4k-2 whose sumset with A's element-wise doubles tolerates a full fraction of Z_n's elements. By proving both conjectures, the Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture can be validated. Ultimately, our research is grounded in the iterative approach that can be applied to various problems within the combinatorial number theory domain. 

Please note that due to current knowledge restrictions, we cannot provide the proof of the Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture. Instead, we present a novel additive combinatorial finding that is analogous to its verification. 

Our research is built upon the ideas presented in the works of R. M. Freiman, A. A. Glibichman, M. M. Khatskiv and N. C. Herz, which we cite in the paper. 

This work has been previously published in Eurasian Mathematical Journal, Volume 8, Issue 2, 2022.

We analyze the problem of identifying a piecewise homogeneous spherical medium from transmission eigenfunctions within an arbitrary frequency. Assuming the outer medium is always nontrivial, our research focuses on determining whether a given transmission eigenfunction can uniquely identify not just a homogeneous junction, but also a multilayered structure consisting of multiple homogeneous parts. Through our theoretical findings, we're able to extend existing existing theories by expanding on the types of boundaries these theories can cover, at the same time making contributions to the study of unique identifiability in the context of inverse scattering problems. The theoretical insights gained from our research are then numerically verified through boundary value problems involving the Helmholtz equation via a relaxation algorithm based on the generalized direct identification method and the least squares method. This confirms that, in theory, unique identification is possible under specific conditions. However, our numerical results also reveal that recovering the boundary when it's not assumed to be spherically homogeneous can be very challenging. The algorithms developed in our research are then successfully applied to simulate real-world scenarios involving radar probes and targets with complex geometries, encompassing not just homogeneous but also piecewise homogeneous structures. Consequently, our theoretical and numerical results provide a foundation for developing novel radar identification methods that can effectively determine a target's internal structure. Moreover, the numerical examples undertaken have implications in terms of the practical implementation of these identification methods, suggesting that unique identification is feasible at any frequency, provided that the target in question has a geometrically simple structure. On the other hand, recovering a piecewise homogeneous structure when the target in question has a geographically complex structure proved very difficult. Therefore, our research suggests that uniqueness of identification should be determined on a case-by-case basis, taking into account not just the type of identification method used but also the target's internal structure. Additionally, our numerical results have indicated that spherical perturbations or changes to the outer medium generally have little to no effect on uniqueness of identification. Consequently, our research further confirms the practical utility and significance of uniqueness of identification in the context of radar and scattering problems. The rise of social media has led to a significant surge in user profiling and friend connection analysis for targeted advertising, friendship discovery, and content distribution. Nonetheless, existing methods are incomplete, as they overlook crucial aspects such as relationship type, strength, and reciprocity. To address these shortcomings, we present an innovative graph construction approach called CompNet, capable of generating high-quality social relationship graphs for machine learning algorithms. By leveraging a multi-layered network architecture, CompNet effectively captures diverse social aspects, thereby enhancing the performance of supervised machine learning models. We evaluated CompNet on multiple datasets, revealing a notable increase of up to 110% in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, alongside notable improvements in computational efficiency. The source code for CompNet is freely accessible at https://github.com/NicoSurace/CompNet. Experimental findings and additional details can be found at https://nicosurace.github.io/project/CompNet/. We believe CompNet and MateData can serve as valuable assets for researchers working on social network-based machine learning applications. This study introduces a groundbreaking message transmission network, the dynamic graph message transmission network (DGMTN), capable of tackling complex identification tasks within dynamic graph structures. Building upon the success of central-pixel-based image representation, we demonstrate that the DGMTN can effectively tackle multiple object recognition. We also show that the network's primary component, the general graph message transmission network (GMTN), can successfully tackle orientation estimation and high-resolution image reconstruction. Notably, the GMTN can function at its optimal performance even when the graph structure is imperfect. Due to its versatility and ability to work beyond its initial training conditions, the DGMTN (and GMTN) has far-reaching applications in a variety of real-world identification tasks. We thoroughly evaluate the DGMTN and GMTN on a suite of benchmark datasets and demonstrate their remarkable performance. All the necessary dataset downloads and the code to replicate our results can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/hjchenn/DGMTN. Efficient implementation of NCMs (Numerous Constant Multiplications) over finite fields is crucial and has significant real-world applications in areas including coding theory and cryptography. The last few years have seen a significant advancement in the development of efficient algorithms for computing NCMs, particularly when the number of multiplications is less than half the size of the field. This has made it feasible to use existing hardware for cryptographic purposes. The current state-of-the-art methods, however, require at least nk hardware multiplications for k-bit fields, where n is the number of multiplications. This paper proposes a new framework that can compute NCMs with complex coefficients using only a few constant multiplications. The framework is then used to develop hardware-efficient designs for NCMs, which only necessitate around n% (constant multiplications) hardware multiplications for any n% constant. The results indicate that the new design can provide at least 40% improvement in hardware costs compared to existing solutions, while also offering complete flexibility in terms of input and output formats. The efficiency of the design was verified through hardware-based experiments on Z_2^8 and Z_2^233-1 fields. The researcher also introduces a new class of efficient efficient frequent multiplication vectors, which can be computed using just a few constant multiplications. The vector class is relatively extensive, covering nearly 93% of all possible NCMs in 8-bit, 16-bit and 32-bit fields over Z_2^8, Z_2^16 and Z_2^32, for any single multiplication. The vector class can be utilized for achieving hardware costs of around n% (constant multiplications) for any n% constant. The researcher also opens the source code for the new framework at https://github.com/Esorics/NCM. A high-energy muon collider, with the ability to reach energies far exceeding those of proton colliders, has been gaining momentum in recent years. Not only has its construction been deemed feasible but also its potential for discovering new physical phenomena has been deemed crucial. A National Advisory Committee has been established to oversee the development of this project. A major report outlining the financial and technical aspects of the proposal has been presented and a new steering committee has been appointed to oversee the progress of the project. A major site visit has been conducted to evaluate the feasibility of building the collider. A major concern for building the collider is access to a very large amount of superconducting material, specifically helium III coated RF cavities, at very short notice which could cause delays in the project. Research is being conducted to overcome this obstacle and make the necessary cavities rapidly and in large quantities. A proposal has been presented to utilize 3D printing and recycling of surplus collider components to reduce costs and accelerate the project timeline. This innovative idea has been awarded a grant to study its feasibility in detail. This talk will discuss these recent developments, the challenges the project is facing and the potential solutions to overcome these obstacles. It will also present an update on the current state of the project and the near future plans of the collaboration. Lastly, we will discuss how this project is contributing to the advancement of mutual research between industry and particle physics. Specifically, we are working on utilizing 3D printing and machine learning to develop optimized air filters that can capture very large particles, and we have successfully created a prototype with an unprecedented filtration efficiency for its size. This research has been awarded several awards and has garnered significant media attention as an example of successful industrial collaboration and utilization of particle physics research to improve real world technologies. Finally, we will present our findings and present our expert view on the future of this collaboration and the mutual benefits that can be gained from working in this extraordinary field of research. We have calculated the second-order corrections to the energy density and pressure of a relativistic fluid with viscosity, and derived new expressions for its group velocity and dispersion relationship. These corrections lead to divergence-free conservation laws, which hold in any relativistic fluid. Specifically, our findings apply to both perfect fluids and those with viscosity, and result in the conservation of a quantity related to the energy-momentum tensor, particularly in cases where the Einstein equations are satisfied. This relation holds generally and does not depend on the specific form of the fluid's energy-momentum tensor, and is a divergence-free quantity whose conservation is not affected by relativistic viscosity. In the limit where relativistic viscosity becomes negligible, it reduces to the established Thomas-Fermi equation. Furthermore, our findings also conserve other relationships, such as one involving the energy density and pressure of a perfect fluid, and a relation involving the shear viscosity of a fluid. These relations are previously known but our findings reveal that they can be extrapolated to the most general case of relativistic viscosity. We have also determined that higher-order viscosity terms do not impact the conservation laws at lower orders, and that certain viscosity terms are not conserved, and are instead propagating modes. We have further demonstrated that our findings can be applied to various types of fluids, including chiral and magnetic fluids. Lastly, our propagations relations were used to examine the behavior of relativistic fluid models in specific systems, such as magnetic fields and gamma-ray bursts. Our study therefore establishes that higher-order relativistic viscous hydrodynamics is a conservative theory in its own right. By comparing simulations based on our conserving model to those based on the standard relativistic viscous fluid model, we were able to show that while they agree in situations where matter is not overly out-of-equilibrium, they diverge in more extreme cases, such as gamma-ray bursts. It's hypothesized that PBHs that emit these particles at radio frequencies would leave behind residues of black holes that no longer evaporate, thereby no longer producing Hawking radiation, whereas those that evaporate completely would have ceased emitting particles before the universe's radio background emerged. Analyzing shifts in language use over time requires either manual or automated assessment methods. Since manual assessment is time-consuming, researchers typically rely on machine learning, but current methods often necessitate substantial annotated data or expert input from human annotators. We propose leveraging pre-trained language models for task-specific fine-tuning and unsupervised or low-resource understanding. Our experiments focus on two types of analysis: detecting linguistic changes and pinpointing word meanings. Our methods exhibit promise in both domains, particularly when few examples are available for training. Interestingly, our unsupervised approach consistently outperforms the supervised option in identifying linguistic changes, whereas the opposite is true for word meaning identification. Our findings show that pre-trained language models can effectively handle both monitoring and analysis in text, reducing the reliance on extensive annotated datasets. Instead, they can utilize existing pre-training to understand temporal or domain-specific language use or to make informed inferences from context. Our proposed techniques, coupled with a new pre-trained language model called ProtoNet, facilitate understanding and identifying linguistic changes without requiring any annotations at all. Furthermore, our results indicate that ProtoNet can accurately pin down word or sentence meanings from a minimal number of examples. Building on this finding, we thoroughly analyzed the RAM with addition for common mathematical operations and identified which of these operations can be performed efficiently in constant time.
Specifically, we established that only multiplication by a constant value can be executed quickly in constant time; in contrast, multiplication by a variable value cannot be performed rapidly in constant time.
Notably, although division by a constant value is mathematically equivalent to multiplication by the reciprocal, it cannot be executed quickly in constant time.
We further showed that division by a variable value must be executed sequentially.
Moreover, we identified that taking the square root, logarithm, exponential, or power of a variable value requires a factorization of n approximation and thus cannot be executed quickly in constant time for all values of n. Ultimately, we concluded that only a limited set of mathematical operations can be executed quickly in constant time.

To tackle the inherent data scarcity issue in personalized recommendation, we have developed a novel framework that utilizes user interaction histories to enhance the quality of recommendation models. These interaction histories, organized into user sessions, provide valuable implicit feedback and natural grouping structures. Drawing inspiration from the co-training method, our framework leverages both individual and aggregated session information for superior performance. Notably, we have designed a self-guided approach to ensure that each session learns from the others and an adaptive graph without a specific task in mind to facilitate seamless knowledge transfer between sessions. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework surpasses state-of-the-art benchmark recommender systems on real-world datasets. Furthermore, the theoretical underpinning of our method has been verified through rigorous analysis. Additionally, we have conducted rigorous empirical evaluations to confirm the efficacy of our algorithm and the importance of the proposed graph technique. These findings validate our hypothesis that session-oriented recommendation can be a powerful tool for improving recommender systems. In recent years, direct product codes and reversible product codes have gained attention due to their efficiency in correcting symmetric errors. This has led researchers to develop various variants of product codes, including reverse product codes, which offer improved error correction capabilities. Furthermore, researchers explored the use of group LCM codes as an extension of product codes, demonstrating their capability to correct a wider range of errors compared to product codes. Building upon this knowledge, this study introduces group reversible LCM codes as a generalization of group LCM codes, capable of correcting additional error patterns. By developing a standard method for encoding group reversible LCM codes and determining their minimum distances, researchers were able to evaluate their error correction capabilities. Specifically, group reversible LCM codes of size $q^6$ and $q^7$ were found to correct all errors of distance less than $q/2$ and $q$, respectively. Additionally, under certain conditions, group reversible LCM codes of size $q^5$ or larger were found to correct all errors of distance less than $q/2$. Using these results, researchers were able to create codes that can correct any $k$-error pattern, provided that $k$ is less than $q/2$, or $q$ but only occurs in at most $5$ codeword positions. Notably, this study offers the first known code capable of correcting any $7$-error pattern in addition to offering improved reversible LCM codes. Specifically, group reversible LCM codes of size $q^7$ were found to correct more error patterns compared to direct product codes of size $q^7$ and group reversible LCM codes of size $q^6$. Furthermore, researchers were able to create group reversible LCM codes using binary field $GF(q)$ for any $q$ based on polar codes, enabling the development of high-performance group reversible LCM codes. Specifically, a group reversible LCM code of size $2^7$ was constructed, which can correct every $6$-error pattern and demonstrated superior performance compared to direct product codes of the same size. Interestingly, when it comes to correcting error patterns that occur in at most $6$ positions, researchers were able to create group reversible LCM codes of size $2^7$ that could correct more error patterns compared to group reversible LCM codes of size $2^6$ and group LCM codes of size $2^7$. In one-dimensional systems with point-gap topology, topological properties remain unchanged when a point gap appears at the origin. We've found that in non-Hermitian point-topological systems, interactions between points can transfer the topological characteristics to a new point gap, resulting in the original point gap closing. This phenomenon allows for multiple pATK cycles and a broader range of topological transitions. The required interactions are strictly singular, meaning they have vanishing amplitudes, and can be realized through coupling with an auxiliary system. We've applied these concepts to the case of fermions coupled with a two-level system via a singular interaction, resulting in a topological transition in the system's wavefunctions and showing static edge entanglement that remains unaffected by system parameters. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that implementing a singular coupling with an auxiliary point gap can lead to a Hermitian system with zero-energy edge states, exhibiting a topologically nontrivial character. This is evident through a non-zero Chern number derived from a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model simulation, complete with a zero-energy localized state in real space at the edge of the system. Lastly, we've explored the dynamic responses of zero-energy edge states in pATK cycles via a spectral density analysis and discovered that edge states from interacting point gaps display a flat spectral density, distinguishing them from edge states arising from individually isolated points gaps. Our research thus shows that singular interactions can modify and control the properties of point-gap topology, facilitating a range of topological transitions. Additionally, we've found that implementing such interactions can lead to auxiliary systems that trap non-Hermitian topological properties, providing a means to preserve topological characteristics in systems that may not initially support them. These findings could enable innovative designs for non-Hermitian topological devices and provide new insights into understanding topological properties in interacting systems. Additionally, these results could be experimentally verified using extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models simulated to display topologically nontrivial characteristics. We design a novel system where $N$ participants share a secret key, and each participant selects a random $x_i$ within a predetermined range, and a related secret $y_i$ is calculated using the square of $x_i$. Participants then record their findings in publicly available channels. Our research shows that, given sufficient data points, it's impractical to deduce individual secrets ($y_i$) without knowing at least $(\frac{logN}{loglogN})^2$ participants' contributions, and we prove that this threshold is both necessary and sufficient. This achievement represents a significant advancement, as the earlier known lower bound was quadratically larger. Based on these findings, we devise an algorithm that can efficiently calculate the collective knowledge, and also present a strategy for updating existing square-based key exchange protocols. The technical foundation of our work is rooted in an unconventional application of the Freiman 4/9 theorem, along with a detailed mathematical analysis. Utilizing Petz-McLaughlin inequality, we establish a minimum bound for the collective entropy of participating participants. Additionally, we propose an innovative approach based on the Bruck- Bennett inequality to evaluate the optimal entropy growth rate. This research has potential real-world implications as the underlying theory can be applied to cryptographic systems involving multiple entities. Interestingly, the underlying theory can be applied to cryptographic systems involving multiple entities. Interestingly, these parameters can be achieved using simple random selections. Furthermore, we establish the applicability of our key exchange protocol to existing cryptographic techniques, along with presenting alternative variants of our solution. This article examines the concept of quantum objects within a non-commutative spacetime, focusing on the paradox that arises when their properties are defined, particularly in relation to position operators that fail to commute. We argue that the identity of a quantum object is inherently tied to the specific set of measurable properties that can be used to identify it. Since different measurable properties yield different identities, the notion of identity is inherently multifaceted. Furthermore, identifying a quantum object via one set of properties inevitably means excluding other possible identities based on different properties. We illustrate this point through the example of a charged particle in non-abelian gauge theory, where the accessible identities of an electron and a photon vary as they traverse a magnetic field. We conclude that the identity of a quantum object is not solely inherent but is also influenced by its environment. Moreover, the object's identity is not constant, as it can change in response to modifications in the measurable properties that are used for its identification. We propose that this dynamic nature of quantum objects is a key factor that should be considered in any attempt to resolve the paradox of their properties in a non-commutative spacetime. Ultimately, this paradox may reflect a deeper ambiguity that arises when translating the measurable properties of quantum objects into classical descriptors within a non-commutative spacetime. We suggest that this ambiguity might be a necessary aspect of working with measurable properties and is not inherently contradictory. In support of this claim, we demonstrate that similar arguments about identity can be applied to the derivatives of an object's properties, which represents a more fundamental description. However, this does not alter the fact that the identification of an object's nature is a complex multifold process. We acknowledge that the object's identity is not solely a function of its properties but is also influenced by its interactions, as well as its wave-like characteristics. We propose that this inductive relationship between the object and its interactions should be seen as a multifaceted identification process. We can draw parallels between the identification of quantum objects and other concepts, such as personal identity, where interactions and measurable properties play a crucial role in determining who we are. We recognize that describing the identity of quantum objects may not suffice on its own but rather needs to be complemented by an examination of their behavior and interactions. Arabic language social media platforms are contaminated by abusive content that harasses and intimidates women. This type of online harassment has severe emotional impacts on women. In response to the need for a solution, we introduce a novel task known as Misogyny Identification and Categorization (MIC). We define misogyny as a form of abuse that targets women based on their gender. In our research, we source data from Twitter by collecting 26,919 Arabic tweets that contain misogynous content, across five distinct sub-categories. Additionally, we suggest two innovative approaches to address MIC: a non-supervised approach that measures the correlation between two disparate datasets, and a supervised task that combines text data with visual information. Our experiments reveal that the integration of visual elements enhances the system's performance, yielding the highest F1-score rates of 53.74% for MIC-quadruplet classification and 57.16% for MIC-five classification tasks. These findings demonstrate that the incorporation of visual elements can positively impact the system's performance in detecting misogynous content on Arabic social media. Our research is the first to tackle the misogynous content classification task in the Arabic language, enabling regulators and platform operators to develop more effective content moderation policies and systems. Meanwhile, the availability of this data can be utilized by developers in creating more accurate online abuse detection and prevention systems. In doing so, we aim to inspire researchers to address this critical issue, proposing a new direction for online research. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/aliPashai/MisogyniyDetection.

We introduce an effective approach to develop robust controllers in complex systems prone to failures and changes. Our method employs a stochastic search algorithm within a simplified model of the target system. This controller is designed to mitigate the effects of disruptions and adapt to shifting system conditions without requiring precise knowledge of those changes. We demonstrate the long-term benefits of our approach by showing that over an infinite number of trials, the controlled system converges towards stable dynamics similar to those of the optimal solution. The benefits of our method are illustrated through examples involving the stabilization of an unstable system and generating resilient flight trajectories. Unlike existing techniques that focus on preparing robust controllers for anticipated threats, our approach prepares controllers for a wide range of potential threats. This contrasts with traditional methods that typically focus on preparing controllers for anticipated threats. Furthermore, our approach yields a more straightforward and less cumbersome controller design compared to other adaptive methods. Valuable insights into the performance of our approach are obtained by analyzing the similarities between our algorithm's performance and optimal solutions in terms of stability and performance. These results are facilitated by a novel theoretical framework that establishes a connection between simplified model-based policy search and optimal robust control. This framework, which we refer to as the 'robust policy gap', provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between search algorithms and optimal robust controllers. Furthermore, we prove that the effects of imperfect modelling and dynamic changes on controlled systems can be quantitatively measured and standardized. Our work offers a comprehensive theoretical framework that can be applied to develop robust controllers and estimate the effects of uncertainty on controlled systems. Developed in collaboration between modeling and control experts from the aerospace and automation industries, our approach offers a novel and practical long-term solution for developing resilient systems. decentralized computation schemes. Our proposed encoding, analyzed within a probabilistic tensor framework, reveals itself as an extension of the encodings used in compressed sensing and randomized matrix techniques. By developing a universal decoded computation scheme based on our developed encodings, we demonstrate that the specific graph constructions previously required in decentralized computation settings can be eliminated. Our generalized framework is exemplified through a universal computation scheme for multiple access channels with cognitive radio constraints. This new approach enables a centralized encoder to produce a publicly available encoded signal and multiple privately obtained encodings, all generated from a common set of random variables. This leads to several key findings: (1) we can always find a common rate for all receivers such that secure communication is possible; (2) this rate is equal to the diversity order of the multi-access channel; and (3) it matches the capacity of the multi-access channel when it exhibits high secrecy capacity. Our novel scheme achieves this by allowing the receivers to perfectly recover any message that is below the common rate without needing knowledge of the other receivers' encodings. Additionally, our multi-access code can be optimized to reach the highest possible rate by using an iterative water-filling algorithm. This rate is shown to be the best possible for this specific scenario as it reaches the secrecy capacity when it can be achieved. Our approach allows both the encoder and receivers to use any available information without needing to know the other's strategies, thus enabling a decentralized computation scheme that is fully compatible with cached encoded data. Furthermore, our framework reduces the required encodings in the cache and receivers by using a probabilistic tensor analysis, thus resulting in a more compact encoded signal than previously known methods. We have shown that the Scott framework of PCF can be constructed within a type theory that is based on univalence, and we have formulated the basic operations of PCF in terms of types and families of types. By doing so, we have provided a way to interpret PCF within any univalent type theory that includes a universe of propositions, and we have demonstrated that the interpreted PCF retains the same equality semantics as the original Scott PCF. This involves mapping PCF's recursion, precursors, and Boolean operations to their corresponding type-theoretic equivalents, and we have established that two PCF expressions are equal in the interpreted type theory if and only if they are equal in the original Scott PCF. Furthermore, we have shown that the interpreted PCF recursion scheme satisfies the fundamental equality with respect to uniqueness. We have also placed the interpreted PCF construction within a specific instance of the Scott framework's universal property, and we have established that the types and families of types constructed by PCF's recursion scheme are a universal model for domains in univalent type theory. This provides a connection between the interpreted PCF and the latter part of the Scott framework's development. Throughout our construction, we have paid close attention to ensuring that the types and families of types constructed by PCF's recursion scheme are compatible with equality, and we have made extensive use of the univalence hypothesis in the form of propositional univalence. By doing so, we have provided a way to understand the equality semantics of PCF as a fundamental aspect of the interpreted type theory, and we have shown that the equality semantics of PCF is a corollary of the univalence hypothesis. Finally, we have established that the results of our construction also apply to bi-recursive PCF, and that the interpreted bi-recursive PCF retains the same equality semantics as the original bi-recursive PCF. The latter result relies on biunivalence. The development of this paper has been conducted entirely within the unfolding of univalent type theory, and we have provided detailed proofs of each of the key results in the accompanying notes. Furthermore, Martino Ciotti has provided an additional set of proof scripts that demonstrate the interpreted PCF construction within univalent type theory. The interpreted PCF construction that we have presented has been shown to be compatible with a range of different univalent type theories, including but not limited to Coq, Agda, and CaRast. We analyze the spaces of Eisenstein series for $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, specifically those generated by the standard parabolic subgroups $P_n$. According to the Rallis-Sayed strategy, expressing an Eisenstein series as an intertwining operator application of a ScherKerind type Eisenstein series of $GL(m, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ involves a determinant expression. An initial computation by Rallis-Sayed concerning the characters of determinants of Eisenstein series enabled the elimination of certain linear factors, leaving behind a product of specific Eisenstein series and a generalised Gauss sum. Building upon this computation, we are able to eliminate the Gauss sum completely, thereby simplifying the expression. Notably, the resulting formula contains a novel product of Eisenstein series attached to a certain symmetric matrix, calculated via an alternate method. This calculation, although related to a result by Gurevich, requires an independent proof which we provide. Additionally, our strategy involves a related but novel calculation concerning the Eisenstein series associated with the cyclic shift parabolic subgroup, also providing an independent proof of a related result by Gurevich. The resulting formula contains a product of Eisenstein series and a finite product of Dirichlet L-functions. The proof utilises an important observation by Friedlander-Klassen concerning the characters of certain powers of Dirichlet L-functions. The key to our proof lies in an initial combinatorial calculation which we had initially intended to prove via an unrelated strategy, instead revealing a significant generalised result. The significance of this problem and its solutions lies in their connection to stabilising components of the asymptotic tempering system on the generic irreducible representations of $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. The latter is an ongoing project by Gurevich. The solutions provided therefore also contribute to this project. The solutions rely on an important technique, namely the calculation of certain "generalised Gauss sums", which had hitherto been unresolved. The critical technical innovation which enables the calculation is the generalised result which emerges from the novel combinatorial calculation mentioned above. This critical innovation can be applied not just to the solutions presented, but also to a related but distinct problem, namely the calculation of certain "Gauss sums" which had hitherto been unresolved. The solutions present two distinct strategies, which we label the 'Gurevich strategy' and the 'Rallis-Sayed strategy'.

This research introduces a novel algorithmic approach to text summarization, which employs graph theory to select key sentences that comprise summaries with precise boundaries. The proposed method generates two graphs - a similarity graph and a relevance graph. The similarity graph calculates weights for each sentence pair based on their similarity, whereas the relevance graph determines a sentence's relevance to a cluster of similar sentences. By integrating these graphs, the algorithm identifies sentences with high relevance and low similarity, effectively avoiding redundant information in the summary. Furthermore, the algorithm optimizes summary length by incorporating a diversity score, which measures diversity within and between graphs. The results demonstrate that this method surpasses established benchmarks in the NEWS and CNN/DailyMail datasets. Nevertheless, the method falls short in capturing sentence overlaps and is susceptible to graph partitioning challenges. Potential enhancements are suggested to address these limitations. The proposed method is comparable to graph-based summarization approaches and surpasses several leading deep learning architectures in terms of performance. Consequently, this algorithm has significant implications for text summarization tasks. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/pulkitd Jayant/Graph-based-Text-Summarization. Additionally, pre-computed vertex weights and summary lengths have been uploaded to the GitHub repository for convenient use. The proposed algorithm is grounded in the theory of graph theory and machine learning, making it an essential contribution in these domains. Specifically, this research addresses the long-standing challenge of bounding summary length, a topic extensively explored in graph-based summarization literature. The theoretical framework provides a precise analysis and proves the algorithm's optimality. Moreover, the algorithm is scalable and efficient, processing large datasets quickly even in high-resource computational environments. The integration of similarity and relevance graphs offers a comprehensive understanding, surpassing the capabilities of established graph-based summarization methods. The proposed algorithm is empirically evaluated and demonstrates superior performance on datasets, including NEWS and CNN/DailyMail. A special case involves the instance of maximal distinctness, and we establish the conditions under which this occurrence takes place. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the concept of distinctness for meromorphic mappings and the intersection properties of the associated analytic subsets within the complex manifold. Additionally, we prove a new theorem that addresses the conditions for a meromorphic mapping to achieve its maximal distinctness when viewed from a particular domain within the manifold. Importantly, this work rectifies an error present in a prior study by Chow. A significant consequence of our research is the establishment of a connection between the complex manifold's holomorphic embeddings and the meromorphic mappings exhibiting maximal distinctness. In this paper, we present a novel approach to determine the non-degenerate components of a polynomial system based on its solutions that exhibit signature zero. This methodology hinges on the application of signature coefficients to filter out degenerate solutions, a concept inspired by Laitinen's work. By incorporating an improved encoding scheme, we increase the likelihood of obtaining signature zero solutions, thereby calculating the non-degenerate components of a polynomial system. A case study using the solutions of a family of polynomial systems, known as the ordinary singularities of a rational map, demonstrates the efficacy of our proposed method. Furthermore, we provide a command set based on the Mathematica language to facilitate the calculation of non-degenerate components via signature-oriented techniques. This includes an implementation of the signature filtering mechanism, an algorithm for identifying non-degenerate components, and a utility for graphing these components in 2D and 3D systems. An interactive 3D visualization was also developed using Mathematica to aid in visualizing non-degenerate components in three-dimensional systems. We evaluate the immediate photon production at low momentum in Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV using ATLAS and PHENIX data along with theoretical simulations. The comparative analysis across different system sizes shows that the produced photons are predominantly a result of final-state interactions. The measured counts are found to be 3.6% (ATLAS) and 4.8% (PHENIX) of total hadronic counts within the specified momentum range, which is in line with the theoretical prediction of 4.1% (ATLAS) and 5.1% (PHENIX). The theoretical estimate itself comprises a component stemming from final-state interactions (4.0% ATLAS, 4.8% PHENIX) and another stemming from prompt photons (0.7% ATLAS, 0.3% PHENIX). The relative impact of final-state interactions increases with decreasing momentum and system size, which corresponds with the theoretical prediction. The measured counts at low momentum (less than 1 GeV) exhibit a statistical relative uncertainty of 4.2% (ATLAS, in-plane), 4.6% (ATLAS, out-of-plane), 4.5% (PHENIX, in-plane), and 5.2% (PHENIX, out-of-plane). The relative uncertainty in momentum measurement is the dominant factor in the counting uncertainty. The detected photons at low momentum are found to be uniformly distributed throughout the entire rapidity range. Additionally, the counts at low momentum (less than 2 GeV) are found to be insensitive to geometric effects observed in Cu$+$Cu and Au$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV, which corresponds with the theoretical prediction. Furthermore, the observed geometric issue at low momentum (less than 1 GeV) is found to be smaller than 1%, which is beyond the current measurement precision. The measured counts at low momentum exhibit a correlation with centrality and are found to be insensitive to $\Delta \eta$ coverage changes between 2 and 6 units. Nonetheless, the counts at low momentum remain below the 2% threshold for $\Delta \eta$ coverage changes. In conclusion, the immediate photon production at low momentum in Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV is found to be in agreement with the theoretical prediction, which attributes 4.1% (ATLAS) and 5.1% (PHENIX) of total hadronic counts to final-state interactions. As these particles interact with light emitted from the neutron star, they cool down, losing energy, leading some to speculate that a substantial amount of energy is lost through the creation of a shell of high gamma-ray emission. Researchers have suggested that such gamma-ray-emitting shells could be used to locate unseen pulsar wind nebulae, which in turn could help in estimating the total number of pulsars in the galaxy. Climate classification is a critical task that has far-reaching implications for regional economic and social development. Accurate climate classification is essential for agricultural production planning and can significantly impact economic outcomes. Existing classification methods are often restricted to specific regions, such as the CKD dataset which only covers Scotland's 13 climatic regions. We have developed a new dataset consisting of 3500 CKD dataset images enhanced with synthetic data, representing the full range of Scotland's climate diversity. This dataset spans 26 classes, offering a more detailed and comprehensive climate classification system. Our experiments comparing various Convolutional Neural Network architectures, such as MobileNetV2, ResNet50, and SqueezeNet, reveal that MobileNetV2 outperforms the other models, achieving a 2-3% higher accuracy. One major issue with neural network training is getting stuck in local minima.
The gradient descent method, used widely in machine learning, has a significant
shortcoming: it often falls back on suboptimal solutions. To address this, a
new global optimization technique known as the all-optimal gradient descent
(OGD) algorithm was developed. OGD outperforms standard gradient descent in
many cases. Building on OGD's principles, a new algorithm, the organic OGD
(OGC), was created to mimic natural evolution by selecting and combining the
most successful training runs. When applied to existing OGD models, the OGC
resulted in superior performance and generalizability. Notably, the OGC achieved
encouraging outcomes even when trained with much smaller dataset sizes. 
Importantly, the OGC trainined models displayed improved resistance to
overfitting. Notably, a notable benefit of the OGC was its increased efficiency
since training sessions were reduced in both the training and testing phases. 
To better understand the behavior of the OGC, a new theoretical framework was
developed based on the concept of "organicism," which explains how the OGC's
selection and combination of training sessions could lead to generalization. 
The selected parameter ranges for the ogd-mat algorithms were analyzed using
this new theoretical framework. Furthermore, a new metric, the organicity
score, was created to gauge the generalization capabilities of the OGD algorithms.
Lastly, a comprehensive study was conducted using public datasets to evaluate
the effectiveness of the OGC. To facilitate future research, the code used to
develop the OGC was made openly available on GitHub.

This paper presents an innovative technique for controlling a group of drones to capture dynamic scenes while maintaining a stable structure and avoiding collisions among the drones. We propose a novel approach to achieve decision-based black-box adversarial example protection, where the model itself remains unchanged and only undergoes modified preprocessing. For instances not affected by adversarial inputs, our method exhibits equivalent performance to the original model. Conversely, adverse inputs detected in the training phase are effectively thwarted in the testing phase. Notably, this method's effectiveness transpires without any overlap between the training and testing datasets, showcasing zero-shot knowledge transfer. Moreover, our method's benefits extend to models constructed with different architectures, demonstrating cross-model generalization. We thoroughly evaluate our approach on three distinct models, showcasing its superiority to existing methods. Under a limited threat scenario, our method can be replicated with $O(N\log N)$ time complexity, where $N$ denotes the dataset's size. Nonetheless, we outline potential optimizations and propose additional controls to achieve comparable processing times with deep learning models of a similar size. For example, when applying co-OHL to a simple navigation task using a virtual character, we found that the agent successfully learned to navigate through a virtual maze using information transferred from another agent that had trained its depth sensor modality.

Research on Programmable Additive Combinatoric (PAC) codes has increased due to their versatile properties. Unlike traditional error-correcting codes, PAC codes don't rely on the Hamming distance but instead utilize the minimum weight of a code that resists additive noise. Measuring PAC code performance involves complex computations, making some analysis methods impractical. As a result, researchers often resort to theoretical assessments or straightforward numerical evaluations. This study focuses on developing numerical techniques to analyze PAC codes, including a novel approach to determine the minimum weight that provides accurate decoding performance and another method to identify the noise tolerance based on a code's auto-correlation properties. Additionally, we propose a heuristic to identify the optimal PAC code decoder and investigate the impact of parity-check matrices in PAC code construction. Our findings are demonstrated through numerical studies, with the source code available upon request. We introduce a novel task that involves utilizing sequential depth sensors to track the physical interactions between objects in a real-world setting. Current approaches to analyzing hand-object interactions are typically confined to controlled conditions, such as through the use of rendered data based on 3D models. In contrast, we aim to analyze and rebuild the hand-object interactions captured within a real-world point cloud series, as demonstrated in the KITTI hand dataset. To accomplish this, we develop a network called HandRebuild that not only estimates the pose of hand-object groups but also generates a point cloud reconstruction of each frame, thereby enabling the monitoring of hand-object interactions and their dissemination through video supplementation. HandRebuild employs a multi-stage approach, beginning with a detection network that identifies hand-object interactions and their poses, before being refined and reconstructed through engagement poses estimated by a kinematics-based network called HandKinematics. To accommodate the KITTI hand dataset's outdoor environment, we introduce an auxiliary network called RegGround, which uses ground information to further refine the reconstruction of hand-object interactions. Through testing using KITTI hand dataset, we find that HandRebuild outperforms other state-of-the-art hand and hand-object reconstruction methods. Additionally, we analyze and rebuild the hand-object interactions captured within the KITTI hand dataset. Our work is the first to monitor and rebuild the hand-object interactions captured within a real-world setting, thereby paving the way for future research in this area. The proposed approach also holds significant practical applications in areas such as human-action analysis and robotic arms, as well as robust vision systems. The transmission properties of dissipative optical grids were initially found to follow a high degree of anisotropy and associated unusual statistics in number distributions, characterized by a logarithmic correction. This was later attributed to dimerized optical grid structures, which facilitate coherent momentum transfer between grid layers. For non-dissipative grids, anisotropy is absent, and associated statistical behaviors do not apply. However, in the presence of dissipation, anisotropy emerges, and associated statistical behaviors are observed. We extend our previous studies to examine laser-cooled particle flows through dissipative optical grids, focusing on unusual statistical properties and associated logarithmic corrections. For non-dissipative grids, a standard Poisson distribution is expected, and most properties can be explained through convolutions of independent, uniformly distributed particle velocities. Nonetheless, in the presence of dissipation, anisotropy introduces novel logarithmically corrected distributions, affecting overall distribution shapes and resulting asymptotic behaviors. Notably, when considering time-resolved transmission measurements, effects of dissipation and anisotropy are reflected in the distribution of time intervals between successive particles transmitted through the grid, where a logarithmic correction becomes apparent. This leads to distinct domain behaviors in the distribution, which stem from velocity spread caused by photon-phonon absorption and can be mitigated by a high absorption rate. Moreover, effects of anisotropy are observable in the transmission's angular distribution, where unusual statistics manifest as a logarithmically corrected power-law behavior. This, in turn, Triggers research into the origin of such statistics in nature. Lastly, in an attempt to connect our findings with real-world phenomena, we discuss the implications of our studies for understanding the distribution of alpha particles and their potential connection to the phenomenon of Jordan blocks in particle dynamics. This potentially allows the application of similar approaches to analyze data from particle physics experiments, particularly in relation to alpha decay. This new perspective on particle dynamics may provide novel insights into the transmission of particles through grids and their associated statistical behaviors. This study is a stepping stone towards a broader investigation of unusual statistical behaviors in nature, where a detailed analysis of particle trajectories and associated logarithmically corrected distributions will be examined in detail. This includes the transmission of particles through grids, as well as real-world phenomena like alpha decay and pure collisions. The presence of quantum nature in molecules is crucial but its influence often diminishes rapidly as molecules interact with their surroundings. This research investigates the extent of quantum behavior in tiny clusters of sulfuric acid and water using variational perturbation theory, a method that considers the interaction with surrounding environment at the quantum level. To put this phenomenon into perspective, the study looks at the properties of 2-amino-sulfuric acid and compares them with those of hemiammonic acid, both systems having a shared sulfuric acid core but differing in their surrounding environments. Our results indicate that the quantum nature of these small clusters is more substantial than anticipated, with significant zero-point contributions. Furthermore, the research reveals that the clusters' quantum properties are largely governed by their first solvation shell. Interestingly, the study finds that increasing the cluster size through the addition of water molecules actually reduces the impact of quantum behavior. Another key discovery is that the clusters' quantum behavior exhibits strong parity-dependent variations. To confirm these theoretical predictions, a series of experiments known as ion solvation thermodynamics were designed to investigate the relationship between quantum behavior and temperature. These experiments aim to answer a pressing question in physical chemistry - can we detect the influence of quantum behavior in chemical reactions at room temperature? This framework is akin to the Riesz compactification of operators. Building on this structure, we establish the concept of compactification of operator pairs and spaces of group-equivariant non-dilating operators. This new framework exhibits surprisingly rich and intricate properties. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the compactification of operator pairs yields a compact topological space. This research provides a systematic approach to extending existing operator theoretic results to the Riesz compactification. The Holographic Thermal Hall Effect exhibits unique properties in quantum systems far from equilibrium, which defy intuitive explanations. By connecting this phenomenon to gravitational analogues, we demonstrate that conventional methods, such as Einstein relations and fluctuation-dissipation theories, fall short. Specifically, we show that Holographic Thermal Hall currents do not adhere to proportional relationships with temperature gradients and that heat fluctuations do not necessarily mirror dissipation rates. Furthermore, we derive distinct criteria for generating Hall currents and eliminating charge gaps, highlighting the distinct behaviors driven by boundary drives and internal spin charges. Lastly, we explore the system's response to multiple drives and discuss the implications for understanding complex, driven quantum systems. Please see arXiv:2205.10042 for the full discussion.

During training, complex models are simplified by neural networks, an inherent characteristic that has sparked significant debate. We observed that this simplification results from a network's tendency to avoid complex architectures and discovered that geometric complexity in neural networks acts as a robust regulator, surpassing other factors such as parameter counting. We found that the topology of a network significantly influences its training dynamics and predicted the optimal topology for a given task, leveraging insights gained from studying the geometric properties of artificial neural networks. These results offer a new perspective on the interplay between neural network complexity and its ability to generalize, empowering the development of more effective and generalized models. Additionally, we provided a method for constructing geometrically simple and generalizable Neural Networks, called GeoNN. The effectiveness of GeoNN was evaluated in two real-world scenarios - resource-limited edge devices and generalization challenges - and demonstrated a notable improvement in test performance compared to the top-rated models, achieving a 14.7% and 13.5% increase in accuracy respectively. Notably, GeoNN also increased the efficient deployment of models on tiny edge devices by a substantial 48.3%, further solidifying the value of geometric complexity in neural networks. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate the creation of more practical and effective neural networks, empowering innovative applications on resource-constrained edge devices. A new approach for determining the four $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay differential distributions' Wilson coefficients is developed. These Wilson coefficients are key indicators of new physics influencing semileptonic $B$ meson decays. Due to difficulties in fitting Wilson coefficients to data, researchers have proposed testing them directly using decay distributions. However, this requires overcoming difficulties in parameter correlations. Our method utilizes decay distributions that are insensitive to hadronic uncertainties and can be used with present data to constrain Wilson coefficients. An example fit with Wilson coefficients alone is demonstrated, and we find that further data will significantly improve our understanding of these coefficients. To this end, we provide fit functions for all relevant decay distributions. Additionally, we considered the impact of new physics in leptoquark representations on our results, and we find that several scenarios can significantly improve our likelihood fit. A new standard model prediction for the $q^2$ distribution around its minimum is also provided. This work represents an extension of a public code package for $B$ meson decays that includes new functions for decay distributions. Furthermore, we provide publicly available fits that include Wilson coefficients from our new approach, in addition to standard Wilson coefficients. This code package, named ${\rm GeoBayes}$, can be downloaded at bayesfit.hep.qcd/. A visual representation of the Wilson coefficient correlations is also available at bayesfit.hep.qcd/wilson_coefficients.html. Lastly, the Wilson coefficient correlations are stored in the database wilson.hep.qcd. This work is also described in a review article, and a shorter summary is available at bayesfit.hep.qcd. The increasing demand for automatic music composition evaluation systems necessitates robust datasets, leading to a significant challenge in creating synthetic data through composition mutation and enhancement processes. This research focuses on exploring enhancement techniques in a neural transformer framework to facilitate compositional modifications. Initially, a neural composer based on transformer is trained to model a reference audio track, followed by the application of three distinct enhancement techniques to produce varied outputs. The objective function of composition evaluation is then applied to each enhanced output. Furthermore, a novel mutation technique grounded in probability theory is proposed to address issues in synthetic data generation for multiple evaluation criteria. The findings demonstrate that the employed enhancement strategies can efficiently mutate compositions according to different objectives. Additionally, the developed method exhibits potential in creating synthetic data with relevant variety for composition evaluation. The code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/jbwhittal/MusicCE.

related to the behavior of empirical processes and the properties of high-dimensional
data. Ultimately, the review investigates the practical applications of
marginal dependence frameworks in estimating a broader class of joint laws and
the resulting implications for high-dimensional statistics. Research opportunities
related to empirical dependence frameworks are also identified. This research was

A probabilistic model, known as the prospect theory mobilility model, is developed to account for dynamic changes in social mobility across successive generations through the application of forward-looking utility theory. Within this framework, a non-interactive game is established where young adults make educational choices based on their personal characteristics, which in turn influence their children's opportunities, also taking into consideration their children's educational choices. By applying probabilistic models to both parents, the theory's ability to predict stability in social mobility patterns is tested, particularly when incorporating uncertainty into the system. The use of a stability measure in social mobility, known as the Matyas theorem, is utilized to evaluate the influence of parental prospects on their children's outcomes, revealing a significant yet reduced effect size. Ultimately, the integration of uncertainty, specifically the likelihood of intergenerational mobility, is found to be crucial in determining the replicability of social mobility patterns. By employing Bayesian estimation techniques on data from the Census of 1980, the results support the use of probabilistic models in social mobility research rather than traditional approaches. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the likelihood of intergenerational mobility is higher when both parents have stable prospects compared to either parent having uncertain prospects. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the precision of intergenerational mobility is higher when both parents have stable prospects compared to either parent having uncertain prospects. By factoring in the impacts of prospects and their distributions, the study provides a more comprehensive understanding of social mobility dynamics. Lastly, the research highlights potential areas of further investigation, including the application of the mobility model to data sets containing repeated observations of the same individuals or families. Potential beneficiaries of this study include policymakers, social scientists, and other scholars in the field. Furthermore, the data and related code are publicly accessible for duplication purposes. Based on these findings, the study makes significant contributions to theoretical and empirical knowledge in the field. Firstly, the study offers a novel theoretical approach that integrates the concepts of dynamic social mobility and the distribution of prospects. Secondly, the results provide a thorough and literature-based justification for using probabilistic models in social mobility research. Thirdly, the data and related code are publicly disclosed for the first time. Lastly, the study provides empirical evidence and a new method of estimating the likelihood of intergenerational mobility. Additionally, the study raises crucial questions and hints at potential areas of further investigation. Using magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we study how hot gas within galaxy clusters responds to cooling and how it may recover through thermal equilibrium with the surrounding environment. Our model incorporates non-ideal processes such as radiative cooling, magnetic fields and thermal conduction. We've identified two key factors that influence gas behavior: the strength of magnetic fields and the conditions at the cluster's boundaries. Groups with weak magnetic fields experience a severe 'fizzling out' effect when the surrounding hot gas cools, whereas those with strong magnetic fields can maintain their gas density. At the cluster edges, a thermal conduction effect occurs that can lead to gas expansion, relieving pressure and potentially preventing 'fizzling out', unless magnetic fields are present to restrict this movement. These findings indicate that magnetic fields and thermal conduction play a crucial role in shaping the internal dynamics and growth of galaxy clusters. As a result of our research, we've developed equations that can predict the rate at which gas density changes based on these processes. Our analysis lays the groundwork for a revised model that may improve the current self-similar model used to describe galaxy clusters. Additionally, our research could help to clarify discrepancies between simulations and observations of galaxy clusters, particularly regarding size and luminosity. Our predicted timescales for gas changes align with supernova feedback timescales, suggesting a potential connection between active feedback and the development of galaxy clusters. Finally, our research implies that magnetic fields and cooling processes may have contributed to the formation of large-scale galaxy structures through similar mechanisms. Our simulations also suggest that thermal conduction could serve as a bridge between kinetic and hydrodynamic descriptions of the gas dynamics. To further investigate these processes, we recommend running simulations with larger numerical resolutions and varied physical initial conditions. To achieve this, we've developed a cloud formation method that can help develop galaxy clusters. Its application is described in a companion paper. For the purpose of this research, we've developed 27 simulation sets that can be accessed at https://simdb.sharcnet.ca/. A total of 654 simulations based on different galaxy cluster models are included in the SimDB. This research explores the feasibility of synthesizing speech without prior knowledge of linguistic structure, using only auditory-based unit representations obtained directly from audio data. In the absence of textual information, the transcription process is crucial to developing a meaningful representation for voice synthesis. Unlike standard transcription methods that utilize existing knowledge of language, this study leverages a data-driven approach to identify and define the boundaries of acoustic units and generate a sequence of transcriptions that can be used to create a neural voice model. By employing a range of acoustic and perceptual metrics, including salience, rhythm, and intonation, the proposed method is comparable to state-of-the-art transcription techniques based on acoustic units. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the proposed transcriptions can be utilized to create a neural voice model for synthesis, although the generated speech exhibits a limited sentence length capacity due to the lack of additional linguistic structure. To evaluate the synthesized speech, a subjective listening test is conducted, revealing ratings comparable to those obtained from human data and a deep learning-based system that assumes knowledge of linguistic structure. Crucially, this study shows that the synthesized speech obtained from the proposed method is capable of conveying the long-term rhythmic and intonational characteristics essential to natural speech. Importantly, the proposed approach does not require a transcription error rate to train the voice model, making it suitable for domains like sign language synthesis. Additionally, this study provides an implementation detail that enables the long-term rhythmic and intonational characteristics to be learned gradually over extended periods, analogous to human language acquisition. Ultimately, this research showcases that voice synthesis is feasible without prior knowledge of linguistic structure and that the resulting speech can be comparable to human-level speech in terms of naturalness. To facilitate the replication of this study's findings, the proposed method, along with the implemented code and acquired acoustic units, are made publicly available. Furthermore, this study's proposed transcription-based approach can be utilized to improve existing speech synthesis models that assume knowledge of linguistic structure. In particular, this study demonstrates that the proposed method can be employed to enhance deep learning-based voice models by incorporating a transcription-based representation of acoustic units, thereby expanding the synthesizable sentence length capacity while maintaining naturalness. To validate the effectiveness of this training method, a listening test is conducted, revealing improved ratings for the synthesized speech obtained from the modified model. Optimization plays a vital role in motion planning for autonomous vehicles. The underlying convex optimization problems often become complex and intractable due to issues like missing or imperfect convexity in sensor data, which necessitates relaxation techniques to yield computationally feasible solutions. However, without specific problem structures, parameterized complexity reductions are generally difficult to achieve. Toward this end, a new framework incorporates linked convex optimization and data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations to address this challenge. A convex model is created from non-convex sensor data using McCormick envelopes and then optimized in a sequence of connected convex problems. To speed up computation, each optimization stage can take advantage of data-driven and problem-specific properties to reduce the problem's dimensionality. This method is successfully tested on autonomous vehicle motion planning tasks using both simulated and real datasets. Compared to existing approaches, this novel strategy delivers better quality solutions with significantly less computational time. With further advancements, this technique has the potential to be used in a variety of optimization-driven autonomous applications. A related video can be found here: https://youtu.be/kX-0fP7OgTo. We examine the properties of quantum states that can be transformed into others under the constraints of probabilistic manipulation, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the basic principles of quantum state manipulation. We began by revisiting the fundamental theorem regarding the minimum success rate required to convert one quantum state into another via sequential measurements and subsequent replenishment. Our analysis reveals that this success rate is always influenced by the maximum overlap between the two states, demonstrating that it cannot drop below a certain threshold as the overlap increases. We also show that when two states have an overlap of one, the success rate must be at least fifty percent, a finding that can be easily verified through simple examples. Furthermore, we established that when the overlap between two states is zero, the success rate cannot be less than fifty percent. Additionally, we proved that when the dimension of one pure state is much larger than the other, the success rate must be at least fifty percent. We also showed that when one state is a mixture of another, the success rate must be at least fifty percent under specific conditions. Finally, we established that when the success rate is less than fifty percent, the diameter of the sets of achievable probabilities for both states must be greater than or equal to fifty percent. We view this latter finding as particularly significant because it represents a previously overlooked constraint on quantum state manipulation. We also discovered that when the success rate is less than fifty percent and the target state is pure, the sets of achievable probabilities for both states must grow larger as the overlap between them increases. Furthermore, we established that when one state is a mixture of another and the success rate is less than fifty percent, the sets of achievable probabilities for both states must become more dissimilar, or larger in diameter, as the overlap between them increases. We also show that when the success rate is less than fifty percent and the target state is a mixture, the sets of achievable probabilities for both states must become more dissimilar, or larger in diameter, as the overlap between them increases. Finally, we developed a conjecture based on these findings, stating that the sets of achievable probabilities for both states must always be more dissimilar, or larger in diameter, as the overlap between them increases, a phenomenon we believe to be a fundamental aspect of quantum state manipulation. In our research paper, we address the challenge of decentralized learning over graphs by leveraging diversity between local data distributions. Using a theoretical framework that accounts for distributional variations and communication constraints, we develop a robust optimization framework for DR-DSGD, a decentralized stochastic gradient descent method. We rigorously prove that our approach is capable of achieving a balance between communication efficiency and performance robustness. Through experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that DR-DSGD significantly enhances robustness while only marginally increasing communication costs compared to the standard DSGD method. Furthermore, DR-DSGD outperforms existing robust methods, such as DR-DQN and Stabilized-DSD, by a substantial margin when data distributions significantly differ. Notably, our method exhibits superior communication efficiency and robustness compared to centralized baselines, thereby verifying its efficacy in practical decentralized learning scenarios. Ultimately, DR-DSGD emerges as a versatile and performant method for stabilization in decentralized learning applications. For further information, refer to our research paper at arXiv, ID: arXiv-2109.10691. Additionally, our implementation details and additional results are available online at dr-dsgd.github.io.
