We investigate how the units and scales of light-matter interactions are affected when adjusting the strength and duration of optical drives in first-principles tight-binding models. By using a fixed profile to drive the optical excitation, we demonstrate the invariance of results for key light-matter interaction parameters regardless of the drive's shape, provided they reach the same high intensity level. This implies a general validity of this invariance for any light-matter interaction scenario reaching such a high intensity level. To further confirm this, we develop a new semi-analytical approach, approximating the electronic dynamics and allowing for the calculation of light-matter coupling constants directly from first-principles models without the need for a specific drive profile. This method yields results consistent with those obtained using more traditional approaches. We evaluate the invariance of light-matter interactions for a silicon material based on a high-density starting state and achieve a high level of precision for the bulk band structure and exciton properties. This allows us to calculate accurately the exciton volume of a silicon bulk, despite limitations in our model which only captures vertical excitations. Additionally, we find that while the exciton radius and coupling constants may change significantly as optical excitation intensify, the overall pattern of this change is consistent across different types of tight-binding models and represents an inherent property of the material itself. Finally, we establish a relationship between the weak and strong optical excitation limits of light-matter parameter definitions and validate a general correspondence between first-principles tight-binding models and phenomenological Peierls models. Throughout our research, we provide clear explanations of complex theoretical concepts and the development of new methods and tools to facilitate the calculation of light-matter coupling constants and exciton properties in complex materials based on first-principles models. These include novel variations of the Bethe-Saunders-Lancaster approach and a general method for calculating the charge density and current profiles of ground and excited states. Additionally, we create and make available a comprehensive software package, called TBAEM, which is based on a tight-binding model to simulate electron matter interactions and enable the calculation of light-matter coupling constants and exciton properties in complex materials. This software includes a number of novel algorithms and representations of tight-binding model sub-lattices that we developed to facilitate the simulation of light-matter interactions and the reconstruction of charge and current profiles. These include, for instance, the eBB and eCC profiles, which allow us to model the interaction between electrons and their spatial relationships in a more precise way

The Cauchy distribution, characterized by a single parameter known as the location parameter, can be used to model data that follows an asymmetrical, bell-shaped pattern. This paper assumes that we have a set of independent data points that follow a Cauchy distribution with unknown parameters. We are tasked with constructing intervals that capture a specified percentage of the data, as well as scoring functions to quantify coverage errors. Traditional methods for achieving this goal are based on assuming a common distribution for the data, whereas the proposed approach integrates Bayesian and frequentist ideas to develop wide-range distributional regression estimators. These estimators utilize a scoring function that incorporates both a frequentist and a Bayesian component. Focusing on the most efficient scoring function, we demonstrate its asymptotic vanishing behavior. We also explore the use of the wide-range distributional regression interval method, revealing that it can produce intervals with nearly perfect coverage up to the sample size's power. This method is comparable to a Bayesian approach, but is more robust and doesn't rely on the specification of prior distribution. Prior work by Chandra et al. (2013) considered a related problem and found that classical methods are unable to produce intervals with specified coverage up to the sample size's power. In contrast, we show that by integrating Bayesian and frequentist ideas, we can achieve this goal. Additionally, we define a scoring function for the data's scale parameter, resulting in a quantity that can be used as a measure of the data's dispersion. We provide an asymptotic justification for this measure, as well as a simple way to calculate it. Furthermore, we establish that it captures the data's variability, producing a value that is unique to the data and is preserved under common data transformations. This paper is a extension of a previous work, specifically: Chandra, R., Roy, S., and Chakrabarty, R. (2013). Bayesian and frequentist integration based interval methods for the Cauchy distribution, Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference, Vol. 192, pp. 102-114. Additionally, this paper has been published in the journal: Journal of Statistical Theory and Testing, Vol. 24, No. 2, 2020. (formerly known as Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference).

A new statistical approach is developed for estimating the required sample size in basket trials that study multiple subgroups within a single trial. This approach utilizes Bayesian methods to incorporate information across various subgroups in the trial. A simulation study compares this approach with traditional methods that assess each subgroup independently. The results show that our approach can significantly reduce the needed sample size by up to 40%, without compromising the overall Type I error rate, by sharing information between subgroups. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable to different clinical trial designs and scenarios. Examples illustrating the practical application of our approach are also provided. Keywords: Basket trials, Bayesian sample size estimation, Subgroup analysis.

To achieve high precision in motion control, it's essential to consider slight variations in system parameters that can affect performance. This work addresses such performance issues by utilizing linear parameter-varying models to create advanced control strategies. These control methods are designed to adaptively adjust parameters in real-time, making them particularly useful for motion control applications. This study evaluates the effectiveness of two cutting-edge control techniques: full-scale predictive control and sequential loop shutting, which are compared with a conventional predictive control method. To facilitate comparison, the study recovers a linear model from an LPV system and demonstrates that full-scale predictive control can be efficiently replaced by the sequential loop shutting technique, resulting in significant computational savings without compromising performance. This replacement is shown to be feasible in both simulation and real-world tests using a high-precision motion platform. The resulting implementation is completed using the open-source LPV Toolbox for MATLAB. To further optimize the control algorithm, the study incorporates time-scheduling techniques, which are shown to be instrumental in enhancing system performance and reducing computational costs. To validate the proposed approach, the study involves two parts: a simulation-based assessment and a real-world test involving a high-precision motion platform. The test reveals that the proposed modification results in a substantial reduction in computational costs without compromising system performance. To facilitate comparison, the study involves two metrics: the computational cost and the actuator positioning error. The results show that full-scale predictive control and sequential loop shutting lead to identical performance in terms of error, while the sequential loop shutting technique offers significantly better computational efficiency. Based on these findings, the study recommends sequential loop shutting as the preferred control strategy due to its superior performance and computational efficiency. This work is expected to contribute to the development of advanced control algorithms for motion control applications. We introduce a innovative deep learning approach dedicated to aligning partial human body scans. The task is critical but poses significant challenges for machine learning algorithms due to partial scan visibility, varying visibility levels, and ambiguous interpretations without contextual information. Our network addresses these complexities by focusing solely on aligning visible body parts while incorporating internal references within each scan to enhance its representations. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through rigorous experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets, which showcase superior results relative to existing state-of-the-art methods. The code and dataset used in this research are openly accessible at https://github.com/JDing2015/PRNet.

In this context, the $D^*$ density functions are determined by solving this equation, which facilitates a deeper understanding of the meson's internal structure. To extend this approach, we apply it to the $D^*_s$ meson, which is then compared to existing data and theoretical results. Additionally, we re-evaluate the form factors $D^*\to D\gamma$ and $D^*_s\to D_s\gamma$. To do this, we compute the electromagnetic current matrix element using a three-body scattering Bethe-Salpeter amplitude, which is then related to a finite momentum interval by a continuous function. This enables us to express the form factors as functions of a single variable for specific momentum cases. Moreover, we find that our form factor results align with the light-cone sum rules prediction. To evaluate the reliability of our form factor outcomes, we also calculate the direct and transverse components of the electromagnetic current within the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons as functions of the momentum ratio $x$. These components, along with the longitudinal component, are found through the projection of the Bethe-Salpeter wavefunction. Notably, the direct and transverse components then contribute to the hadronic parton distribution functions of $D$ and $D_s$ mesons, which are also determined in this research. Finally, to further verify the validity of our approach, we compared the obtained density functions and form factors with those reported in the literature using a kernel-defined Bethe-Salpeter equation and lattice QCD data. While our results are consistent with these sources, minor discrepancies are observed which can be attributed to differences in approach or the incorporation of lattice QCD data. To bring our results in line with lattice QCD data, we would need to incorporate lattice QCD corrections to the density functions and form factors. This would require modifying the Bethe-Salpeter wavefunction in accordance with lattice QCD rules. By doing this, we are confident that our results will be in agreement with lattice QCD data. To conclude, we have successfully applied a Bethe-Salpeter framework in conjunction with wave patterns to obtain density functions and form factors, which have been validated through comparisons to various sources. Through cyclic training, the Cycle-GAN learns to segment the dataset into equal parts based on distinct visual features, effectively creating a dataset replication function. Predicting future actions of individuals is crucial for numerous applications in social sciences. Existing models, including those using state and action embeddings, often assume direct mapping of states to actions, which is impractical given the vast potential actions and contextual influences on decisions. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel approach that uses a radial basis function to map state and social context to a joint action-space feature space. This representation enables the learning of complex decision processes. Complemented by a feature mapping LSTM network, our model synthesizes state and context features to produce a probabilistic distribution of future actions. We evaluate our approach on the NUSPMDS dataset, achieving superior results compared to existing action prediction methods. Additionally, we provide a theoretical justification for our feature mapping strategy by establishing an upper bound on the distortion of our feature mapping function. Experimental results demonstrate that our model systematically outperforms baseline methods across various context lengths. The code for our model is available on GitHub. Experimental findings reveal that our feature mapping method exhibits more efficient generalization compared to a motion prediction model utilizing a self-organizing map. Specifically, our approach performs 57% better in terms of generalization than the motion prediction model. Notably, incorporating a context-aware feature mapping function further enhances our model's action prediction capabilities by 23%. To better comprehend this event, a detailed physical model incorporating all observed UV optical emissions has been developed. Utilizing the MAGIUS Monte Carlo atmosphere model, a comprehensive pre-flare brightness inventory was created, accounting for all extraterrestrial optical emissions. Subsequently, a one-dimensional radiative transfer code was employed to determine the necessary hydrogen and helium line opacities, followed by the integration of these components into a semi-empirical model of the UV optical spectrum, which was then combined with observational data to refine the measurements. Furthermore, both numerical models have been utilized to define the physical characteristics of the enormous flare that occurred on September 16, 2004, observed through the FERMI Gamma Burst Monitor, as well as the huge X-ray eruption detected by the MAXI telescope on March 11, 2019. These model applications demonstrate that both events can be accurately explained by the same underlying physical processes. Additionally, the potential occurrence of comparable events that could impact radio communications and device operations is being considered. Based on the maximum rate of energy released observed during the 1985 flare, as well as the carrier densities of major flares, including the Carrington Event and the 1909, November 5 Geophysical Institute Magnetogram Network event, it appears that this event ranks second in terms of energy release rate and third in terms of total energy release. Importantly, the frequencies of such huge events observed from Earth may significantly exceed previously estimated values. Given that these events could have a detrimental impact on Earth's infrastructure and communications systems, as seen during the Carrington Event, it is crucial to understand the likelihood of their occurrence. Neural network-based point cloud representation learning has been successful, but a significant issue has been identified, namely the loss of local geometry during the transformation (translation, rotation, and scaling) applied to representational data. This has been found to particularly affect representational data in the early stages of training, resulting in inaccurate reconstruction of the original point cloud. A novel method called Transformation-Dependent Smoothing (TPS) has been proposed to mitigate this issue. TPS involves adjusting the smoothing process in representational data based on the effect of transformation on its class. Experimentation has been conducted on three benchmark datasets (Shapenet, ModelNet10, and ModelNet40) using a network designed to learn point cloud representations, and the results have shown that TPS significantly improves the accuracy of the model across all datasets, averaging a 4.64% improvement, making it a crucial step in the representational data generation process. Additionally, the implementation of TPS is easily integratable into existing representation learning methods, yielding improved accuracy with no additional computational cost. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/TPS. Additionally, the performance of the model can be evaluated using the provided benchmark datasets, along with the generated point clouds during training and the dataset statistics at https://github.com/asharakeh/TPSBenchmark. A video demonstrating the effectiveness of the model is available at https://youtu.be/6kx4UkYHhHk. The research findings provide insights into the local geometry issues prevalent in neural point cloud representation learning, as well as the accuracy of the model across various configuration settings. It has been observed through experimentation that the issue of local geometry loss is prevalent across multiple datasets and geometric transformation types, and arises during both the training and testing phases. Additionally, the accuracy of the model heavily depends on the effect of the transformation on its class, which has been confirmed through analysis of the dataset labels. Based on these research findings, a new smoothing process, TPS, has been developed to mitigate the issue of local geometry loss and enhance the accuracy of point cloud representation learning. The accuracy of the model was evaluated across multiple benchmark datasets, and the results show that TPS significantly improves the accuracy of the model, reaching as high as 98.57% on ModelNet40. The research also identifies potential areas for further improvement, including the extension of TPS to other types of geometric transformations and its application to other machine learning methods for point cloud representation. ALOHA offers simple implementation but poor efficiency in high-demand scenarios, whereas CSMA optimizes bandwidth usage, though at the cost of greater computational complexity. Our development of a continuous-time Markov chain for CSMA reveals that, unlike traditional ALOHA, this method exhibits throughput capacity when closely scrutinized. To facilitate reliable digital communication in high-risk radar environments, we propose a new QoS-based ALOHA technique that incorporates adaptive coding theories. This allows radar networks to achieve nearly optimal efficiency while maintaining high data integrity. A key data privacy solution has also been introduced to safeguard sensitive radar data, utilizing an untrusted ALOHA helper node that assists the main node while preventing eavesdropping by a third party. This scheme successfully balances data transmission efficiency and security, solving a long-negotiated trade-off. Comprehensive simulations validate our analytical findings, offering clear visual representation of ALOHA performance across varying parameter values. Moreover, a thorough comparison of ALOHA and CSMA is provided, along with specific recommendations for designing practical radar networks that prioritize both efficiency and security. Detailed step-by-step implementation details for both ALOHA and CSMA are included, enabling direct emulation of our proposed schemes. Two-photon experiments, particularly in the form of Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, have become essential for examining the fundamental properties of quantum mechanics. A key area of investigation involves studying how linked photons interact through various processes. A notable focus lies on exploring the consequences of entangled photon absorption via two-photon autoionization. To gain insight into the properties of quantum mechanics, researchers evaluate how this phenomenon influences outcomes measured in Hong-Ou-Mandel interference setups. To this end, various models are employed to describe the optical response of quantum systems, with the spectral width being defined as a measure of how quickly these systems respond. According to the Wigner function perspective, the FROG second-order correlation signal distribution can be seen as encapsulating the entire Wigner function at a specific time point, which suggests a complete quantum description via correlation function-based approach. Through this approach, the quantum connection between the optical response and the correlation signal becomes evident, enabling the utilization of the optical spectrum for forecasting the correlation signal shape. It is demonstrated that the entangled photon absorption via two-photon autoionization leaves its distinct mark on the predicted correlation signal, which can be further utilized by experimentally determining the lifetime related to this phenomenon. Moreover, the predicted correlation signal associated with two-photon autoionization provides an accurate means of detecting this phenomenon in experiments. To verify these predictions, a quantum optical model is compared with the semi-classical approach, which indicates that the distinct quantum features of the correlation signal can be revealed even under semi-classical conditions. Consequently, the absorption via two-photon autoionization can be correctly modelled using the semi-classical approach, which implies that this phenomenon can be reliably detected through Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiments. Based on these predictions, the necessary experimental conditions for observing this phenomenon in a practical setting can be determined. Specifically, the required experimentally-induced spectral width can be determined by cross-correlating the optical and SFG signals. It is found that this detection method is feasible using current technology. A concise summary of the discovered relationships and the relevant recommendations for experimental procedures in detecting entangled photon absorption via two-photon autoionization through Hong-Ou-Mandel interference are provided. Additionally, potential future research directions focusing on quantum-connected photon absorption and coherent phenomena are identified and outlined. To facilitate these studies, the implemented approaches and related mathematical models are described in further detail. A comprehensive mathematical framework is provided to support these research areas. Several complex quantum systems are examined to illustrate the universal applicability of the distinct spectral evaluations

This paper investigates the impact of ground noise on noise robust automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. We demonstrate that ground noise can adversely affect the performance of ASR systems, leading to decreased word error rates. Furthermore, we identify three key factors contributing to this decline: ground noise intensity, microphone directivity, and system training method. To better understand these factors, we conducted experiments using a NeAR-SYS platform with human operators, subjecting it to various noise levels. Notably, we found that ground noise in real-world settings can harm ASR performance, contradicting previous indoor noise studies, which showed little reduction in performance. We hope these findings will guide researchers in developing noise-resistant ASR technology. We also provide suggestions for system developers to mitigate ground noise's detrimental effect, including using an external microphone, adjusting the camera's position, using head movements to adjust the microphone's angle, or implementing beamforming techniques. Prior research had suggested that this composition might be a superconductor at pressures exceeding 20 GPa, with temperatures below 10 K. However, our calculations indicate that it is actually not possible for the HfB4 compound, which contains 37.5% H, 75% B, and 87.5% H, to be a superconductor at such pressures. Specifically, we found that as the number of H atoms in these compounds decreases, their cohesion and resistance to compression increase, while their ability to be bound by electrons also increases. The $k$-Center problem is an NP-hard issue where we pick $k$ facilities to minimize the greatest distance from these facilities to the $k$ hottest locations. Researchers proposed a $2$-doubling approximation algorithm for this problem, which leads to an approximately $2$-factor increase in distance. We studied this problem further under a specific point-process model, resulting in a $4/3$-factor increase in distance. This new method outperforms the previous $2$-doubling approach by approximately $0.47$ factors. We studied an analogous problem in which customers' connection rates changed over time, known as the $k$-Center $w$-Offpeak problem. Utilizing a modified version of the Fourier transform, we developed a $3/2$-factor increase algorithm for this problem. This method was initially based on a $2$-factor increase provided by Epstein and Mathieu. We further analyzed this problem under a multi-facility setting, resulting in a $4/3$-factor increase in distance. This research was initially based on a $2$-factor increase provided by Ananth and Svitkina. We studied an analogous problem in which customers' connection rates were constant but facilities' placement rates changed over time, known as the $w$-Offpeak $k$-Server problem. Utilizing a Fourier series, we developed a $2$-factor increase algorithm for this problem. This method was previously known to be at least $1.83$ times larger than the optimal solution. Additionally, we studied a multi-facility version of this problem, resulting in a $4/3$-factor increase in distance. This research was previously known to be at least $2$ times larger than the optimal solution. Lastly, we studied a $k$-Server problem where customers' connection rates were constant, revealing a connection between this problem and the Matroid Intersection problem. We demonstrated that combining $k$-Center and $k$-Server algorithms results in a $2$-factor increase in distance. This research was previously known to be at least $1.5$ times larger than the optimal solution. Furthermore, we studied a $k$-Center problem in which customers' connection rates changed over time, combining it with the Minimum Spanning Tree problem, resulting in a $7/3$-factor increase in distance. This research was previously known to be at least $4$ times larger than the optimal solution.

This research paper explores the challenges of accurately processing polynomial linear systems that contain errors randomly distributed across coefficients. Even without noise, such systems often have multiple solutions to choose from, and this diversity poses an obstacle in finding the optimal solution that maximizes polynomial values at specific points. In the presence of random errors, this task becomes even more complicated, and current algorithms fall short of taking advantage of available randomness to find the best solution. Our research provides an evaluation of the minimum amount of randomness needed to solve this problem accurately and proposes a new early cessation technique that helps speed up computation. These findings are validated through comprehensive experiments. Additionally, we investigated the effect of random errors on solving polynomial linear systems and established a criterion for determining when it becomes more efficient to restart the computation rather than refining the current solution further. These insights are grounded in statistical analysis. Furthermore, we studied the effect of random errors on solving a crucial subproblem in accelerating polynomial linear systems that contain errors randomly distributed across coefficients. Our research provides the theoretical foundations for solving this problem under controlled randomness and establishes a statistical analysis of its accuracy. These findings led to the development of the \matryoshka algorithm, which uses the early cessation technique and stochastic errors to speed up solving polynomial linear systems efficiently. This insight is further utilized in the matryoshka package, a software tool that accelerates solving polynomial linear systems under certain conditions. These developments are based on comprehensive numerical experiments and theoretical analysis. Our research sets two new limits on the amount of randomness needed to solve polynomial linear systems under controlled conditions, providing precise mathematical demonstrations. These findings resolve an open problem and reveal an underappreciated connection between solving polynomial linear systems and testing whether a matrix has full rank. Moreover, our research provides an evaluation of the effectiveness of various algorithms for solving polynomial linear systems under certain conditions, and these insights are also useful for improving the performance of algorithms that solve a related problem. Finally, our research offers two new techniques, early cessation and switching, which significantly accelerate solving polynomial linear systems under certain conditions, and these algorithms are already showing promising results in practice. These techniques are grounded in comprehensive numerical experiments and theoretical analysis. Moreover, our research provides precise mathematical demonstrations that these techniques are efficient and accurate. These algorithms are further utilized in the matryoshka package, a software tool that accelerates solving polynomial linear systems under certain conditions. We propose a novel concept called parity-symmetry-guarded bundle emission, which occurs when bundle states at the edge of a topological insulator interact with multiple light modes, displaying multiple bundle edges that can be triggered by a single photon. This interaction results in a highly entangled photonic state, spanning multiple channels, and their findings demonstrate that bundle emission is possible without requiring edge states to be in proximity to light. This theory, harnessing the properties of a topological insulator, offers a potential pathway for generating highly secure multi-photon entanglement for quantum communication. Simulation data has been provided.

We suggest a highly sensitive method to detect ultralight bosonic dark matter, which uses the inelastic scattering of this matter with a rigid lattice material for detection. Due to the rigid lattice structure, the primary Scattering signal would arise from a lower frequency mode than that of the photon mode we use for detection, which is in the infrared to radio frequency range. To extract the dark matter quasiparticle mass from this scattering signal, we would use a technique similar to neutron star radii probe, known as 'probes', by utilizing multiple materials with different lattice structures. This method is particularly effective for masses in the picogram range and has the potential to be tested using current technology. Furthermore, this method could be improved by using pulsed laser systems to enhance its sensitivity, which would allow it to detect dark matter even if it has masses slightly higher than the maximum allowable mass as per Planck observations. Finally, we propose that the revised method from the Hanbury Brown and Twyson tests, combined with the radio frequency signal detection via magnetic field detection in a superconducting material such as niobium, could be an effective way to detect dark matter in the picogram range through the revised RCT method. Additionally, we propose that the radio frequency signal detection in a material such as tellurium could be an effective way to detect dark matter in the femtogram range through the HF version of the RCT method. Finally, we outline that the proposed method could be improved upon by using an actual tellurium target in the setup. Lastly, we establish that the primary challenge associated with implementing the RCT method would be the requirement to know the specific litterature used for the production of the material whose dark matter quasiparticle mass we are attempting to measure. If this challenge can be overcome, we propose that the RCT method could be an effective way to detect dark matter in the femtogram range. This paper explores the mathematical concept of basis pursuit in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. It presents two distinct methods for solving basis pursuit problems even when the design matrix has restricted information. This research provides a detailed analysis of the solutions generated by these methods, including proof of the existence and uniqueness of the solutions. This outcome has significant practical implications, demonstrating that in certain situations, basis pursuit problems can have a singular solution. This research is a continuation of the authors' previous work on regularization methods for basis pursuit in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. P4 has become the standard language for programming Network Functions Forwarding Tables. Despite its versatility, implementing the subset required by production-grade switch firmware can be challenging due to language restrictions. This paper introduces an open-source compiler framework that translates programs from the P4v16 subset to RMT (Reconfigurable Match-Table) switches. Our compilation method focuses on forwarding table instructions and is adaptable to various target platforms. This paper also outlines an algorithm to optimize tables for reduced memory usage on target switches. We conducted comprehensive testing to validate our compiler framework and examined its performance across different scenarios. Furthermore, we investigated the compiler's efficiency in converting programs and assessed its quality through a series of experiments. This study demonstrates that our compiler framework can effectively convert P4 programs to code compatible with RMT switches, and we found that using our compiler and fixed-size tables can significantly reduce compilation time while still achieving low table memory usage. Differential privacy has become the standard for protecting sensitive information in machine learning research. A training process known as federated learning, which utilizes decentralized datasets, has been successfully integrated with differential privacy. However, the alignment of justice and differential privacy reveals discrepancies. Specifically, the differential privacy framework treats all individuals equally, whereas justice requires the consideration of disproportionate impacts on vulnerable groups. Furthermore, differential privacy may inadvertently exacerbate vulnerabilities during federated learning. This work reexamines the foundational relationships between justice and differential privacy, focusing on distributed training, to identify opportunities for modifying the differential privacy paradigm and developing new evaluation criteria that promote justice. Specifically, we investigate whether justice can be achieved through utilization of utilization weights in federated learning, which can be incorporated into the differential privacy framework. If this incorporation is not possible, we analyze alternative strategies for integrating justice and differential privacy during distributed training. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that employing utilization weights during federated learning results in data owners who are not vulnerable becoming the primary contributors to the aggregation process. Moreover, theoretical findings indicate that utilizing these weights enables the achievement of a form of justice, while maintaining a comparable level of generalization. When such weights are not applicable, we propose a novel evaluation criterion that balances the differential privacy violations experienced by data owners, with a focus on mitigating vulnerabilities. This evaluation criterion is grounded in the concept of justice and does not require compromising on differential privacy. Finally, we discuss potential research directions on integrating justice and differential privacy during distributed training. This work is currently available on arXiv. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/yokohai/fed-diff. The federated learning experiments can be replicated by visiting https://federatedscope.org/fedlearn/diff. Note that differential privacy is utilized in federated learning to safeguard aggregated gradients instead of the datasets themselves. Therefore, the source code may appear to violate differential privacy, but this is a methodology-driven artifact that does not compromise differential privacy. Similarly, the source code involves downloading some public datasets, which may not be compliant with differential privacy due to justice considerations. However, these datasets are not used during federated learning, and the experiments can be replicated without downloading these datasets. Furthermore, we have removed some code that is not compliant with differential privacy when performing localized training. The current version of the code only supports decentralized, stochastic, and localized training processes that are compatible with differential privacy. This paper proposes a new computational approach to estimating thermal states and entropy in statistical systems, employing a method of nested sampling originally developed for cosmological applications. By leveraging this approach, we simulate the behavior of the Ising and Poincaré planes across various temperatures and magnetic field strengths. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to apply the method to observables beyond the energy, highlighting the calculation of thermal entropy as a significant benefit. Notably, we observe that thermal entropy derived from nested sampling exhibits a second-order phase-transition behavior, in line with the predictions of third-order thermodynamic perturbation theory. In addition, we investigate the extent of statistical fluctuations in our estimates and discover that they diminish in proportion to the square of the number of spins simulated. In light of these outcomes, we argue that nested sampling provides a valuable tool for computational thermodynamics, allowing physicists to study thermodynamic phenomena that are challenging to model mathematically. In particular, we believe that this method could be valuable in analyzing lattice gauge theories and other extended-field models that are difficult to tackle analytically. In these contexts, we anticipate that nested sampling will prove to be a versatile and indispensable tool. Furthermore, we observe that combining our approach with high-order perturbation theory and other analytical techniques can help mitigate the long computational times associated with nested sampling, particularly at very low temperatures. In this regard, we find that the methods of Refs. [arXiv:2104.13831] and [arXiv:2006.14167] can be very effective in this regard. In the future, we intend to integrate these techniques in order to create a highly efficient, dynamically-adaptable simulation tool for computational thermodynamics. In this regard, we propose the name "NanoTS" for this code. In the present work, we have primarily used NanoTS to verify its performance and accuracy on a range of well-studied statistical systems. Researchers have shown an increasing interest in Distributed Denial-of-Service attacks, which overwhelm networks by flooding them with traffic from multiple sources. To identify whether a device is involved in a DDoS attack, we propose NBcoded, a lightweight classifier based on Naive Bayes and Binary Classifier. NBcoded distinguishes ordinary devices from those participating in a DDoS attack by analyzing packet characteristics such as size, header patterns, and timing. For our initial study, we selected two key features: packet size and interarrival time. An NB-coded model is trained on remote sensors, then tested on resource-constrained IoT devices, which are confirmed to be involved in a DDoS attack. Our experimental results indicate that NBcoded achieves high accuracy in identifying DDoS participants, with a substantial reduction in computational overhead. Currently, NBcoded can detect attacks with accuracy rates of 95.3% for packet size and 96.1% for interarrival time, with a computational complexity of 0.0003 MIPS. This pioneering work lays the foundation for a fast, efficient, and reliable DDoS detection system. Future developments will focus on enhancing feature selection and training using deeper Binary Encoder. Additionally, we aim to integrate NBcoded into standard network operating systems. Our long-term goal is to develop a robust and robust DDoS detection system utilizing NBcoded. This work is the initial step in that goal. For a finite solvable group G, the number of Sylow p-subgroups in G is a multiple of p,
with the exact power depending on certain properties of G. In this paper, we determine the
minimum value of the exponent in the expression for the total number of Sylow p-subgroups in
G, thereby providing an expansion of the previous result by Knuth and Chan. Furthermore, we
establish a generalized inequality for the total number of subgroups in G that are isomorphic
to D_{2^n} for any positive integer n. Additionally, we find a lower bound for the total number
of subgroups in G that are isomorphic to D_{p-1}, specifically for odd prime p. Lastly, we
investigate the minimal generating sets of semidirect products in the form V \direct M, where V
is a noncyclic abelian group of order p^2 and M is a cyclic group of order p-1. In the process,
we identify the subgroups of V that can be expressed as a semidirect product in the aforementioned
form and establish a connection between the minimal generating sets of such groups and those
of D_{p-1}. This research aims to expand our understanding of the total number of subgroups in a
finite solvable group G, specifically its noncyclic subgroups of certain orders. Through our
investigations, we strive to identify the intrinsic characteristics of G that influence its subgroups.

This paper presents a novel computational method for tracing the movement of living organisms in video footage. The proposed method boasts higher accuracy compared to existing methods, particularly in cases where the target organism undergoes partial occlusion. We have meticulously evaluated our approach against four prevalent human motion analysis methods and discovered that it surpasses their performance by a significant margin. Our state-of-the-art algorithm has been successfully applied to analyze the movement of capuchin monkeys during a feeding interaction, showcasing its efficacy. The proposed method is comprised of a systematic framework that automates the detection, tracking, and representation of biological movements within video sequences. Comprehensive experimental outcomes validate its superiority. The detailed findings of our research are accessible through a dedicated open-source platform. Furthermore, we have accurately quantified the outcomes and provided transparent recommendations for future research in a scholarly report. Research has shown that quantum methods, particularly quantum-inspired classical algorithms, can efficiently handle complex optimization problems. This has led to interest in applying these algorithms to classic systems. This study investigates whether such algorithms can improve conventional methods used to optimize the performance of gas networks. By utilizing the quantum-inspired MaxCut algorithm, researchers were able to surpass the Lagrangian Relaxation method, a standard approach employed in the industry. Further analysis revealed that this quantum-inspired algorithm avoided getting stuck in local optima, a common issue with conventional methods. However, it also exhibited high computational complexity. Ultimately, the findings suggest that hybrid approaches, combining quantum-inspired and conventional techniques, could offer valuable insights for optimizing energy networks. Potential future applications involve developing more advanced quantum algorithms capable of handling additional constraints naturally, something that classical methods often struggle with. Nevertheless, the potential breakthroughs prompted this research to examine the feasibility of using quantum-inspired algorithms to improve gas network efficiency. Interestingly, the study discovered that implementing such algorithms was more complicated than expected, mainly due to technical difficulties with optimization problems that arise from the relaxed linearization of the network. Despite these challenges, the research was able to develop a modified version of the MaxCut algorithm, tailored to the specific requirements of gas network optimization, and demonstrate its superior performance when compared to the standard Lagrangian Relaxation method. Moreover, the research found that the MaxCut algorithm was resistant to getting stuck in local optima, a characteristic that, while beneficial, also contributed to its high computational complexity. Recent advancements in applying information theory to physics have made significant progress, yet the underlying physical concepts still rely heavily on information theory. This thesis proposes that physics should be derived solely from physics, without relying on information theory. To achieve this, we must redefine the fundamental aspects of physics. This study introduces new globally applicable postulates for physics, including a non-classical version of the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle. Notably, the revised principle does not contain the Gaussian factor commonly found in existing formulations. By reinterpreting Pauli's Exclusion Principle in relation to this new uncertainty principle, we arrive at a novel expression for the Exclusion Principle, thereby eliminating the need for wave functions to apply the principle. Additionally, we demonstrate that the existing wave function formalism is actually a by-product of the proposed uncertainty principle and can be derived from it. However, we also identify a contradiction between our formulation of the Exclusion Principle and the existing many-body formalism, indicating an inconsistency in physics. To resolve this inconsistency, we propose a correction to the Exclusion Principle, which has far-reaching implications for our understanding of physics. Furthermore, we derive a generalised expression for the Exclusion Principle that applies across all domains of physics. This study also explores the concepts of entanglement and non-locality, revealing that they are not distinct phenomena after all. To test our proposals, we demonstrate that the revised uncertainty principle, combined with existing electromagnetism and the de Broglie hypothesis, can accurately calculate the electron g-factor. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the new perspectives and discoveries that arise from the proposed derivation of physics. Additionally, we clarify any potential ambiguities in the study. Lastly, we introduce an innovative research strategy known as 'Revealism' to expedite the advancement of physics. This approach involves an in-depth examination of existing physical concepts, followed by a straightforward and efficient re-interpretation of these concepts to arrive at novel and innovative results. This study illustrates the 'Revealism' method in action. We also discuss how 'Revealism' can be applied to strengthen our findings and accelerate the development of physics. Furthermore, we utilise 'Revealism' to identify an unrecognised aspect of Einstein's photoelectric effect experiment. To facilitate the development of revealism, we also derive key mathematical operations, including a novel form of division, without using information theory. This study exploits the potential of revealism. Lastly, we discuss the profound implications of deriveism, a method for which this study is an exemplary case.

A key objective in evolving optimal solutions is to maximize phenotypic variety, as it enhances discovery and prevents solutions from becoming too specialized. Currently, there is a disjoint between optimization techniques and methods for measuring variety, potentially hindering its utilization in multi-objective optimization. This study connects phenotypic variety with multi-objective optimization by analyzing its benefits and identifying its inherent limitations. Variety in phenotypes offers advantages such as comprehensive understanding, improved generalization, and enhanced innovative potential. However, maximizing variety may not always lead to optimal solutions and sometimes compromises exist between variety and performance. This study introduces new approaches for evaluating phenotypic variety and demonstrates their application in multi-objective optimization problems. The proposed methods are compared with established variety measurement methods and used to guide an evolutionary algorithm aimed at optimizing solutions in both single and multi-objective problems while considering variety as an additional objective. The study confirms the significance of phenotypic variety but also identifies its potential limitations and suggests future research directions. We've demonstrated in a stable matching framework that when preferences are nonlinear and distinct in a three-dimensional stable housemates problem, a key condition results. A formal condition, known as "not much destruction", reveals that in instances where a stable and optimal solution exists, it's possible to achieve the maximum destruction value of zero. This condition's name stems from a concept where the minimum value of the sum of individual preference levels for each house member is close to the maximum destruction value. A key finding related to this concept is that the maximum destruction value of zero is synonymous with the existence of both stable and optimal solutions. This concept is further extended to apply to situations with larger numbers of agents and houses. A one-to-one correspondence between the destruction value of a given situation and a particular ideal house configuration allows us to establish a boundary for the maximum destruction value in situations with larger numbers of agents and houses. This ideal house configuration, known as a "chain", holds key importance in understanding this concept. A formal examination of the destruction value of each possible house configuration, known as a "box", and its relationship to the destruction value of a "hook", a house configuration with one member having lower preference levels than the others, reveals that a stable and optimal solution always exists for situations with a "hook" configuration. A discovery related to this concept is that in situations with a "hook", it's always possible to achieve a destruction value of zero. This concept is further extended to explore the relationship between the destruction value of a given situation and its topological properties. A one-to-one correspondence between the destruction value of each possible house configuration and its Euler tour allows us to establish a boundary for the maximum destruction value in situations with larger numbers of agents and houses. A key finding related to this concept is that both a stable and optimal solution, as well as an efficient time-complexity for finding it, can be achieved if the given situation's Euler tour is a chain. A demonstration by means of a drawn illustration shows that in situations with a house configuration that resembles a "star", it's not necessarily the case that a stable and optimal solution is equivalent to an optimal solution. This concept is further extended to explore the relationship between the destruction value of each possible house configuration and its topological properties in multi-dimensional situations. A key finding related to this concept is that both a stable and optimal solution, as well as an efficient time-complexity for finding it, can be achieved if the given situation's Euler tour does not contain any inner-point cross-over. Lastly, we have explored how these electron-phonon interactions can be utilized to generate optically measurable valley polarization. To strike a balance between optimizing performance and ensuring robustness against different environments, we developed a set of evaluation criteria called 'wealthy attributes.' These attributes help analyze the characteristics of models based on various criteria such as data they use to train, location where they are trained, and the level of difficulty in their tasks. We utilized wealthy attributes to investigate the performance of models on different clustering tasks and found that certain models exhibit a 'targeted optimization,' where they heavily invest in features that provide performance boosts but also make them more prone to disruptions from unexpected changes. We found that using wealthy attributes to evaluate models during training facilitates generalized optimization. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jmnystrom/wealthy. 

Keywords: Generalization, Performance optimization, Rich attributes,

When conducting meta-analyses with mixed effects, such as when modeling random effects in binary or continuous outcome data with correlated variances, the frequentist closed testing procedure can be quite conservative. This leads to a low rate of rejection under a true null hypothesis, but also results in overly broad confidence intervals when they are calculated. To address this issue, we developed new estimators for combining random effects in bivariate mixed models, focusing specifically on the case of correlated variances. These new estimators have the desired asymptotic properties and perform well even when the sample sizes are relatively small. To evaluate their effectiveness, we conducted simulations using a wide range of data distributions and transfer functions, comparing our new estimators to existing methods. The results show that they offer significant improvements, producing shorter and more efficient confidence intervals while maintaining the desired level of accuracy. To test these new estimators in practical applications, we also developed a comprehensive R package, metaanomb. Notably, similar discrepancies have been found in other lattice QCD-based calculations and black tensor perturbation theory predictions for gravitational waves in the early universe, indicating a common physical phenomenon underlying these findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the first solution occurs at $n=2$ with solutions $a=7, b=3$. To generalize these findings, we developed a method for creating entire families of solutions for any $n$ greater than 2, revealing that the solutions for each $n$ are linked to the irreducible polynomial $x^2+(1-d)z=b^2$ over the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{7})$ for certain values of $d$ and $z$. We establish two techniques for translating probabilistic lambda terms into classical proofs and investigate their relationship. One method involves probabilistic lambda terms being mapped to propositional proof nets by ignoring random variables, a technique similar to the propagation of probabilities to determinism in the probabilistic propositional lambda calculus. This mapping is shown to be surjective. An alternative method, inspired by the lifting of intuitionistic proofs to classical proofs in the Curry-Howard framework, involves lifting probabilistic lambda terms to deterministic lambda terms while preserving the notion of equality. It is demonstrated that every deterministic lambda term can be obtained through either of these methods, revealing a connection between the probabilistic and deterministic lambda calculi. Furthermore, by interpreting these lifting techniques as notions of implication, a corresponding notion of probabilistic predicate logic emerges, offering a fundamental way to understand probability within a logical framework. An equivalent mapping between probabilistic lambda terms and classical proof nets was previously proposed by Ehrhard and Ghini, which we show to be a specific realisation of our more general connection between the probabilistic and deterministic lambda calculi. We conclude by examining the key similarities and differences between our development and the previous work. Specifically, while our study is grounded in a purely functional interpretation, Ehrhard and Ghini's work draws on a more general understanding of the probabilistic lambda calculus as a directed complete partial order, which allows for a deeper mathematical analysis but results in a more complex and distributional understanding of probability. Ultimately, we believe that both interpretations have value and can provide distinct perspectives on the logic of probability. 

Keywords: Probabilistic lambda calculus, Probabilistic predicate logic, Proof nets, Lifting, Curry-Howard interpretation.

A new approach to extending the proximal gradient algorithm is developed for solving optimization problems involving a smooth data-driven loss function and constraints defined by measurement-equipped smooth manifolds. Building on a theoretical framework for parametric surface identification through proximal gradient techniques, the method utilizes gradient measurements to compute local normal vectors to each point in the surface. It is theoretically proven that an iterative algorithm combining these vectors with incremental gradient measurements achieves a geometric convergence rate of O(1/k), even when the surface is partially unknown or poorly estimated. The method is empirically validated on several experimental platforms, including a 2D batch identification problem and a 3D real-time 2D camera calibration application. The resulting surface points can be used as initialization for Newton-type optimization methods, and a novel adaptation of the Quasi-Newton algorithm is proposed for efficiently optimizing the loss function along the surface curves when the Hessian is partially unknown. The algorithms' designs are motivated by the challenge of minimizing the number of expensive Hessian measurements, and a theoretical analysis of the Quasi-Newton method's convergence rate is provided under the assumption that the Hessian remains relatively constant over small regions of the surface. The proposed algorithms are empirically validated on several applications, and their results demonstrate the benefits of combining low-complexity proximal gradient techniques with informed optimization methods to exploit knowledge about the underlying surface structure of the problem. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jmlorenz/prox-Newton-surfaces. This research aims to investigate the application of Hidden Markov Models in detecting irregularities in data. Our method involves using the output gauge probability distribution to identify abnormalities. The process begins with training a model on normal data to establish a baseline probability distribution. Next, we adjust the model's transition probabilities to match this standard distribution. The gauge probability distribution of new, unseen data is then calculated to determine its similarity to the original, training-based distribution. The similarity between these distributions is quantified as a similarity score, which informs our decision to classify the data as normal or abnormal. The research compares three methods for classifying data as normal or abnormal: one-class, two-class, and minority class detection. The experiments were conducted using HMM models implemented in Keras with Gaussian and Mixed-Dimensional Gauges. The outcomes demonstrate that using an adjusted transition probability of one can effectively identify abnormalities across all datasets, regardless of their size or distribution type. Furthermore, the research reveals a significant advantage of using HMMs over a Nearest Neighbor classifier and No HMM model, particularly in accurately classifying data when the datasets are imbalanced. However, it's worth noting that using an adjusted transition probability of zero resulted in poor classification outcomes. The proposed method also offers desirable results in terms of computational efficiency and classification accuracy. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, the research involves evaluating HMMs on six real-world datasets, including datasets with zero, one, two, and three classes. The outcomes of these experiments provide substantial support for using HMMs to detect irregularities in data. Based on these findings, it's recommended that HMMs be trained with a transition probability of one and used to classify data into normal or abnormal categories. The proposed method is suitable for use cases where the datasets are imbalanced and can help avoid the development of anomalies in automated systems. The research is likely to be of considerable benefit to anyone working with Hidden Markov Models, particularly in the areas of quality control and bioinformatics. The proposed approach can be effectively applied to a wide range of problems, including detecting irregularities in data, analyzing sequences, and understanding context-dependent language. The HMM-based method offers a simple and efficient means of detecting irregularities in data, requiring less data and computational resources compared to other classifier types. We analyze average field games originating from optimal control theory, where players' actions are constrained by a state-dependent constraint, leading to a counterexample demonstrating the impossibility of achieving a gentle solution in all situations. However, under the condition that the right-hand side of the continuum limit equation has a bounded Lipschitz norm, we establish the existence of a gentle solution. Furthermore, this condition can be relaxed in the case where the right-hand side of the continuum limit equation is a measure with a finite Lipschitz norm on the solution space. Notably, this property distinguishes average field games from the classical case involving a single control actor. Moreover, it is speculated that similar results could be applied to a broader class of macro models derived from microfoundation theories. Finally, the relationship between the continuum limit equation and the measure-valued solution is investigated, with a particular focus on the case where the right-hand side of the continuum limit equation is a measure with a finite Lipschitz norm. This analysis enables us to resolve an inquiry initially posed by Delarue and Rasse de Grandpremarie.

When subjected to external forces like pressure and bending, it develops elastic deformations, ultimately leading to fracture-like cracks in areas of high bending stress as predicted by theoretical models and confirmed through recent experiments. Unlike previous observations, we found fewer fractures in higher cross-linking densities and fewer fractures under stress than in air. Additionally, we observed more complex fractures under stress, which can be attributed to the greater stiffness of the raft, allowing it to withstand external forces but develop more intricate fracture patterns. This review re-examines the estimation of conditional expectation functions, a broad concept that encompasses multiple applications including growth curve analysis, function regression, and missing data imputation. Initially, the focus is on nonparametric techniques which often rely on kernel-based estimation. Notably, these estimators can be inconsistent when conditional heteroscedasticity is present, highlighting the need for more robust methods such as those proposed by Newey and Wooldridge (1993). This review also considers more recent developments in the field, driven by evolving computational capabilities and the increasing availability of high-dimensional data. As a result, novel approaches like machine learning methods and empirical Bayes estimation have emerged, which can be viewed as modern contributions to nonparametric estimation. This article aims to provide an up-to-date summary of the subject, informed by the 2019 special volume on panel data in International Statistical Review. Key topics such as time series, high-dimensional data, and missing data have been addressed. Notwithstanding the extensive existing literature, this review necessarily lacks a comprehensive treatment of every aspect, instead providing an entry-point and a synthesis of existing knowledge. Crucially, this review focuses on the theoretical underpinning of nonparametric estimation, encompassing consistent estimation and asymptotic distributions. Furthermore, it addresses context-specific challenges and outlines emerging areas of research. Ultimately, this review is intended to provide readers with a deeper understanding of nonparametric estimation of conditional expectation functions. Keywords: Empirical Bayes, Functional Bayesian Polya, Gaussian process, Imputation, Inference, Kernel, Partially observed, Regression, Replication, Variance estimation. Furthermore, we found that the direction of the magnetic field affects the heavy quark interaction by up to 10 percent. For instance, in a magnetic field of 10 Tesla, the real part of the heavy quark potential increases by about two percent when the quarks are aligned parallel to the field, as opposed to being perpendicular. We used a first-order approximation to analyze the imaginary part of the heavy quark potential, which shows that it becomes significant at lower separation distances in all directions, but particularly harsh directions. Our analysis suggests that the imaginary part could influence ground state binding energies by up to 10%. Our research also suggests that the direction of the magnetic field can impact the critical temperature of quarkonia by as much as 5%. We introduce a new framework for developing high-dimensional expansions based on covering arguments in probability theory. This framework surpasses existing methods, enabling the creation of new and intricate asymptotic results that were previously inaccessible. To illustrate the power of this framework, we will use it to establish several novel high-dimensional expansions for the probabilities of random graphs and combinatorial structures exhibiting certain properties. The underlying concept of this framework is rooted in the remarkable recent findings of Alemann-Garreti and Rossi, whose work on covering-based inequalities for the probabilities of random combinatorial structures serves as the foundational hypothesis for our proposed framework. Furthermore, we will non-trivially demonstrate the applicability of this framework by proving a new, sharp asymptotic result for the probabilities of random graphs that are k-regular and coloring-complete. This result is an extension of a prior finding of Kohlerber and Sörgel. Next, we will utilize the introduced framework to establish a novel high-dimensional expansion for the probabilities of random bipartite graphs that are k-regular and coloring-complete. The underlying concept of this result is rooted in the findings of Alemann-Garreti and Rossi, whose work is also connected to the outcomes of a poll conducted among the participants of the 2020 Probability and Combinatorics online seminar. Lastly, we will establish a novel high-dimensional expansion for the probabilities of random hypergraphs meeting specific divisibility criteria, thereby resolving an open issue first raised by Bollob's and Riordan in their work on divisible random hypergraphs. The underlying concept of this result is rooted in the coalescent random hypergraphs studied by Alemann-Garreti and Rossi. The proposed framework is an integration of ideas originally presented by Alemann-Garreti in her PhD thesis and a high-dimensional expansion framework for random graphs and combinatorial structures developed by Rossi and Kohlerber. The structure of this paper is organized such that sections 1-4 provide a comprehensive introduction to the underlying concepts and the proposed framework, whereas sections 5-8 serve as a self-contained presentation of the new high-dimensional expansions achieved through the incorporation of the introduced framework, and section 9 comprises a detailed discussion of the obtained results along with suggestions for further investigation. The appendix contains an originally presented alternative proof of a critical inequality that is an extension of a finding of Alemann-Garreti and Rossi. This paper was initially distributed as a preprint under the arXiv ID 2102.041

Our work in this paper builds on this framework, using it to study p-adic Artin modules and derive properties of both the modules themselves and the modular forms that arise from them. The LHC's lead-lead collisions at ultra-peripheral distances involve the exchange of high-energy photon and Z boson mediations, leading to forward J/psi production. Utilizing the ALICE detector's precision sensors, researchers analyzed a 0.36 microbarns dataset from 2015's Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. By leveraging the ALICE's Forward Physics Apparatus, composed of a highly inductive quartz fiber detector and a highly sensitive silicon tracker, researchers analyzed events featuring exclusive forward J/psi production. Utilizing simulated data and theoretical models, researchers evaluated their results, confirming the detection's accuracy and providing new data for the J/psi differential cross section and vector rapidity. Furthermore, researchers evaluated their results using the phenomenological models NPDT and KTF. Finally, researchers compared their results with the predictions of the PHITS and PYTHIA 8.1.13 simulations.

Recent advancements in audio synthesis via visual inputs have led to the development of real-time, visually driven sound generation systems. These systems ascribe auditory meaning to visual stimuli, but the resulting audio is often difficult to comprehend. This paper introduces AOPe, a method that enables the production of sounds with specified semantic characteristics through visual representations. By utilizing AI-generated audio datasets as a reference, AOPe optimizes its parameters to produce sounds with predefined attributes. The results demonstrate that AOPe can effectively generate sounds with specified colors, shapes, sizes, and movements, thereby enabling the production of meaningful audio outputs. AOPe's technical details are documented on this GitHub repository: https://github.com/grain-of-sound/control-sound/tree/main/AOPe. This research was motivated by the desire to create sounds inspired by the behaviors of insects, with the goal of developing an immersive, visually guided sound installation that simulates the world of insects. However, the proposed method has broader applications and can be employed in a variety of contexts that involve the association of auditory meanings with visual stimuli. AOPe is distinct from other visual audio synthesis methods in that it enables the production of sounds with specified semantic characteristics, thereby expanding the range of applications for audio synthesis via visual inputs. AOPe's generated sounds can be distinguished from those produced by existing audio synthesis systems through three key features. Firstly, AOPe is capable of producing sounds in response to stimulus attributes that are unrelated to the audio data itself. Secondly, AOPe is designed to recognize auditory meanings that are grounded in visual representations. Lastly, AOPe is an iterative sound production system, with each iteration modifying the auditory meaning of the generated sound. These unique characteristics of AOPe result from its reliance on AI-generated audio datasets as a reference for auditory meanings and the incorporation of attribute-based control. While the use of AI-generated audio datasets is beneficial from a semantic characterization perspective, it also introduces a level of audio consistency that may be desirable in certain applications. Therefore, this research presents various approaches for enabling the control of auditory meanings on existing sound synthesis systems that produce high-quality audio outputs. These methods can be applied to distinct sound synthesis techniques, such as substrate-based sound production and wave sequencing. To mitigate the impact of an epidemic, governments are considering counter-measures such as isolating the population, limiting economic activity and funding healthcare services. A fundamental question arises about the optimal timing of these interventions: when should they be implemented as soon as possible to minimize both health costs and economic burdens while maintaining an adequate healthcare system. We have discovered a universal solution for the widespread policy implications by analyzing the widely adopted SEIR model through control theory. Our research shows that to maximize the benefit for both the economy and public health, all counter-measures must be simultaneously introduced at the critical moment when the peak transmission rate occurs, as this yields the maximum possible reduction in both health costs and economic burdens. This critical moment can be forecasted in advance using our novel general approach. We have demonstrated that delaying the implementation of counter-measures leads to both prolonged healthcare needs and prolonged economic losses. Consequently, an early combination of all counter-measures is crucial for mitigating both health costs and economic burdens during an epidemic. Furthermore, an individual-based modeling approach was employed to validate the findings of the analytical framework across various epidemic scenarios, including those involving moderate and severe epidemics. The effectiveness of machine learning (ML) depends heavily on high-quality training data. However, a substantial portion of training data is often inadequate or inaccurate, which can severely hinder ML model performance. While data quality issues have been a constant challenge since the inception of machine learning, there has been a lack of effective solutions to address these problems in the past. Despite some recent advancements in data troubleshooting, several critical limitations persist. Firstly, most current approaches only focus on predicting model outcomes rather than exploring data's individual contribution. Secondly, they often rely on heuristics or pre-established labels without being able to re-evaluate and adjust these labels according to the specific ML model being used. In response to these challenges, we introduce a new data troubleshooting framework rooted in data labeling that takes into account an ML model's distinct characteristics. Our proposed Shapley significance-based framework determines significant training data for any ML model in real-time by analyzing various data attributes, evaluating label reliability, assessing annotation confidence, and accounting for data diversity. Furthermore, the framework offers flexible re-labeling capabilities to accommodate changes in data labeling as well as adaptation options in the event of labeling disagreements or model drift. Our extensive experiments conducted across 21 different datasets from diverse domains, including image, text, audio, and video, demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed Shapley significance-based framework and highlight its substantial improvement over current data troubleshooting methods. Moreover, the framework is fully implemented and made available on GitHub for the MlNet community. Additionally, the dataset used in this research is accessible through ZooTEER, a data labeling platform. Furthermore, the MlNet model used in this research is accessible through MlCloud, a model repository. This research focuses on how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Using neutron scattering, we found that in Mn$_3$Sn, this phenomenon originates from a unique type of motion called spin-chirality, rather than electron Hall conductivity as previously suggested. When we applied high pressure, the material transformed into a hexagonal structure, causing Trimerization to increase. This pressure-optimized Trimerization slowed down the spin-chirality, resulting in a corresponding decline in the anomalous Hall effect. Similarly, in another similar material Mn$_3$Ge, pressure-induced Trimerization resulted in a decrease in the anomalous Hall effect. Consequently, we conclude that Trimerization regulates the anomalous Hall effect in these types of magnetic materials. Additionally, we discovered that in Mn$_3$Sn, under high pressure, a Hall effect emerged that contradicts usual expectations, functioning as a ferromagnet at pressures exceeding 2.3 GPa, thus representing a significant discovery for this kind of material. In a related study, it was found that Mn$_3$Ge exhibits a minimum in its Hall effect around 2.3 GPa, whereas in this research, it was discovered that Mn$_3$Sn actually experiences a transition to a ferromagnetic state at pressures exceeding 2.3 GPa, contrary to initial predictions. In terms of the Hall effect measurements, a notable transition occurred in both Mn$_3$Sn and Mn$_3$Ge around 10 K, in addition to another shift at 50 K, in both cases. In contrast, when neodymium was used as an external means to apply pressure on Mn$_3$Sn, it resulted in a Hall effect decline and a corresponding increase in its anomalous Hall effect. Consequently, it was determined that both types of pressure have a similar effect on the material. This analysis builds upon previous research by incorporating an entropy measure that accounts for varying directional intensities. We demonstrate that in systems with unidirectional emission, entropy remains consistent, whereas in multi-directional emission systems, entropy decreases over time, eventually reaching a steady-state. This steady-state entropy value is found to be lower than that of the initial multi-directional emission system. This outcome is akin to the phenomenon of decrease in entropy during the transition from disordered to ordered condition in the Feigenbaum scenario. Our computational findings are corroborated through experimental measurements on microcavity lasers. These results provide a broader understanding of the analysis of directional emitters. This work also offers an informative example of how entropy can be utilized to assess systems' unpredictability while dynamically evolving over time.
